en: Oṃ, salutations to the illustrious Gaṇeśa.
Oṃ, salutations to Nārāyaṇa.
Now begins the third section, the Viṣṇudharmottara, of the glorious Viṣṇu Mahāpurāṇa.
Vajra said:

And having seen the gods even in the Kṛta age and others, O best of men.
They worship according to the prescribed rite, with special attention directed toward the image.
The image of the deity fashioned according to the rules for painting and thread-measurement;
The wise man should worship Surūpā; she will then be present there.
The man who worships her, who possesses her own form and is endowed with the auspicious marks, [attains the fruit].
He obtains all his desires; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He shall always be possessed of happiness in this world and in the next as well. || 8 ||
Now, if a man worships an image that is deficient in its characteristic marks, [he incurs misfortune].
His misfortunes increase; therefore, one should avoid her.
The merit of constructing a temple, as well as that of performing worship of the deities, [is likewise great].
The worship of the image of the Lord is meritorious; therein, an act of salutation is meritorious.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform the worship of the gods according to the prescribed characteristics.

Thus ends the first chapter, titled "The Citra-sūtra," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.

Mārkaṇḍeya said:

Now, the methodological principles (*tantrayukti*) are as follows: the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*), the connection (*yoga*), the meaning of the term (*padārtha*), the meaning of the reason (*hetvartha*), the brief statement (*uddeśa*), the detailed exposition (*nideśa*), the reference to a previous section (*pradeśa*), the extension of a rule to another context (*atideśa*), the exception (*apavarga*), the specific statement (*vākyaviśeṣa*), the implication (*arthāpatti*), the consequence (*prasaṅga*), the categorical (*ekānta*), the non-categorical (*anaikānta*), the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*), the final determination (*nirṇaya*), the synonym (*vidhānaparyāya*), the retrospective observation of what has passed (*atikrāntāvekṣaṇa*), the doubt (*saṃśaya*), the explanation (*vyākhyāna*), the assent (*anumati*), the technical terminology (*svasaṃjñā*), the etymological definition (*nirvacana*), the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), the exclusion (*viyoga*), the alternative (*vikalpa*), the conjunction (*samuccaya*), and the purpose (*artha*).

That which serves as the locus by which the meaning of the sentence is joined is *saṃyoga*; that which is a modified word from the aphorism is the *padārtha* (word-meaning); that which is the proof for another reasoned matter is the *hetvartha* (meaning of the reason). A concise statement is *uddeśa* (enumeration); a detailed statement is *nirdeśa* (definition); "it is just so" is *upadeśa* (instruction); "by this cause" is *apadeśa* (designation). Proof of what is present by means of what is yet to come is *pradeśa* (reference); when there is a location, moving beyond it is *atideśa* (extended application); the drawing forth of an intention is *abhiprāya-anukarṣaṇa*; and that by which the matter is brought to completion is *apavarga* (conclusion).

That remainder of a sentence which, through an implied word (*āhārya-pada*), reaches a limit not explicitly stated is presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). When that which was mentioned in the context is again referred to by some introductory remark, it is a relevant topic (*prasaṅga*). Wherever it is thus, it is "exclusive" (*ekānta*); where it is otherwise in some cases, it is "non-exclusive" (*anekānta*). A statement of negation is a definitive conclusion (*nirṇaya*). Arrangement according to the sequence of the context is "prescription" (*vidhāna*); its opposite is called "reversal" (*viparyaya*).

To say "I shall speak later" regarding a moment that has already passed is anticipation of the future; seeing a cause in both respects constitutes doubt. Therein, an elaborate description is an over-explanation (*ativyākhyāna*). An opponent's view that is not refuted is accepted. A word not agreed upon by others is one's own technical term (*svasaṃjñā*). An example is what is well-known in the world. Etymological derivation (*nirvacana*) is the demonstration of its reasoning; thus, it is indeed an illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*). Restriction (*niyoga*) is expressed as "this alone" or "this or that. Option (*vikalpa*) is "this and that. Conjunction (*samuccaya*) is "both this and that. Whatever is not explicitly stated but is to be understood through reasoning is to be inferred (*ūhya*).
The purpose, the resolution of doubt, the specific method of exposition, and the brevity of qualities [are the characteristics of a commentary].
The *kṛtavyudāsa*, the *kṛtaśāsana*, the *sāṃvartika*, and the *dharmaguṇoṣṭaka*.

Now follows the definition of song (*gīta*). It has three places of articulation: the chest, the throat, and the head; from these arise the low (*mandra*), middle (*madhya*), and high (*tāra*) registers. There are three scales (*grāma*): *ṣaḍja*, *madhyama*, and *gāndhāra*.
There are seven notes (*svara*): *ṣaḍja*, *ṛṣabha*, *gāndhāra*, *madhyama*, *pañcama*, *niṣāda*, and *dhaivata*.
There are twenty-one *mūrcchanās*, seven for each scale (*grāma*).
Their names are as follows: Sauvīrī, Hāriṇāśvā, Kalopanatā, Śuddhamadhyamā, Mārgī, Pauravī, and Ṛṣyakā.
These seven are the Madhyamagrāminīs, known by the name Uttarā.
Prāñcinī, Uttarāyatā, Śuddhaṣaḍjamatsarīkṛtā, Aśvakrāntā, and Udgatā—these seven belong to the Ṣaḍjagrāma.

Ālāpī, Kuntīmā, Śraddhā, Uttarā, Ṣaḍjā, Pañcāyatā—these seven belong to the Gāndhāra scale (*gāndhāragrāmika*). Now, as for the forty-nine *tānas*: Agniṣṭomika, Atyagniṣṭomika, Pauṇḍarika, Āśvamedhika, Rājasūyika, Vahusuvarṇika, Gosavika, Mahāvratika, Brahma-tāna, Prājāpatya, Nagāśraya, Yajñāśraya, Godānika, Hayakrānta, Ajakrānta, Viṣṇukrānta, Araṇya, Mattakokila, and Ujjīvika—these twenty belong to the Madhyama scale (*madhyamagrāmika*).

*Prasvāpana*, *paiśāca*, *jīvana*, *sāvitra*, *ardhasāvitra*, *sarvatobhadra*, *suvarṇa*, *viṣṇu*, *jiṣṇu*, *viṣṇuvāra*, *śārada*, *vijaya*, *haṃsa*, and *jyeṣṭha*—these fourteen belong to the Ṣaḍja grāma.

*Tumburupriya*, *mahālakṣmaṇa*, *gandharvānumata*, *alambusapriya*, *nāradapriya*, *bhīmasenapriya*, *vitāna*, *mātaṅga*, *bhārgavapriya*, *abhirāma*, *saṃśrāvya*, *kinnarapriya*, *puṇya*, *manohara*, and *kalyāṇakara*—these fifteen are based on the Gāndhāra [grāma].

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now follows the classification of stringed instruments.

There are four kinds of musical instruments: stringed (*tata*), wind (*suṣira*), solid (*ghana*), and percussion (*avanaddha*). The stringed includes the lute (*vīṇā*) and so forth; the wind includes the flute (*vaṃśa*) and so forth; the solid includes cymbals (*tāla*) and so forth; and the percussion includes the drum (*muraja*) and so forth. Among these, the notes (*svaras*) are similar in both the human body and the lute. However, while there is an ascending and descending scale (*āroha-avarohaṇa*) in the case of bodies, it is the reverse for the lutes and flutes. As for the cymbals (*tāla*), they are employed according to the time-measure (*kāla*).
The three modes (*vṛtti*) consist of three measures (*mātrā*), each being the duration required to pronounce five short syllables.
The *citrā* mode is twofold:
in the *mātrākalā-citrā*, which is a four-measure mode, there are eight measures; in the *dakṣiṇā* mode, there are two measures.
From the eighth measure on the right, there are *avayā*, *niṣkraya*, *vikṣepa*, *praveśa*, *śampātāla*, and *saṃnipātabheda*. A collection of *kalās* is joined [with these].

There is *capuṭastha*, *ayuk*, *cañcatpuṭala*, and *plutānta*; *pañcapāṇi* and *kha* are the *tāputrā*s situated according to the syllables (*yathākṣarastha*). In that regard, the tempos (*laya*) are fast (*druta*), medium (*madhya*), and slow (*vilambita*). The *tāla* possesses these tempos.

The *prakaraṇa* is of two kinds: the *kulaka* and the *chedyaka*. Now, regarding the *avanaddha*, it is characterized by resonance like that of a drum (*pauṣkara*) and is imbued with pathos (*karuṇa*).

In this context, there are sixteen syllables: *ka, kha, ga, gha, ṭa, ṭha, ḍa, ṇa, ta, tha, da, dha, ya, ra, la, va*. Among these, *ka, ṭa, ra, tha, u, ga*, and so forth, belong to the right side; *gha, dha, mā* belong to the left; *ga, da, kāra* belong to the head; *ṭa, ṇa, la, ha* belong to the embrace (*āliṅga*). The vowels *a, ā, i, ī, u, ū, e, o, ai, au* are applied as appropriate. Furthermore, *kha, ga, dha*, and *nāṃ* are joined with the letter *repha* (the letter *r*).

The *Nalasthava* of the Kaha-bhadas: from the simultaneous falling of the hands, with the movement of the fingers and the upward raising of one [hand], there is the *yoga* of the *ḍallas*, characterized by the simultaneous falling of the hands and the forefinger (*pradeśinī*). There are the *samapāṇi*, *ardhapāṇi*, *adīrghapāṇi*, and *ekapāṇi*. In the *samapāṇi-prahata*, there are the *upakāra*, *ghathagaḍara*, and *adhyardhapāṇi* [varieties]. In the *adhyardhapāṇi*, there are the *ṭhaṇala*, *hāsna*, *hā*, and the two-hand [movement] with the striking of the palm and forefinger. In the *ahitavitasta*, there are the *ālipta*, *gomukhī*, and *mārga* [styles]; the *andhita* occurs in the *śṛṅgāra* and *hāsya* [rasas].
In the heroic, the furious, and the marvelous sentiments, the *vitasta* [drum] is used; in the pathetic and the peaceful, the *ālipta*.

In the loathsome and the terrifying, there follows the playing of the *gomukha*, the *dardura*, the *paṇava*, and the *mṛdaṅga*. Furthermore, in these instances, there occurs the looking upon the stage from the door of the dressing room (*nepathyabhavana*).

When the index finger is curved over the outstretched thumb of the *vāsas* [hand], that is the syllable *oṃ*.

By means of the index finger of the opposite hand placed at the base of the thumb, the *ka*-group (*kavarga*) is formed sequentially.

By means of the [index finger] placed on the line furthest below, the *ta*-group (*tavarga*) is formed. Above that, by means of the [index finger] placed on the third line from the bottom, the *pa*-group (*pavarga*) is formed.
The *p*-group [is formed] by the first joint of the index finger (*tarjanī*) and so forth;
the *ś*-group [is formed] at the tips [of the fingers];
and with the touch of the nail of the middle finger (*madhyamā*), [one says] "ra kṣa."
A is Vāsudeva;
Ā is Saṅkarṣaṇa; Aṃ is Pradyumna;
Aḥ is Aniruddha.

The *añjalipuruṣa* (clasped-hand) mudrā consists of the two hands with their backs joined to one another; when the little finger is joined to the little finger, the forefinger to the forefinger, and the thumb to the thumb, it is the *tārkṣya* mudrā. The *patāka* (banner) mudrā has the palm slightly curved at the tips; the *makara* (crocodile) mudrā has the thumb extended obliquely;
and the *ardhacandra* (half-moon) mudrā has the fingers curved inward.
The two visible peaks are joined at the tips of the little fingers;
with the thumbs pressed together, it is the *śaṅkha* (conch) mudrā;
the two hands joined with fingers clearly extended are the *padma* (lotus) mudrā.
The hunchbacked thumb is Lakṣmī;
the crocodile is the extended fingers;

The syllable *Aḥ* itself, with the middle finger extended, is *Ga*.
With that same [hand], the middle finger held at its tip is *Garuḍavāhana*.

And Vanamālā was also renowned, O scion of the Yadu clan.
By him the earth is supported, together with its mountains, forests, and groves.
By him the earth must be fashioned upon his central hood.
O chief of the Yādava lineage, may you, who are anointed with the hood [of Śeṣa], attain your desired stability through her.
For this form of the supreme lord Viṣṇu, who is inconceivable, has been described to you by me.
Thus ends the sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Infinite Form," in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The lord, the god Tumburu, should be depicted situated in the midst of the Mothers.
Seated upon a bull, he should be fashioned with four faces like Śarva. || 1 ||
But he should be made to sit down, O best of kings.
Mahādeva said to him: "I have described your entire form to you."
A skull should be fashioned for him, held in a hand that grasps a citron.
And a citron (mātuluṅga) should be made; that was proclaimed by Tryambaka. || 3 ||
To its right, two Mothers should likewise be placed.
And to his left, the pair of Mothers should likewise be fashioned.
Both Jayā and Vijayā should indeed be placed on the right side.
Jayantī should be placed on the left, and likewise Aparājitā.
And all [the deities] should be made with two arms and likewise with four faces.
One should, however, cause skull-bowls to be fashioned in the left hands of all of them.
O Great King, the staff should be held in the right hand, while Jaya is in the left.
In the hand of Vijayā, a sword should be depicted, having the luster of crushed collyrium.
O King, one should have Jayantī fashioned holding a rosary in her hand.
The Bhindipāla should be made in her hand, and likewise the Aparājitā goddess.
One should cause the feet of all [the goddesses] to rest upon a footstool.
O King, the right leg, which is extended, should be made slightly bent at the left.
Jayā should be performed like a man, while Vijayā is comparable to a female owl.
Jayantī was mounted upon a horse, and Aparājitā rode upon a cloud.
Mahādeva Tumburu, however, should be made white as the rays of the moon.
Then, for the sake of pleasing the Goddess, the Blessed Lord, the Protector of the World and Master, stood in their midst.
Thus remains that slayer of the enemies of the gods, distributing desires among his devotees; he is worthy of worship.

Thus ends the sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Creation of the Form of Tumburu Together with the Four Goddesses," in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vajra said:
The formation of the forms of the Moon and the Lord of Water was previously described by you.
Tell me another form of those very two, who possess the nature of the moonless [and the full] moon. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Ravi should be depicted with auspicious whiskers and the luster of vermilion ornaments.
He was brilliantly attired, possessed of a beautiful form, and adorned with all ornaments.
He had four arms, possessed great splendor, and was completely covered by armor.
And his girdle should be made of that which is known as *yāvyāṅgī*. || 3 ||
His rays should be fashioned in his left and right hands.
They are auspicious, adorned with all kinds of flowers, and arranged in the form of upward-pointing garlands.
He should be depicted with a beautiful form, handsome appearance, and holding a staff to his left.
On the southern side, in the tawny region, one who is exceedingly tawny should be made. ||5||
O Yādava, both of them should be depicted with their garments ablaze.
The two hands should be placed upon the heads of those two [fires] of the fire-god.
One who holds a pen and a leaf of a manuscript in his hands becomes tawny in complexion.
The god bearing a shield and a spear is likewise fashioned with great care.
A lion and a banner should likewise be made to the left of the Sun.
And four sons should be appointed by him for his two wives. ||8||
Revanta, Yama, and likewise the two Manus.
The Sun, the king of planets, should be depicted, either surrounded by the other planets or alone.
And Queen Rikṣubhā, as well as Queen Chāyā and Suvarcasā.
And four wives should be placed by his two sides.
Then, upon that supreme chariot, which has one wheel, seven horses, and is marked with six lines;
The god whose charioteer is Varuṇa should be depicted as seated. ||11||
The Gāyatrī, Uṣṇih, Anuṣṭubh, Bṛhatī, and Paṅkti;
The Triṣṭubh and the Jagatī—these seven meters are the horses on the chariot of the Sun. || 12 ||
With rays situated in his hands, he sustains the entire world.
And a lion upon his banner is proclaimed to be Dharma himself in visible form. || 13 ||
In the same way, the Lord sustains the entire world situated upon his girdle.
The queen Bhūrikṣubhā and Dyau are proclaimed as Chāyā; she is known as Chāyā. ||14||
Prabhā and Suvarcasā are said to be the wives of that god.
That Blessed One is red in color because his abode is the source of splendor.
And likewise, his limbs are concealed because he bears unbearable splendor.
Thus, the abode consisting of all things is proclaimed to be the Sun alone.
Thus have I described the form of this Lord of the Day, who pervades the entire universe.
Of the treasury of splendor, supremely radiant, the eternal sovereign of all. || 17 ||
Thus ends the sixty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Form of Āditya," in the Māgha-vrata section of the third book of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The Lord Candra should be depicted with a white body and likewise clad in white garments.
He had four arms, possessed great splendor, and was likewise adorned with all ornaments.
And two white water-lilies (kumuda) should be placed in the hands of that deity.
Beauty (Kānti) should be depicted in embodied form at his right side.
On the left, Śobhā should likewise be fashioned, peerless in form upon the earth.
Likewise, his mark should appear as a single lion on his left side.
Or a chariot with ten horses should be made, having two wheels, a canopy, and a charioteer.
A garland, a triple-minded one, a bull, a speaker, a man, and a horse. || 4 ||
Furthermore, there are Vāk, Saptadhātu, Haṃsa, Vyoma, and Mṛga.
All these ten horses of the moon are on your left side. ||5||
Then, indeed, twenty-eight wives, endowed with exceeding beauty and named after the lunar mansions (nakṣatra), were to be made for him.
One hundred and two states, or rather the various distinctions of the body, are to be produced.
Formerly, in the war between the gods and the asuras, by means of his sovereign power, [the king] with the stars... || 7 ||
O delighter of the Yadus, many of your own bodies have been created.
Then those Dānavas were slain by the forms of their own lords, the gods.
Whatever form belongs to whichever deity was created by a particular constellation.
And that very deity is proclaimed as belonging to that lunar mansion. || 9 ||
Then, O Yādava, the battle between the gods and the asuras proceeded with unrestrained intensity.
An equal number of gods were then created by him, assuming the forms of women.
O knower of dharma, the moon is indeed remembered as the father of the entire world.
And when he has created all this world, it attains supreme joy.
That supreme form of the high-souled Viṣṇu is to be known as gentle in appearance.
Joy and clarity are to be understood as the two white lotuses in the hands of Candra. || 12 ||
O descendant of Bhṛgu, splendor and beauty are declared to be its essential nature.
For the moon is white in color because it consists of the essence of the waters. || 13 ||
For they say that the immortal essence of the waters is the primordial food; that is declared to be equal to the moon.
O King, they declare that the lion-banner represents Dharma, while the horses are assigned to the quarters of the moon.
Thus ends the sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Form of the Moon," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
O mighty-armed one, explain the manifestation of the forms of the planets.
By this very argument, you are considered by me to be omniscient.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The terrestrial fire-altar (bhauma-agni) should be constructed on a golden chariot drawn by eight horses.
Viṣṇu’s couch should be made by a wise man, as should that of Bhauma on his chariot.
Bṛhaspati should be fashioned out of refined gold and depicted with two arms.
One should cause a book and a rosary to be placed in his two hands.
And likewise, the Guru is adorned with all ornaments and wears yellow garments.
Upon a divine golden chariot yoked with eight horses, which was enchanting to the sight.
Śukra should be depicted with a white body and likewise wearing white garments.
His two hands are said to be joined with a treasure and a book.
O descendant of Bhrigu, a chariot drawn by ten horses should be made of silver.
Likewise, Saturn should be depicted as dark-complexioned, dressed in black garments, and with veins prominently visible.
He is adorned with two hands, joined by a staff and a rosary of beads.
It should likewise be placed upon a chariot made of black iron and supported by eight serpents.
Likewise, Rāhu should be skillfully fashioned as having eight horses on a silver chariot.
Only the head should be made, joined with a single arm.
However, one hand must be made empty; that is, the right one.
And likewise, one who understands the form of Ketu should perform the rite for Bhauma.
And, O King, only ten horses must be provided for this sacrifice.

Thus ends the sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Formation of the Forms of the Planets, Mars and Others," in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vajra said:
O Lord of such splendor, please describe to me the form of these two Manus.
And you have spoken, O knower of dharma, concerning Yama, the lord of the gods.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The present Manu should be made, endowed with the characteristics of a king.
He should be made to appear thus, devoid of all ornaments. || 2 ||
He wore matted hair, held a rosary of beads, and likewise carried a water-pot.
Though emaciated, he was endowed with splendor and likewise devoted to asceticism.
And other future Manus who are to come shall also be established through yoga.
O Yādava, he should be fashioned in a form equal to that of Sāvarṇi Manu.
The past Manus were to be honored, for they were endowed with the marks of royalty.
On the back of the horse, Revanta, the lord, should be fashioned like the sun.
Thus ends the seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Form of Manu," in the third section of the first part of the glorious Viśvaprakāśa.
Vajra said:
The deities of the planets have already been declared by you previously.
O Lord of such splendor, please describe the nature and the manifestation of those [energies].
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I have already previously described the forms of the lords of fire and water.
And so it was told to you in the past by Viṣṇu and the Lord of the Gods.
O Yādava, I shall describe to you the form of Kumāra, who possesses four manifestations.
And likewise Kumāra, Skanda, Viśākha, and the Preceptor (Guru). || 3 ||
The youth should be depicted with six faces, adorned with a tuft of hair.
He should be depicted wearing red garments and having the excellent peacock as his vehicle. || 4 ||
And likewise, a cock and a bell are in his two right hands.
And a banner, a Vaijayantī flag, a spear, and a sword should be fashioned in the two left [hands]. || 5 ||
Skanda, Viśākha, and Guha should be fashioned like Kumāra.
They should not have six faces, nor should they be mounted upon peacocks.
For the eternal Blessed One Vāsudeva is indeed fourfold in nature.
The youth appeared, indeed, with the desire to lead the army of the gods.
The enchanting Bhadrakālī should be depicted with eighteen arms.
Standing in the ālīḍha posture, she is seated upon a chariot drawn by four lions. || 8 ||
O Yādava, [he holds] a rosary, a trident, a sword, and a shield.
The arrow and the bow are to be fashioned, and likewise the conch and the lotus.
Likewise, the two small ladles (sruk and sruva) should be prepared, as well as the altar and the ritual basin (kamaṇḍalu).
And when the power of punishment must be exercised, [it is like] the black antelope skin and the sacrificial fire.
The hand of Bhadrakālī among the hands shall be the bringer of peace.
And one person of great fortune should be the bearer of the jewel-vessel. || 11 ||
He should be depicted as having a swan-vehicle, and he must not be made four-faced.
The other form spoken by Brahmā is all the activity of Prajāpati.
Vināyaka, however, should be fashioned with the face of an elephant and four arms.
And a trident and a rosary are in his two right hands.
A bowl filled with sweetmeats and an axe are on the left.
And its left tusk must not be fashioned, O destroyer of enemies. (14)
One foot should be placed upon a footstool while the other remains on the seat.
One should cause a bowl full of sweetmeats to be placed at the tip of his hand.
Likewise, O Yādava, he should be made with a protruding belly and stiff ears.
Wearing a tiger skin as his garment and having a serpent as his sacred thread; || 16 ||
Now Viśvakarman must be made the lord who assumes the form of the sun.
He, possessing ten hands yet two arms, becomes the embodiment of splendor.
Because he indeed creates the universe, he is therefore remembered as Viśvakarman.
The Lord Viṣṇu, the creator of the universe, is called Viśvakarmā.

Thus ends the seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Forms of Kumāra, Bhadrakālī, Caturvaktra, Gajavaktra, and Viśvakarman," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
O God, my form belongs to the Vasus, and likewise that of the auspicious Aṅgirasas.
And [he is] the deity of all the gods and also of the Rudras. ||1||
And likewise for the Bhṛgus, the Sādhyas, and the Ādityas.
And likewise, O one honored by the gods, describe the form of the Maruts.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In the form of Prajāpati, he shall become the Vasu named Dhara.
And in his Vaiṣṇava form, he is celebrated by the name Dhruva.
Soma [is established] by means of the lunar form, and likewise Anila by means of the aerial form.
The fire-altar (anala) is to be constructed with the Āgneya [sāman], and Prabhāsa with the Vāruṇa.
Likewise, the Viśvedevas, the gods who bear the form of Śakra, should be fashioned.
The king of serpents was avoided by the side-glance and the eye of the forehead.
Likewise, the gods and the descendants of Aṅgiras should be fashioned in the form of living beings.
The Rudras [were subdued] by the Māheśvara [weapon], and the Sādhyas and Aśvins by the Vaiṣṇava.
And the Ādityas in the form of the Sun—thus, O Yādava, there are twelve.
But when they are considered individually, they are remembered as being like the rising sun. ||7||
Viṣṇu, Indra, and Varuṇa are to be fashioned just as previously described by me.
The deities named Maruts are to be fashioned in the form of semen.
Thus ends the seventy-second chapter, titled "The Creation of the Form of Vasu," in the third section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vajra said:
And likewise, the creation of the forms of other gods as well.
Speak, O highly fortunate one, for you are indeed said to be all-knowing.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The lord Kaśyapa should be fashioned in the form of Prajāpati.
Aditi, Diti, Danu, Kāṣṭhā, Danāyus, Siṃhikā, and Muni. ||2||
Kadru, Krodhavasa, Danayu, Pradha, Vinata, Surabhi, and Khasa.
All the primordial Mothers should be depicted as beautiful, possessing two arms.
Aditi and Diti, as well as Vinatā and Surabhi.
But their gaze, O delighter of the Yadavas, must be made gentle.
Indeed, all the divine mothers are truly of this very form.
O best of the Yadavas, it must be performed through the act of fashioning a form.
Kaśyapa’s other wives must be made to have eyes filled with agitation.
Dhruva, the lord of the host of planets, should be fashioned bearing the form of Viṣṇu.
The glorious one, with two arms and a gentle appearance, emits rays of light from his wheel.
The great sage Agastya should be made to appear in accordance with what is to come.
Thus has the form of the great-souled Bhṛgu and others been described.
And Jayanta, the son of Śukra, should be fashioned endowed with beauty.
The glorious one has two arms, holds a bow and an arrow in his hands, and possesses a serene appearance.
The son of Yama is Bala, the lord who holds a shield and a trident in his hands.
And the Puṣkara should likewise be made, possessing a luster equal to that of a lotus petal.
One should have both a sword and a book fashioned for his two hands.
The daughter of the Moon, as well as Jyotsnā, were peerless in beauty upon the earth.
On the left side, however, she should be fashioned, adorned with all ornaments.
The omnipresent Lord should be fashioned with a beautiful form, holding a jewel-bowl in his hand.
Nalakūbara has a face endowed with two tusks and possesses wealth and other such riches. ||12||
The wise know Maṇibhadra to be the very form of the Giver of Wealth (Dhanada).
A palanquin should not be prepared for him, as he, along with his wife, is borne by men.
The son of Vāyu, however, should be made in the form of Vāyu, swift as the wind.
The powerful lord Varca, the son of Soma, was to be made exceedingly handsome in form.
By which one becomes radiant, with a hand like a playful lotus.
Nandi should have three eyes, four arms, and mighty limbs. || 15 ||
Resembling the crimson hue of vermilion, he was clothed in a garment of tiger skin.
And one should have a trident and a bhindipāla made for his two hands. || 16 ||
The third is located on the head, and likewise another is threatening.
One should observe people coming from afar. || 17 ||
And in this very form, the wise know him as Vīrabhadra.
I shall describe the nature of Dharma to you hereafter.
The purpose, however, was to be accomplished through the form of the high-souled Dhanada.
Kāmadeva, moreover, should be fashioned as peerless in beauty upon the earth. || 19 ||
He should be depicted with eight arms, adorned with a conch and a lotus.
With bow and arrow in hand, his eyes were rolling with intoxication.
Rati, Prīti, Śakti, Madaśakti, and likewise Ujjvalā.
Four wives, enchanting in their beauty, should be appointed for him.
And four marks on his hands should be made, reaching toward his wife's breasts.
And Ketu should be made as a great makara with five-arrowed faces.
Then, one should induce sleep with the left hand placed upon the hip.
Likewise, on her right side, there should be Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Likewise, Vāsudeva is on the left, and Maikāneśa is likewise his son.
O sinless one, I shall describe the form of Lakṣmī to you hereafter.
And the goddess Sarasvatī should likewise be depicted as four-armed.
An akṣamālā, a trident, a book, and a water-pot. || 25 ||
O delighter of the Yadus, her duties should be performed by her hands according to the rules.
The goddess Vāruṇī, exceedingly beautiful, should be fashioned with all her limbs complete. || 26 ||
Lambodarī, however, should be depicted with red garments and breasts.
The highly fortunate one has a trident in her hand, and likewise uses her arms as weapons.
And she should be made large-bodied (Bṛhadrathā), likewise possessing many arms.
She herself is declared to be Cāmuṇḍā, the subduer of all beings. || 28 ||
In the same way, the intestine-mouthed [vessel] should be made especially dry and withered.
The goddess possesses many arms and is encircled by serpents. || 29 ||
She is garlanded with skulls, fearsome, and likewise a bearer of the khaṭvāṅga staff.
The auspicious messenger Śivā, however, should be made with the face of a jackal.
O King, she likewise stood in the ālīḍha posture, possessing four arms.
The goddess likewise holds a cup of blood, as well as a sword and a trident.
But her fourth hand should likewise be made to hold something with meat.
By a mark equal to that of a deity, according to its form, [they are known as] mothers. || 32 ||
The seals marked with the names of the deities, which were previously described by me to you, must be made.
They should be depicted with hands holding vessels of blood, and likewise with hands containing meat.
The illustrious ones were dancing, though their forms were not described.
The eastern direction shall belong to a young woman with the gait of an elephant, who is red in color. || 34 ||
Kareṇugā, Bṛhatkanyā, and Padmābhā are in the southeast.
Standing upon a chariot, she should be fair-complexioned, and likewise in the full bloom of youth. || 35 ||
The Varuṇa river flows south-westward, riding upon camels and being blackish-yellow in color.
Kṛṣṇā, having fallen from her youth, is situated in the west, mounted upon a horse.
O delighter of the Yadus, the mare was dark blue with white hairs appearing near her head.
The Śveta, Narabhṛtā, Vṛddhā, and likewise the Uttara [are situated] there. || 37 ||
The ativṛddhā [yoga] occurs when the moon is situated in Vṛṣa (Taurus) and is in the eastern or northern part of the sky.
Below it is equal to the earth, and above it is situated in the sky.
Time has a terrifying countenance, it is ever-moving, and it is fearsome.
And he should be made with a noose in his hand, possessing the hair of a snake or a scorpion.
Jvara should be depicted with three legs, three eyes, and three faces.
Fierce, with three arms and agitated eyes, he had ashes as his weapon.
And Dhanvantari should be fashioned, beautiful in form and pleasing to behold.
And in his two hands there should be a jar containing nectar. || 41 ||
The Sāmaveda must indeed be composed, but the Lord has a dog’s face.
Alternatively, the wise should compose the Vedas in the form of deities.
The Rigveda is remembered as Brahmā, while the Yajurveda is Vāsava.
Likewise, Viṣṇu is the Sāmaveda, and Śambhu is the Atharvaveda. || 43 ||
The training (śikṣā) is to be known as Prajāpati, and the ritual manual (kalpa) is proclaimed to be Brahmā.
Sarasvatī is grammar, and the Lord Varuṇa is etymology (nirukta). || 44 ||
Chandas is the earth, and likewise Agni is the Lord Sun, the light.
The Lord Soma is Mīmāṃsā, and the Wind-god is the Path of Logic (Nyāya). || 45 ||
Dharma, the treatises on Dharma, the Purāṇas, and likewise Manu.
The Lord of Creatures [received] history, and Śatakratu [received] the science of archery.
Likewise, the Lord Dhanvantari himself is Āyurveda.
The goddess Mahī [taught] the science of fruits, and Maheśvara [taught] the science of dance. || 47 ||
Saṅkarṣaṇa [revealed] the Pāñcarātra, and likewise Rudra [revealed] the Pāśupata.
And Ananta is the author of the Pātañjala [Yoga], while the sage Kapila is the author of the Sāṃkhya. || 48 ||
All treatises on statecraft (arthaśāstra) are proclaimed as pertaining to the Superintendent of Wealth.
All the arts and sciences belong to Kāmadeva, the teacher of the world. || 49 ||
Whatever other treatises there are that they declare to have various authors;
And he indeed was the embodied deity of that scripture and poem.
But the form of the division of time is its effect, equal to the form of one's own deity, O destroyer of enemies.
O moon of the Yadu lineage, I have thus described to you the form of those most excellent of gods.
Thus ends the seventy-third chapter, titled "The Creation of the Forms of the Deities," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
O sinless one, tell me about the creation of the form of the Liṅga.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
For when worship is performed upon the liṅga, it is as if worship were performed for the entire world.
Its enjoyment should be performed as an eight-sided portion.
Likewise, it should be made square in its divisions and provided with abundant sacrificial fees.
The visible [mandala] should be made circular, while the pedestal should be octagonal.
It should be made square and likewise situated upon the pedestal of Brahmā.
The wise know that below the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) is the seat of Brahmā (brahmapīṭha).
Above the liṅga, however, a line has gone forward; it should likewise be made perfectly circular.
Likewise, its upward-extending quality of intelligence is declared by the wise to be the Brahma-sūtra. ||5||
Thus ends the seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Manufacture of the Form of the Liṅga," in the third section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vajra said:
O best among the upholders of all dharmas, please explain the nature of space.
But when the sky is worshipped, the worship of the entire world becomes accomplished. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O mighty-armed one, it should be square at its base and then circular.
From that, there should be a slightly smaller square, and from that, another square.
Then, it is slightly less than a square and situated like Mount Meru.
This is declared to be the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha), the third division of the sky.
This is said to be the characteristic of all auspicious seats (bhadrapīṭhas).
The central portion is proclaimed to be square in shape. || 4 ||
Then, one should place the auspicious seat (bhadrapīṭha) in that portion and install the lotus there.
In its center, upon the pericarp, is a beautiful eight-petaled lotus with the sun at its core.
There, one should arrange the guardians of the directions upon the leaves according to their respective quarters.
One should visualize the earth beneath the auspicious seat.
Likewise, they know the intermediate space to be the pillar and its upper portion.
There, all the foremost of the thirty gods are present together.
O mighty-armed one, it has been told to you that the sky consists of all the gods.
By performing its worship, one shall obtain all desires.
I have thus described the true nature of space; by performing worship to space, everything [is accomplished].
O sole hero of the world, O foremost of the Yadava lineage, the entire universe, both moving and unmoving, would be honored [by that].
Thus ends the seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Creation of the Form of Space," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
In what forms were Nara and Nārāyaṇa joined together for their task?
And how, O descendant of Bhṛgu, should Hari and Kṛṣṇa be fashioned? (1)
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The man should be made dark-green like dūrvā grass, with two arms and mighty limbs.
Nārāyaṇa has four arms and the complexion of the petals of a blue lotus. || 2 ||
And between those two, a jujube tree (badarī) adorned with fruit should be fashioned.
In Badarī, both of them were engaged in their respective tasks, wearing rosaries of seeds.
They are situated upon a beautiful vehicle endowed with prosperity and possessing eight wheels.
Wearing black antelope skins, self-controlled, and bearing circles of matted hair.

Vajra said:
"Blessed One, by what ritual procedure is the consecration performed?"
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, for the consecration of the deities, there are sixteen officiating priests (ṛtvij).

These were as follows: the astrologer, the architect, the barber, and the reciter; the long-armed Arghabāhu, knower of the Yajurveda; Devahotṛ, knower of the Yajurveda; and Devadravyarakṣitā, knower of the Yajurveda—these four supports of the water-jars were Sāttvatas who were knowers of the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda respectively. Of them, one was the bearer of the image (mūrtidhara), and the second was the knower of the rites for the deity.
The third is the protector of the mantra, and the fourth is the protector of the substances.
In that regard, assistants for those who hold the jars must be appointed along with the Śaktis.

All the officiating priests (ṛtvijas) must be free from physical defects—not tawny-haired, not squint-eyed, and not having extra limbs—and they must be thoroughly proficient in their own scriptures, gentle, and not born of remarriage.

Then, on an auspicious day, the sacrificer, having bathed well, with his limbs anointed with unguents, wearing garlands, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya), dressed in unwashed garments, and holding purifiers (pavitra) in his hands, should take up the initiation (dīkṣā) together with those assistants.

When he has bathed, is clothed in new garments, and stands on a spot smeared with cow-dung, the Brahmins—preceded by the recitation of the *svasti-vācana*—and the ritual specialist (*kalpaka*), having bound white mustard seeds and *vacā* roots with a white thread and a white cloth, shall tie a protective amulet (*pratisara*) or bracelet upon his right hand.
From that time until the moment of the consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*), and for seven nights thereafter, he must avoid meat, liquor, alkaline salts, unchastity, anger, envy, pride, and ignoble conduct.
And there is a verse on this point:
Thus, starting from the day of initiation, the consecration takes place on the seventh day.
For as long as that time lasts, may you remain ever constant, performing sacrifices and well-restrained.
A celibate student who eats sacrificial food, has conquered anger, and is free from envy.
And he slept on the ground, O king of kings, and likewise bathed daily.
Thus ends the ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Chapter on Initiation," in the *Pratiṣṭhākalpa* within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.

at their placement, one should utter "tejo'si śukram.
Then again, one should perform the scattering of white mustard seeds with mantras that destroy demons.
One should mutter: "O gods who sit in the east."
One should recite the account of the Varāha incarnation and chant the Śrīsūkta;
then, one should sprinkle the ground with that fivefold cow-product (pañcagavya).
One should install archways for the purpose of worship and purification; in the case of a grand ablution (*bṛhatsnāna*), it should be done in this manner, and one should not employ anything else.
Now, regarding the *arghya* offering:
O best of kings, when the arrangement of the archways has been thus completed...
All obstacles come to an end and supreme prosperity arises. ||1||
Thus ends the ninety-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Arches," in the section on the Installation Rite within the third part of the second book of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, regarding the five products of the cow (pañcagavya):
therein, the milk is from a tawny cow,
and the curd is from a black cow.
And the ghee of a blue cow;
the dung of a white cow;
the urine of a copper-colored cow.
One should take cow’s urine with the Gāyatrī mantra;
cow dung with "gandhadvārām";
and milk with "āpyāyasva."
With "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," [he offers] curd;
with "ghṛtavatī bhuvanānām," ghee;
and with "devasya tvā," water with *kuśa* grass.
Having joined the Gāyatrī with the Aghamarṣaṇa [verse], one should recite it;
then, one should sprinkle the dwelling with that fivefold cow-product (pañcagavya).
And one should set up archways for the purpose of purification after worship.
In the case of a major ablution (bṛhatsnāna), that same [rite] should be performed, or one may arrange another.
Now follows the preparation of the *arghya* offering.

In that regard, one should place a silver vessel there and arrange within it conch-shell, *bilva*, lotus, *uśīra*, the roots of *darbha* grass, *dūrvā* grass, milk, unbroken rice (*akṣata*), white mustard seeds, and grains of rice;
one should then immerse them in water from a sacred bathing-place (*tīrtha*).
One should recite the mantra beginning with "rathākṣe.

Then, [one should recite] the Draviṇam, Pāvamānya, Drupada, Pavitra, Śaṅkha-mantra, Śrīsūkta, and the Pavitra mantra from the Kāṇḍātkāṇḍa hymn. Thereafter, O auspicious one, one should prepare the water for washing the feet (pādya) in a firm, well-adorned vessel.
And with the three verses beginning with "hiraṇyavarṇā," O King.
With the three verses beginning with "āpo hi ṣṭhā" and also with "śanno devī," [he should sprinkle water]. || 1 ||
And likewise with the sacred thread of Brahmā’s seed, which is pure.
There, the reciter should cause the supreme majesty of the sacred site (tīrtha) to be proclaimed.
Thus ends the ninety-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Five Products of the Cow," in the *Pratiṣṭhākalpa* of the *Māghavratavidhi* within the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*. 99.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now follows the purification of the image (*arcā*).

In that regard, one should purify those made of clay and those fashioned through painting. For both, one should perform purification with *darbha* strainers and the preliminary consecration (*adhivāsana*). Furthermore, at the very outset, one should perform the purification prescribed for whatever material the image is made of. Thereafter, one should perform it with water while reciting the *gāyatrī*.
"Step upon [me]," with these words he takes a second portion of earth; and here there is another mantra:
"O Vasundharā, stepped upon by the horse, stepped upon by the chariot, stepped upon by Viṣṇu!"
O Earth, take away my sin, whatever evil deed has been committed by me. || 1 ||
You were lifted up by the boar, by Kṛṣṇa with his hundred arms.
O Earth, grant me my desire; be the bestower of all wishes.
The third [application] is with ashes, [reciting] "Thou art prosperity";
the fourth is with cow dung, [reciting] "May cattle be here";
and the fifth is with white mustard seeds, [reciting] "Thou art the back of Viṣṇu."
The sixth [mark] is made with the ash of the three sacred fires while reciting the Bṛhat Sāman.
With the Śākvara [sāman] is the seventh; with the five products of the cow [is the eighth].

The eighth [offering] with *kuṣṭha* is performed with the verse "The desire of the mind is intention" (*manasaḥ kāmam ākūtiḥ*). The ninth is performed with golden-colored water using the verse "Golden-hued" (*hiraṇyavarṇā*).
The tenth [offering] is made with *darbha* stalks while reciting "taratsamandī."
The eleventh [layer] is with earth from a sacred ford (*tīrtha*) accompanied by the *pāvamānī* verses;
the twelfth is with earth from a river.
The thirteenth [world] was lifted up by those mountains with earth from the mountain peaks;
the fourteenth was lifted up by Ṛṣabha with earth from his newly grown horns.
The fifteenth [mudrā] is called Aśvakrāntā, made from earth dug up by a plow.
With the earth from the top of an anthill, one performs the sixteenth [rite] known as the Kūṣmāṇḍī.
With the mantra "pṛthvīdevī," [he should apply] the clay from a sacred ford for the seventeenth [mark].
With the clay from a lake and the mantra "brahmajajñāna," he performs the eighteenth [rite].
With the verse "dadhikrāvṇo akāriṣam," he offers the nineteenth oblation with curd;
with "ghṛtavatī bhuvanānām abhiśriyā," he offers the twentieth oblation with ghee.
With the Aghamarṣaṇa hymn, [he should worship] with jewels twenty-one times.
Having thus purified that [sin] with Soma consisting of twenty-one parts, the supremely purifying mantras should be recited: the Aghamarṣaṇa, the Daivakṛta, the Śuddhavatīs, and the Taratsamās.
The Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras, the Pāvamānī verses, the goddess Durgā, and Sarasvatī. || 1 ||
The Cāndrāyaṇa, the Ṛṣabha, the Vāmadevya, and the Rathantara.
And likewise, the Pauruṣa Sūkta, the Śrī Sūkta, or the Āpsara Sūkta. || 2 ||
And [he taught] the supernatural powers, the purifying [rites], and likewise the Vaiṣṇava conduct.
Surrounded by the sounds of musical instruments mingled with shouts of victory from the excellent women of the king,
once the purification is completed, the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) must indeed be performed for the worship of the deities, as I shall now describe.

Thus ends the one hundredth chapter, titled "The Description of Purity for the Worship of Icons," in the Māhātmya of the Madhyama-khaṇḍa, in the Third Part of the Dharmārtha-saṃhitā of the Śrī Viṣṇu Purāṇa. || 100 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, immediately after the ritual for purification, one should perform the worship of the *pavitraka*.
There, upon the pericarp of the lotus, one should place [the image] on the bed with its head toward the south or toward the east, reciting the mantra "dhruvā dyauḥ."
Therefore, one should spread five coverings of five colors;
one should recite the Śuddhāvatya verses;
then, one should offer a veil with the verse "yuvā suvāsāḥ."
And a pillow.
Then, one should fashion Ananta, the serpent consisting of the embryo, with seven heads;
and one should place him upon the bed.

Then one should perform the invocation of Jīva and recite the Śivasaṃkalpa. Next, one should carry out the invocation of Ananta. Thereafter, one should worship each with the Sāvitra mantra using the following: arghya, pādya, ācamanīya, unguent, garland, lamp, incense, madhuparka, and the offering of food.
Then follows the Sarpasāman;
one should utter the mantra "namo astu sarpebhyo ye ke ca pṛthivīm anu" and "yoge-yoge".
Or he may speak of his infinite majesty.
Then, with the mantra "dhruvā dyauḥ," one should place the image of the Blessed Lord upon the sacred thread (pavitraka) on top of Ananta.
Then one should perform the invocation of the individual soul (jīva).
One should recite the Śivasaṅkalpa mantra. Then one should invoke the Blessed Lord.
Then all [the attendants], with their knees placed upon the ground, should perform prostration and say, "The Blessed One has arrived.
Then they should worship him with the sounds of conchs, kettledrums, drums, and cries of victory.

Thereafter, they should worship the illustrious Blessed One individually with the *sāvitra* mantra, offering arghya, pādya, ācamanīya, bathing water, unguents, garlands, incense, lamps, madhuparka, and various foods.
Then one should mutter the mantra, "May it be well with us, O Indra.
Then, with the mantra "The young one, well-dressed," one should cover the illustrious Blessed One with a pair of great garments. With the mantra "They harness the mind," one should scatter flowers.
With the mantra "Awakening and re-awakening," one should scatter white mustard seeds.
One should recite, "Because of their manifestation.
In this manner, the consecration (adhivāsana) should be performed.

Once the Blessed One has consented, the Sāttvata, having established an altar at the site of worship, should purify the altar and the seats according to the rules for the purification of the ritual image.
Then, he should perform the sacrifice according to the procedure taught in the *Śaṅkaragītā*.
Simultaneously with the sacrifice, the Hotṛ priest performs the fire-oblation on the sacrificial mound and carries out the purification of the altar and the seats only once.

Sacrificial offerings and oblations must be performed daily once the preliminary consecration (adhivāsana) has been completed; likewise, worship with songs and dances should continue until the final installation (pratiṣṭhā) takes place. Thus, this preliminary consecration has been fully described by me to you.

Thus ends the one hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Consecration," in the *Māhātmya* of the *Vāsudeva-saṃhitā*, within the third section of the *Dharma-khaṇḍa* of the *Śrī-Viṣṇu-purāṇa*. ||101||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I invoke Jīva, the all-pervading seed and Lord.
It abides within the body in five states, and furthermore, it exists in a fivefold manner.
Furthermore, by means of the nature of Vāyu, it is again established in five ways.
Furthermore, by means of the fiery nature, it likewise exists in five states.
And by means of the Varuṇa-nature, he beheld the Lord established in fivefold states.
Furthermore, it exists in five ways by virtue of being composed of the elements.
The Supreme Self, most formidable yet gracious, the Lord of the universe.
All-pervading, the sustainer of all realms, the Lord of all, unconquered. || 4 ||
The Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña), the Lord, the Sovereign, who is exceedingly subtle and the bestower of boons.
The Lord of the past, present, and future, who is honored by the worlds.
The substratum of all qualities, the source of the universe, greater even than the great.
O Jīvadeva, come hither; enter this worship yourself.
O Lord of the gods of gods, O sinless one, restore him to life.
"Please accept this water for honor, this water for the feet, and this incense. (7)

Thus ends the one hundred and second chapter, titled "The Invocation of the Soul," in the [section on] the Installation of the Deity, within the [tenth] Book on the Worship of the Deity, in the [third] Part on the Rituals of the Temple, in the [first] Section on the Daily Routine, in the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. 102.
Vajra said:
O best of the Bhrigus, tell me the invocations for the deities.
For by means of mantras, the gods are summoned and become present.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O delighter of the Yadus, I shall tell you the invocations for the gods.
Then, excluding those who had already spoken, they spoke once again to some and to others.
At the conclusion of every invocation, half a verse is proclaimed.
May this water for honor and this water for the feet, as well as this incense, be accepted. || 3 ||
I invoke the two divine Nāsatyas, the sons of Sūrya.
The two auspicious Aśvins, the bestowers of boons and possessed of great fortune, arrived.
I shall invoke the eight Vasu deities, the bestowers of boons.
May the boon-granting gods, the Vasus who destroy evil, come hither. || 5 ||
I shall invoke all the gods of wondrous splendor.
May all the Viśvedevas, the givers of boons and possessors of great power, come hither. || 6 ||
I invoke the divine sages of the Aṅgiras lineage, possessed of wondrous splendor.
May the divine Aṅgirasas, possessed of great strength and prowess, come hither. || 7 ||
I shall invoke the Rudras, who have three eyes and ride upon bulls.
May the auspicious Rudras, the bestowers of boons upon the three worlds, come here. || 8 ||
I shall invoke the Ādityas, the givers of boons, who possess blazing splendor.
May all those suns, the bestowers of boons and blazing with intense splendor, come here.
I shall invoke the Bhṛgus, the gods whose wealth is radiant asceticism.
May the divine Bhṛgus, the bestowers of boons and possessed of blazing splendor, come hither.
"I shall invoke the Suras, the Maruts who are preeminent in splendor."
May the Maruts, the gods, the givers of boons, and the lords of the world come hither. || 11 ||
I shall invoke all the gods, the inhabitants of heaven.
May all the gods, desiring the mantra-worship, come here.
I shall summon the Daityas of great strength and prowess.
"O righteous Daityas, followers of the God of gods, come to me! (13)
I shall invoke the Gandharvas, who are endowed with beauty and wealth.
May all the Gandharvas, the givers of boons who can assume any form at will, come here. || 14 ||
I shall invoke the yakṣas together with the lords of wealth.
May the boon-granting yakṣas, renowned throughout the three worlds, come to me. || 15 ||
Likewise, I shall summon various Rākṣasas armed with diverse weapons.
May the heroic Rākṣasas, who follow the God of gods, come here. || 16 ||
In that manner, I shall invoke the hosts of Vidyādharas.
Let various Vidyādharas, who travel through the sky, assemble here. ||17||
Likewise, I shall invoke the Kinnaras, the celestial singers.
May all the Kinnaras, who possess beautiful voices and lovely eyes, come here. || 18 ||
I shall invoke the Nāgas, the serpents whose domain is the subterranean realm.
May the boon-granting Nāgas, renowned throughout the three worlds, come to me. || 19 ||
In that same manner, I shall invoke the auspicious Apsarases.
May the highly fortunate and radiant celestial women come to me.
I shall invoke all you wives of the gods.
May all those who grant boons, possessing the luster of molten gold, come hither. || 21 ||
In that manner, I shall invoke the boon-granting mothers of the gods.
May all of you, the bestowers of boons, well-attired, givers of happiness, and auspicious ones, come forth. || 22 ||
I shall invoke the ancestors who bear subtle forms.
May all the ancestors come, each remaining in their respective groups.
I shall likewise summon the exceedingly powerful Suparṇas.
Let the Suparṇas arrive, augmented by the splendor of Viṣṇu.
I invoke all the Prajāpatis, the bestowers of boons.
May the presiding lords of creatures, the protectors of the three worlds, come together. || 25 ||
I invoke the lords of the gods, the deities who are the leaders of the worlds.
May the lords of the gods, who grant boons and can assume any form at will, come to me. || 26 ||
I shall invoke the Manus who abide in the sovereignty of the world.
May all the sages come, their sins destroyed by austerity. || 27 ||
I shall invoke the auspicious medicinal herbs that sustain all living beings.
And may all auspicious medicinal herbs, which grant all desires, come together. || 28 ||
I shall invoke the sages, whose splendor is illuminated by asceticism.
May all the perfected sages of blazing splendor come to me.
I shall cause mountains endowed with all medicinal herbs to be brought here.
May all the mountain-dwelling deities, the lords of the immovable, come to me.
"I shall invoke the trees, which assume various forms."
May all the trees arrive with the speed of mind and wind.
Likewise, I shall invoke those who range throughout the entire Pātāla.
Let all those from the netherworlds, the abodes of the Daityas, who are indeed beyond reproach, come here.
I shall summon all the continents that possess wondrous qualities.
May those islands, which serve as the abodes of the worlds and are beloved by all beings, come here.
I shall invoke the worlds, which are beautiful and serve as the very abodes [of the deities].
May all the worlds, the creators of all beings, come to me.
In that manner, I shall invoke the oceans, which are dear to the world.
May the oceans, the repositories of essence beloved by the world, come together for me.
I shall invoke the Rain-god here, the refuge of all beings.
And let there come here likewise rains that are enchanting to all.
In that manner, I shall also invoke the four oceans.
"May all the oceans, the bearers of water, come quickly to me."
I shall invoke the rivers, the granter of boons and mothers of the world.
May the auspicious rivers, the bestowers of boons and removers of all sins, come hither.
In that same manner, I shall invoke all the hosts of clouds.
"Let all my noble and cloud-like followers come to me."
In that same manner, I shall summon all the Piśācas.
"Let all the Piśācas, who can assume any form at will, come to me. ||39||
In that same manner, I shall invoke those who stand by the side of Skanda.
Let those of various forms come and stand by my side, Skanda.
In that manner, I shall invoke the attendants of the gods.
Let the various attendants of my deities assemble in manifold forms.
In that same manner, I shall invoke the attendants of Hara.
"Let the various forms of Hara’s attendants come to me."
In that manner, I shall invoke the Mothers, the mothers of the world.
May the divine Mothers come, the givers of boons, all-pervading and auspicious.
I shall invoke the planets, the lords of all the worlds.
May all the planets, the radiant leaders of the world, come together.
Likewise, I shall invoke the stars, which are the bestowers of boons.
May all the constellations and all the lords of the worlds come here.
I shall invoke the most enchanting quarters, beginning with the East.
May they come from all directions, bringing happiness to all beings.
I shall invoke the divine streets that serve as the abodes of the nine planets.
May all the streets come forth, adorned with the circles of planets and constellations.
I shall invoke the subtle-formed moments.
May the auspicious divisions of time, the muhūrtas, quickly arrive.
I shall invoke the six seasons, the lords of the world, for six days.
May all the seasons come, which set the wheel of the world in motion.
In that same manner, I shall invoke the five-year cycles.
May all the years come forth, the movers of the wheel of time.
I shall invoke the four Yugas, which possess blazing splendor.
May all the ages come, established in their fourfold forms.
I shall invoke the fourteen Manus as well. ||52||
May the Manvantaras arrive, established for a duration equal to that of the thirty gods.
I shall invoke the auspicious god Kāla, who possesses limbs.
Come, O Blessed One, O Kāla, O God of gods, O Janārdana!
I shall invoke the gods who bear the form of sacrifice.
May all the gods, the bestowers of boons who assume many forms, arrive together.
I shall invoke the planets and all the branches of knowledge without exception.
May all of them come here out of a desire for the welfare of the worlds.
I shall invoke the peaceful Śāstṛs who abide in the state of vision.
Let weapons quickly arrive, the supreme ornament of the armies.
I shall indeed invoke the weapons that are beneficial to the three worlds.
And may all those who establish the bridge of Dharma assemble here.
"I shall invoke the Vedas and the various scriptures in manifold ways. (58)
May those learned in the Vedas and Shastras, who are intent on protecting the world, come together.
I shall invoke all those who have the gods as their vehicle.
May all come here; may all those who have the thirty gods as their vehicle come.
I shall summon the Nāgas and the sons of the gods who possess great strength.
May the lords of the nāgas, who are the mounts of the gods, come quickly with all haste.
I shall invoke the treasures, headed by Śaṅkha and Padma.
May all the treasures come forth, the sole source of sustenance for the entire world.
O Lord of the Yadu lineage, if the purpose of the summons is for the sake of one person from among the assembly, [then act accordingly].
However, due to the requirements of the ritual action, the invocation mantra should be made to correspond with that [deity] alone, as is appropriate. || 62 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and third chapter, titled "The Invocation of the Deities," in the section on Consecration (*Pratiṣṭhākalpa*) within the Dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third part of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I invoke the god Brahmā, the supreme creator.
The cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of this world. || 1 ||
The Lord who possesses the four Vedas, who has four faces, and who is the master of the four castes.
The protector of the four stages of life, the bestower of boons, and the creator of all beings.
The source of the lotus, the source of the world, the source of sacrifice, the Lord of the universe.
The self-born, the invincible, the sustainer of sacrifice, the lord of the world.
The Lord of Sacrifice, the embodiment of sacrifice, and the sole cause of the three worlds.
To the all-pervading, gentle Nārada, the supreme Lord of lords.
The eternal Lord of the past, the future, and the present, who is to be known through yoga.
Come, O Blessed One, for the prosperity of the sacrificer who offers to Brahman. || 5 ||
"Please accept this water for honor, this water for the feet, and this incense."
I invoke the god, the god of gods, the consumer of oblations.
The cause of the origin, maintenance, and dissolution of this world.
The divine form, the support of that [universe], the mouth of all the gods, the Lord.
The fire-god Vibhāvasu, with tawny eyes and tawny matted hair, whose banner is smoke.
The god who had arrived on a parrot-vehicle, adorned with all ornaments. || 8 ||
The all-pervading, boon-bestowing Sun, who dwells within the bellies of all embodied beings.
He was a form of splendor, invincible, seven-tongued, and possessed of great strength.
He who has seven flames, seven sages, seven fuels, and is infallible.
The indefinable portion of Viṣṇu, who is like the sun and is the knower of all beings.
It is purifying, nourishing, gentle, and increases the prosperity of devotees.
Distribute prosperity in every way to both the officiating priest and the patron of the sacrifice.
Please accept this water for honor, this water for the feet, and this incense.
Therefore, O best of kings, I shall now describe the invocations for all of them.
At the conclusion of every invocation, this verse is proclaimed.
Having entered, [worship] this image which has been properly fashioned by me with devotion. || 13 ||
"Please accept this water for honor, this water for the feet, and this incense."
"I shall certainly invoke Dhruva, the lord of the hosts of all the gods."
By means of the cords of wind, the wheel of time is bound and made to revolve.
"Come to me, O Lord of Gods, O Keśava of inconceivable prowess! (15)
O presiding lord of all the hosts of grahas, you who are honored by all the worlds!
I shall summon the sky, adorned with hundreds of celestial chariots.
The third step belongs to Viṣṇu, the high-souled God of gods.
Come to me, O Blessed One, O gentle one, O supportless expanse of the sky!
Adorned with hundreds of celestial palaces that are immeasurable and exceedingly profound.
I shall invoke from above the great and infinite quarter.
Immeasurable, without support, and devoid of the rays of the moon and sun.
Come here, O illustrious lady, to this place constantly frequented by the Siddhas.
O Goddess, infinite, vast, stainless, and beneficent!
I invoke [the deity] from below, from the direction protected by Śeṣa.
And it was constantly frequented by hosts of nāgas, daityas, and uragas.
It was deep, vast, formidable, and adorned with many locations. || 21 ||
Come to me, O you who possess abundant jewels, manifold forms, and great strength!
I shall invoke the sun-god Divākara, the granter of boons and possessor of a thousand rays.
He is the embodiment of splendor, invincible, and the bestower of fearlessness upon his devotees.
Come, O Lord, O Master of the World, O Lord of the Ṛg, Sāman, and Yajus! ||23||
O lamp of the mandala of the three worlds, destroyer of all diseases!
I invoke the god Āditya, who dwells within the waters.
Varuṇa, who possesses great splendor and resembles smooth lapis lazuli.
"Come, O Lord, Master of the Waters, Great Sovereign of the hosts of aquatic creatures! || 25 ||
O Acyuta, you are constantly served by hosts of Nāgas, Daityas, and Uragas.
I invoke the Moon, the cool-rayed one, whose luster is like nectar. || 26 ||
The lord of medicinal herbs, the presiding deity of the twice-born, who brings delight to the eyes.
Come to me, O Blessed One, O Moon, you who bear the mark of the hare! 27 ||
O you who are ever compassionate toward your devotees, honored by all the constellations.
I shall invoke Bhauma, the embodiment of splendor, who is difficult to approach.
He possessed an auspicious form, with an indescribable face that shone with the luster of blood.
"Come to me, O Blessed One, you who possess the luster of the terrestrial planet Aṅgāraka! || 29 ||
Upon this earth, all that is auspicious and inauspicious is dependent on you.
I shall invoke Skanda, the six-faced one, the granter of boons, the child.
The crusher of the army of the enemies of the gods, the increaser of Pārvatī’s joy.
"Come, O King, today, you who are the thief of Mahiṣāsura's wealth! (31)
O Kārttikeya, Lord of the World, whose vehicle is the excellent peacock!
I shall invoke Budha, the awakener, the Lord of the World.
The lord of the lunar sphere, the presiding authority over the host of planets, whose form is splendor and who is difficult to approach.
Come, O inconceivable one born from the cool-rayed moon, O Janārdana, conqueror of the world! 33.
O you of great strength, O fortunate one, O mighty-armed one, O you of great splendor!
I shall invoke Viṣṇu, the wielder of the conch, the discus, and the mace.
Dark as the flax flower, clad in yellow garments, and infallible.
"Come to me, O Lord of the gods, O creator of the manifestation of living beings! (35)
O Nārāyaṇa, you who are difficult to cross over, great archer, wielder of the bow!
"I shall invoke Śakra, the god who is the lord of the hosts of deities."
To Vajrapāṇi, the long-armed one, who is devoted to the welfare of cows and brahmins.
Come, O thousand-eyed god, destroyer of the strength of the enemies of the gods!
O Airāvata, knower of dharma, delighter of Śacī’s heart!
I shall invoke Jīva, the priest of the Lord of the Gods.
To Bṛhaspati, whose speech is vast and who has reached the further shore of the Vedas and their auxiliary sciences.
"Come, O illustrious one, O you who have become the very life-force upon the surface of the earth! ||39||
O increaser of the earth, your own righteous prosperity is perpetually dependent upon you.
"I shall invoke the Goddess Pārvatī, the boon-granting Umā."
The beloved wife of Hara, who possesses beautiful limbs and increases prosperity.
Come, O Goddess, Mother of the World, who brings joy to the heart of Menā! 41.
O purifier, giver of boons, gentle one, who is eternally dear to your devotees!
"I shall invoke Śukra, the descendant of Bhṛgu, the Lord of the World. ||42||

Four-faced and four-armed, dependent on the qualities yet transcending the qualities.

The lotus, consisting of the form of the waters, is known as the gentle (saumya).

The Gāyatrī, mother of the gods, the Night of Time, and the terrifying one.

Among them, you are declared to be the profound Vaiṣṇavī, who is indeed very difficult to restrain.

Come here, O Lāṅgalāsya, and address these words to the three worlds.
"I shall invoke the lord Musala, the son of Sudhanvan. || 69 ||
Come here from the pestle, O destroyer of the hosts of the enemies of the gods!

"I shall invoke the sword named Nandaka by name. (73)

O Rigveda, embodiment of Brahman, bestower of boons, come here to me.

"O Yajurveda, come hither, O Lord of Gods, Leader of the Gaṇas!

O Atharvaveda, come here, you who bestow the fruits of all ritual actions!

The companion of Lakṣmī, the giver of boons, the witness of the world, and the imperishable.

Difficult to behold, exceedingly profound, you manifest a form through illusion.

"I shall invoke Vālmīki, the treasure-house of asceticism. (99)

Come quickly, O Axe, making the earth your target!

"I shall invoke Rāma, who has accomplished the destruction of the Rākṣasas."

"O Bharata, you who have subdued the Gandharvas, come here!"
"I shall summon Lakṣmaṇa, the destroyer of enemies."
O Lakṣmaṇa, you who are like the sun to the weapon of Meghanāda, come here to me!

O Śatrughna, slayer of the Asura Lavaṇa, come quickly!

"O Arjuna, come quickly to me, you who have lightened the burden of the earth!"

Go alone to the site of destruction, prepared for the sake of protecting Kṛṣṇa.

May all the goddesses, headed by Gāndhārī, come here together.

Wearing a single earring, peaceful, and adorned with a forest garland.
Come, O illustrious Rāma, O infallible beloved of Revatī! 122
The waters of the Yamunā were drawn forth from its source by the tip of the plowshare that had struck deep.
I shall invoke Kṛṣṇa, who possesses the luster of a cloud filled with water.
The destroyer of Cāṇūra’s pride in his strength, the annihilator of the demon Kaṃsa.
Come, O illustrious Kṛṣṇa, you who have taken the earth as your mark!
O best of Danavas, you who have been cast down; O you who held up Mount Govardhana!
I shall invoke Pradyumna, who has the splendor of a sea-monster.
The beloved of Rati, who was the thief of the life-breath of Śambara, the enemy of the gods.

O submarine fire for the ocean of the great army of the demon Bāṇāsura! 127.
O Aniruddha, you of great strength and prowess, come hither!
O sword-handed one, O highly fortunate one, O increaser of the heart of Ūṣā!

Come, O illustrious Sāmba, you who have destroyed all the dānavas!
