Thus ends the one hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Invocation of All Deities with Śeṣa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O hero, this mantra has indeed been declared for the purpose of awakening the denizens of heaven.
O King, I shall speak of Vāsudeva; listen to my instruction.
I shall awaken the divine Vāsudeva, the unborn and all-pervading Lord.
Without beginning, middle, or end, possessing great strength and prowess.
The infinite, all-pervading Lord, greater even than the great.
Extremely subtle, as well as situated at a great distance or even in close proximity; || 3 ||
Nārāyaṇa, the gentle deity who wields the Śārṅga bow.
Dark as the flax flower, clad in yellow garments, and infallible.
The lotus-eyed one has awakened, he who is compassionate toward those who have come for refuge.
O you who have shown compassion for the elephant-like beings submerged and distressed in the lake of saṃsāra!
O you whose tip is severed by the edge of the wheel, O you who are difficult to restrain like the crocodile of bad dreams!
O you whose eyes are closed in the well-practiced sleep of great yoga!
O You who never depart from Your vast bed, which extends as far as the coils of the serpent Śeṣa!
With its upper canopy formed by the rays of the jewels in the rows of his hoods.
O you who are resplendent with two lotus feet being massaged by Lakṣmī.
O destroyer of the great Daityas, you who have brought security to the three worlds!
O Acyuta, who resembles the mass of rays of the moon and reclines upon the ocean of milk!
O destroyer of the fear of falling into the abysses of hell for your devotees!
O you who have extended a helping hand for their return to their own world!
O Janārdana, you are the great ship for crossing the ocean of saṃsāra.
O you who cause the destruction of dense clouds by the mere utterance of your name!
O you who have brought to full fruition the great fruit of all desires, accomplished solely by yourself!
O you who have stepped beyond the pavilion of the universe with the strides of Trivikrama!
O you who playfully lifted the earth with the tips of your fangs, which resemble the crescent moon!
These gods, led by Indra, are awakening you.
And the highly fortunate sages, who perceive the stainless truth of the three worlds.
O Lord, Brahmā, the auspicious four-faced one, awakens you.
O Acyuta, best among gods, the Yajurveda [is worshipped] with maces and with words.
O destroyer of the enemies of the hosts of gods, abandon your sleep today; O Lord of the world, become the remover of my accumulation of sins.

"O Lord, for one who possesses fierce devotion toward you, their inclination toward other deities is indeed surpassed. Thus ends the one hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Awakening of Vāsudeva," in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Vavra said:
O Blessed One, the forms of all the gods have been fully described.
O best of the Bhṛgus, because they are joined with the five elements, therefore [they are so called].
The procedure for invocation has been declared; that which is most appropriate is considered the best.
Wherever they are summoned, they arrive, possessing the power to bring desires to their conclusion.
Relying upon greatness, attainment, and likewise lightness, O gods.
Viṣṇu is the all-pervading God, greater even than the great.
Subtler than the subtlest, all-pervading, and consisting of the entire world.
There is nothing in this world where Janārdana is not present.
O illustrious one, both being and non-being are pervaded by that Great-Souled One.
What purpose is there in invoking Him who is indeed omnipresent?
O illustrious one of great faculties, it ripens everywhere.
Cut asunder this doubt of mine, for you are indeed said to be all-knowing.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Just as all the hosts of gods have forms that are condensed like a vajra.
In this very manner, the Lord, the slayer of Madhu, manifested his appearance.
The entire form, joined with the five elements, becomes adorned.
O best of the Yadus, it is joined with the beginning, the end, and the middle of everything.
Just as Viṣṇu has appeared in his manifestations, so too have the hosts of gods.
The established conclusion is that when it has been deposited, it becomes present. ||9||
The form of the God is twofold: the supreme (parā) and likewise the lower (aparā).
The supreme form of Puruṣa is resplendent with the five elements.
Through that [power], the omnipresent Supreme Lord assumes a physical form.
In this world, nothing whatsoever exists here without the Puruṣa.
He is without beginning, middle, or end, and likewise possesses an immeasurable body.
O King, that power is likewise present everywhere, pervading all the senses and the mind.
Furthermore, that which is his omnipotence even while he has entered into manifestation.
O King, that [attainment] is declared for one who desires it, but not for one who does not desire it.
For that which is the omnipotence of the infinite one in his state as Puruṣa, O King—
O Yadava, it should be known that she is eternally and everywhere established by nature. || 14 ||
Furthermore, the invocation of the Lord of the World is performed here as well.
Even though the Supreme Lord is eternally present everywhere, [he is not perceived]. || 15 ||
In that regard, the sole cause is the cause for the satisfaction of the mind.
The god has been invoked by me, and he is present in this very place.
The invocation is for the purpose of one's own satisfaction, just as it exists for the Supreme Person.
Nevertheless, O highly fortunate one, the purpose of this worship is for my own satisfaction. (17)
For one who is eternally satisfied, what purpose would there be in performing worship?
He accepts [offerings] from his devotees solely for the sake of being pleased by their devotion.
That deity who is worshipped, wherein the gods are worshipped by the wise. || 19 ||
And know that all those entities by which one worships are likewise composed of That.
Know that the performance of its worship has as its purpose the gratification of the agent.
And likewise, the object of knowledge is the Self of that [Self] which is omnipresent.
Therefore, O Yādava, he who is eternally satisfied has no beginning cause.
It has been set forth for the sake of favoring devotees and for [the benefit of] oneself.
O King, how it is that the bodiless one dwells within the body.
For the sake of awakening the devotee to the characteristics [of the deity], that [deity] is likewise invoked.
O Great King, that which is formless is difficult to bind as a target. ||23||
Indeed, the binding of the *lakṣa* can easily be performed by means of the *sākāras*.
For indeed, the manifestation of one who has entered [the womb] occurs according to the rule and in such a manner. ||24||
O tiger among kings, I have already declared this to you previously according to the scriptures.
Whatever state a man may be in during his meditation, let that very state become his.
In that very place, O Yādava, this meditation and worship should be performed by him.
O highly fortunate one, having first performed the binding of the *lakṣa* within the formalized form (*sākāra*). || 26 ||
Thereafter, O best of men, he becomes capable in the meditation on emptiness.
Such is the invocation of him, O Yādava, and likewise his worship.
The awakened ones exert effort for this purpose as a means to benefit themselves.
Being eternally satisfied, he does not offer an oblation for the sake of satisfaction.
O Great King, he who bestows grace upon his devotees accepts [the offering].
O mighty-armed one, you should know that both of these lead to the attainment of liberation.
The path of knowledge and the path of action have been established for those who are free from desire.
An action performed with desire leads to the vajra-bond.
That very same [action], when performed without desire, is ordained for liberation alone.
O King, when invoked and brought near, those [deities] joined with mantras necessarily become present at that very moment.
O Lord, for one's own satisfaction, the wise have prescribed the invocation of the boon-bestowing Viṣṇu with the Vajra-mantra. || 31 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Purpose of Invoking," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
"O Blessed One, explain the procedure for the *homa* sacrifice.
To him the Blessed Mārkaṇḍeya replied:

"The Blessed One, having been consecrated (*adhivāsita*), kindles the fire, sweeps around it, and with the melted clarified butter (*ājya*) and with festivity, offers the previously mentioned oblations of the *rakṣoghna* mantras up to the *ājyabhāga* portions. Then, with the names to be mentioned hereafter—ending in *svāhā*, joined with the dative case—one should offer eight, twenty-eight, or one hundred and eight oblations of clarified butter, using barley, sesame, and white mustard seeds, one by one name."
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Vāsudeva.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Saṃkarṣaṇa.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One Pradyumna.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, Aniruddha.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Supreme Person.
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Truth!
Oṃ, homage to the Blessed One, the Immovable One.
Oṃ, homage to Śrī.
Oṃ, homage to Kālarātri.
Oṃ, salutations to Emanation.
Oṃ, homage to Garuḍa!
Oṃ, homage to Tāla!
Oṃ, homage to Makara!
Oṃ, homage to the Ṛṣi!
Oṃ, homage to Ananta.
Oṃ, salutations to Kaustubha.
Oṃ, homage to Vanamālā.
Oṃ, salutations to the Earth.
Oṃ, homage to Śaṅkha.
Oṃ, homage to the Lotus!
Oṃ, homage to Gadā.
Oṃ, homage to the Wheel.
Oṃ, homage to Halāya!
Oṃ, homage to the pestle!
Oṃ, homage to the bow!
Oṃ, salutation to the hide.
Oṃ, homage to the sword!
Oṃ, homage to Subhadra.
Oṃ, homage to Vasubhadra!
Oṃ, homage to Āṣāḍha.
Oṃ, homage to the one who has reached the end of sacrifice!
Oṃ, homage to Jayā!
Oṃ, homage to Vijaya!
Oṃ, homage to Āmoda!
Oṃ, homage to Joy!
Then the oblation with the *vyāhṛtis* should be performed;
then one should perform the oblation with the *gāyatrī*;
then with the verse "That supreme step of Viṣṇu" (*tad viṣṇoḥ paramaṃ padam*); and then with the Vaiṣṇava *gāyatrī*.
Then [he recites] the section beginning with "They yoke the mind."
Then, with the Puruṣasūkta.
Then, [he offers] with the four verses beginning with "tato ratho akṣeṣu."
And then with the six *camaka* [sections].
Then, however, with clarified butter.
After one year, having performed the ritual beginning with the fire-oblation, he should complete the subsequent procedure.
This is proclaimed as the fire-oblation (homa) to be performed for the consecration (pratiṣṭhā) of Viṣṇu.
And for other deities, one should offer the oblation with their respective characteristic mantras.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Fire-offerings," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, when the day for the consecration and other rites has arrived, one should awaken the Blessed Lord with conchs, kettledrums, and musical instruments.
One should recite the awakening mantra.

Then, assuming forms for ten million aeons with their arms raised, bearing water-pots, and acting as chief architects, they should enter the temple while reciting the mantra: "And here is the Blessed One."
Then, one should bury all medicinal herbs mixed with the five products of the cow (pañcagavya), all fragrances, all gems, and gold into the pit of the pedestal.
And there are mantras in that regard.
The highly fortunate one. ||1||
The bird.
The Trisuparṇa.
The Bhāruṇḍa.
The Plough of Death.
May there be well-being for us from Indra; this is the twelfth [chapter] concerning the internal self.
Then, at the time prescribed by the astrologer, he arranged his own personification before the Blessed One on a perfectly level viewing platform.
One should make it steady with this very mantra: "The sky is firm."
And one should utter his name.
And one should recite the *Pratiṣṭhā-sāman*;
and all the people should create a tumultuous sound with shouts of "Victory! (*jaya*) and by scattering parched grain and flowers.
One should cause musical instruments to be played.
One should utter: "Oṃ, obeisance to the Blessed One Vāsudeva."
And one should recite the Brahmasūkta.
With the mantra "Thou art the life of Agni," he should perform the taking of life.
And the barber, with a water-pot in his hand, should recite.
Oṃ, you are established, O Blessed One; may this [image] be well-established.
Manifest your presence for the prosperity of the sacrificer.
May there be constant peace for our bipeds, and may there be peace for our quadrupeds.
May there be peace for all the world, and likewise may there be peace for the kings.
The sacrificer, together with his servants, his sons, his cattle, and his kinsmen.
This region must be constantly protected by the Blessed One; homage be to you!

Thus ends the one hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Mantras for Awakening the Blessed One," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 110 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, once the Blessed One has been installed, one should begin the great ceremonial bath; thereafter, one should recite the Gāyatrī.
With the words "iṣe tvā," he should give the alms-bowl.
With the Vaiṣṇava-gāyatrī, he places the two sandals; with the verse "yanosi," he takes the earth for the two sandals.
"May the waters be auspicious to us"—with these words, the water for washing;
"O Vanaspati, [be favorable] to the gods"—with these words, the tooth-stick.
"Yāmālikha" refers to the scraping of the tongue.
The sipping of water is performed with the verse beginning "āpo hi ṣṭha."
The arghya offering with the vessel.
With the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," [he puts on] the bathing garment.
The seat is with the verse "Firm is the sky," and the footstool is with the Pratiṣṭhā Sāman.
"Kanikrada" refers to the seed-vessel.
"Thou art the essence of fire and semen"—with these words, [he offers] the lamp.
From the mouth [he recites] "Indra... and [offers] the mirror.
In the same way, there is the smearing of the face.
Rodhra, the bark of kola, majjā, vacā, kuṣṭha, blue lotuses, and saffron—this is a facial paste.
The oil [is prepared] with the mantra beginning "sahasraśīrṣā."
One should perform the ritual rubbing with the verse beginning "bhadraṃ karṇebhiḥ."
With Supratīka, the cups for the ritual bath.
By means of Ṛṣabha, the bath that removes the male organ.
"Ghṛtavatī" refers to a bath with clarified butter.
With curd, [he recites] "Of Dadhikrāvan."
"Payasvatī" means "by means of milk."
With "Gandhadvara," [he should smear] with cow dung.
With the Gāyatrī mantra, [one should bathe] with cow's urine.
With the *aghamarṣaṇa* hymn and the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*);
with the verse "Firm is the sky" (*dhruvā dyauḥ*) and the rite of *niṣpuṃsana*, [one attains] stability.
With honey, [reciting] "The winds are honeyed for the one who follows the cosmic order."
"With *supratīka* means with sugarcane juice;
with *bhauma* means with molasses-water."
With water containing pebbles, reciting the Atharvaśiras.
With the Vāmadeva mantra, [he should take] earth from both banks of a river.
With the earth from a confluence, [he recites] "śāntā dyauḥ."
With the Prāṇasūkta, together with hair and earth.
"By means of the Vārāha [mantra]" means with clay extracted by the Boar [incarnation].
With the Vāmadeva [mantra], one should use clay from an elephant's tusk.
"By means of a bull" means by means of the clay originating from the horns of a bull.
"Ashvakrāntā" [is recited] by all [the goddesses].
With *bhāruṇḍa* and *āmalaka*.
"By Vikarṇa" means by Rodhra;
"by Jyeṣṭhasāman" means by Kāleyaka.
With the *bṛhatsāman*, [one should worship] with a citron.
With "kṛṣṇājineneti," [he bathes] with varṇaka;
with "agna āyurasīti," with tagara;
and with the Śrīsūkta, with priyaṅgu.
With white mustard seeds while reciting the mantra "viṣṇorarāṭam."
"By means of the black gem" means by means of that which has been drawn forth.
"With *śiribhita*" means with water infused with *kuśa* grass;
"those which are herbs" means with all medicinal herbs.
With the seeds [reciting] "O Brahmin, you are a Brahmin."
"Puṣpavatī" means "by means of flowers."
With the formula "O Lord of the Forest, firm-limbed," [he sprinkles] with bundles of wood.
"Flower-bearing" refers to [the tree] by means of its fruits.
"Swift, sharpening [your weapons]!"—with these words, he bestows riches.
"Gandhadvārā" means by means of fragrances.

With the *oṃ* syllable and salutations as purifiers, there are medicinal herbs for bathing the head, such as: kuṣṭha, rodhra, mustā, vacā, mustard seeds, jayantī, viṣṇukrāntā, punarnavā, brāhmī, tagara, atibalā, navabalā, nāgabalā, tvak, patra, aguru, bālaka, hareṇuka, lavaṅga, agara, uśīra, nālikā, cūrakam, and the two types of haridrā.
In this manner, the offering of the ritual jar for the bath is performed.

Therein, at the very beginning, having purified [the site] with salutations consisting of the syllable *oṃ*, one should offer ten lumps of clay that are sweet within and characterized by goodness (*sāttvata*).
Then, with the Sāman chants—the Mahānāmnī, Vāmadevya, Lakṣa, Rathantara, Śākvara, Bhāruṇḍa, and Bṛhat Sāmans—[he worshipped].

The knower of the Atharvaveda [protects] by means of the *Atharvaśiras*, *Pratyaṅgirasa*, *Śaṅkha*, *Maṇi*, *Prāṇasūkta*, *Maṇipratisara*, and *Maṇis*; and the knower of the Ṛgveda [protects] by means of the *Gāyatrī*, *Sāvitrī*, and *Go-sūkta*.

One who knows the Yajurveda should perform [the rite] with the Sūryasūkta, Puruṣasūkta, and Śrīsūkta. Then, with a black antelope skin, a wooden cup (camasa), the six [offerings], the Ṣaḍṛtu, Kūṣmāṇḍa, Rudra, and Draviṇa [mantras], one should offer jars according to one's capacity—whether a thousand jars, eight hundred, five hundred, four hundred, one hundred and eight, twenty-eight, or eight—well-adorned, accompanied by the sound of the chanting of the Vanaspati, Kālāpa-garbha, and conch shells, the noise of musical instruments, shouts of "Victory! Victory!", and the dancing of beautiful women.
Then, having rested the upakalaśas with the purifier, he should place them upon the altar.
With the words "ghṛtavatī," he should show [the butter] while looking at the ghee.
With the *sahasraśīrṣa* [hymn], one should give a garment for the purpose of grasping the crest-lock (*śikhaṇḍa*).
With the verse "yuvā suvāsāḥ," [he puts on] the garment for changing.
With the mantra "idam āpaḥ pravahata," he should offer water for sipping; then, with his knees, hands, and head, he should perform a prostration.
Indeed, that man who performs this great ablution for Hari, [attains the highest state].
Freed from all sins, he is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
One should always act in this manner not only during the consecration ceremony.
This supreme and extensive ritual bathing bestows peace, nourishment, and the fulfillment of all desires.
When there occurs the manifestation of celestial, atmospheric, and terrestrial portents.
O king of kings, one should perform the great ablution for the God of gods.
There is no arising in the world that is not stilled by this.
One who desires health, one who desires prosperity, and one who desires liberation from bondage [should practice this].
And one who desires good fortune and peace should perform the Bṛhatsnapana rite.
One seeking knowledge shall obtain knowledge, and likewise, one desiring sons shall obtain offspring.
He obtains beloved and eminent women, as well as whatever else he desires.
One who desires no desires attains that supreme abode of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of the Great Bathing Ceremony," in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 111 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should worship the Blessed Lord after he has bathed.
One should prepare an ointment using sandalwood, resinous exudate, nutmeg, musk, and camphor, either all together or individually. With the mantra "Gandhadvārām," one should anoint the Blessed One.
With the mantra "vāyuragregā," one should offer a palm-leaf fan.
One should fan [the patient] with the words, "O Wind, you are the medicine for wind."
One should present the fly-whisk with the mantra, "sāvitrāṇi sāvitrasya."
One should offer the seed-syllables (bījas) of the Śrī Viṣṇu-gāyatrī.
With the mantra "yuvā suvāsāḥ," one should clothe the Blessed Lord with garments of great value.

One should worship with ornaments that are not worn out, not blue, and golden in color. With a comb [one recites] "Not a comb, not a comb"; with a comb [one recites] "O Indra and Viśve"; with a comb for the head of the Dūṣya; with collyrium, a jewel, a broom, a self-arrangement, a brush for smoothing, and with flowers [reciting] "The flower-bearing one," both those that are gathered and those placed at the front.
With the verse "O Prajāpati, none other than you [possesses] these," he should perform the rite with the scattering of cloth-powder.
With the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā," one should offer a lamp.
With the mantra "Thou art the bearer; bear [the burden]," he fumigates with incense.
With the verse "abhitvā śūra nonumaḥ," [he should worship] with an umbrella.
With the Viṣṇu-gāyatrī, [he worships] the two shoes.

With the mantra "idaṃ viṣṇurvicakrame," he should proceed by that very vehicle; with the mantra "ketuṃ kṛṇvan," he should proceed with banners, flags, and so forth. Then, he should worship the Blessed Lord with hymns of praise.
Then, with the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā," one should offer [oblations] in this measure for the sake of fulfilling all enjoyments.
Then with stringed instruments, and then with the resounding blasts of conchs, kettledrums, and drums—thus it was exceedingly beautiful.
Having worshipped Janārdana with enjoyments according to this rite, [one should proceed].
One obtains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu. || 1 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bestowal of Enjoyments," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 112 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, one should worship the Blessed One with the honey-mixture offering (madhuparka).
One should offer the guest-offering with the verse beginning "Hiraṇyavarṇā";
curd with the verse beginning "Dadhikrāvṇaḥ"; and ghee with the verse beginning "Ghṛtavatī."
"Sweet are the winds for him who lives according to the Truth"—thus it is honey.
Having combined it with three parts of gold, one should employ it with the Sāvitra mantra.
One should offer the libation with the verse beginning "āpo hi ṣṭhā."
"May the wind blow healing medicine"—with these words, the castration is performed.
"May the waters be auspicious to us"—with these words, the water for sipping is offered.

According to the rite of the Aṣṭaka, one should offer an animal or a measure [of grain] with the hymn beginning "hiraṇyavarṇā," and by means of that, present auspicious objects such as images, conchs, and lotuses.
O sinless one, this procedure for the madhuparka has been described by me to you.
Having performed this, O Great King, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Offering of Madhuparka," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 113 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should offer the guest-offering with the verse beginning "hiraṇyavarṇā."
Then, one should offer it with the Sāvitra mantra, accompanied by edible foods, side dishes, meat, snacks, fruits, and the sacred thread.

According to one's ability, one should worship the Blessed Lord with fragrant and delicious food offerings, water for drinking with the *āpohiṣṭhā* verses and the libation (*tarpaṇa*), the fanning away [of impurities] with the verse *vāta āvātu bheṣajam*, the water for sipping (*ācamanīya*) with the verse *śanna āpaḥ*, and again with this same procedure using the verse *agnirmūrdhā*, followed by the concluding sacrifice (*anuyajña*) consisting of the distribution of portions.
Indra shall offer betel-leaf from his mouth.
With that very same [substance], one should apply fragrant scents and mouth-perfumes; with that very same [substance], one should use a mirror.
Furthermore, one should again worship the Blessed One with songs, instrumental music, and dances.
Having fully worshipped the eternal God of gods with the sacrifice of food.
One attains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Sacrificial Worship," in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, the Sāttvata should perform the worship according to the procedure described in the Śaṅkaragītā.
And one should honor Śacī with enjoyments for those who perform [the ritual].

In front of the gods, he should give to each of the officiating priests (ṛtvij) a large quantity of gold, a garment, a calf, and a bronze vessel; and he should honor them according to his own capacity.
Then one should feed the Brahmins.
And while they are eating, one should cause them to hear the majesty of the Blessed One.
Then the sacrificer should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya).
Then he should remain in a temple for the sake of listening to songs, dances, instrumental music, and sacred texts.
Having performed the consecration of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow according to this rite, a person—
One attains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Sāttvata Sacrifice," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 115 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:

One should perform the worship daily for seven days according to the Vedic ritual procedure, with the offering rites prescribed in the Sāttvata system. Then, on the seventh day, having performed the great ablution (bṛhatsnapana), the ritualist, holding a water-pot in his hand, should sprinkle the archways while reciting the mantra "yā oṣadhayaḥ."
"By means of the gateway of fragrance" means one should worship with ointment;
"possessing flowers" means with flowers.
With the mantra "Agnirmūrdhā," he worships with a lamp;
with "Dhūrasi," with incense;
and with "Sāvitrāṇi sāvitrasya," with the food offering.

Then, one should erect the archways (toraṇas) in the northeast, then in the east, then in the south, and finally in the west, using the Śrī-Viṣṇu-Gāyatrī mantra. All these officiating priests (ṛtvijas), taking the archways, should proceed to the river—mounted on the backs of elephants, or on horse-drawn chariots, or on ox-carts, or seated in palanquins—and there they should cast them [into the water] with the mantra: "svasti na indra."
Those who go to the temple of the glorious deity Bhadra-kaṇṇā and those who enter here saying "The Blessed One is here," [shall attain the goal].
Then, they should follow the procedure for the installation of the Śrī Bhagavān according to the entire ritual previously described for the enjoyment [of the deity].
Then, when the Brahmins have finished eating, the officiant should release the bound initiation of the patron with the mantra "I release you" (*muñcāmi tvā*).
And one should perform protection with the armor-mantra.
Except for the raising of the archway, one should perform the ritual procedure prescribed for seven days every month.
For as long as a year, one should perform this rite daily; it is a practice that grants all desires.
O best of kings, I have thus declared to you this ritual for consecration.
It should be known as the remover of all sins, bestowing long life, and invincible.
Having performed the installation of the wielder of the Śārṅga bow according to this rite, a person—
One obtains all desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
Herbs, trees, and whatever else is used [as medicine], [are all derived from that].
For when established in that state, all of it is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O lord of men, those who even witness the consecration being performed, [attain merit].
Those devotees who rejoice [in this] are also men who have earned heaven.
It is eternally established according to the ritual prescribed by the Sātvata.
One who desires the eternal state should worship the Lord of the gods of gods.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Erecting the Arches," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 116 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now follows the procedure for the festival procession of the deities:
on whichever lunar day (tithi) is prescribed as the specific day for a particular deity, one should perform the procession on that very lunar day.
For one whose lunar day is not known, one should perform [the rite] on the full moon day.

For the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, all lunar days (tithis) are auspicious; indeed, he has no specific day of his own. Therefore, at the very outset, having constructed a temple for the deity white as nectar and beautifully decorated, one should perform the worship of Vināyaka on an auspicious day.
On the second day, there is the worship of the planets and constellations; on the third day, the worship of the Nāgas;
on the fourth day, the worship of the Pramathas; on the fifth day, the worship of Brāhmaṇas and the giving of gifts to the poor and the helpless; and on the sixth day, the ceremonial bathing.

There, having performed the great ablution, all the city-dwellers, dressed in pure white garments and with hands purified by sacred grass (*pavitraka*), should proceed toward the nearest dwelling near the city—situated by lakes, rivers, springs, or reservoirs—to the accompaniment of a great sound of musical instruments and auspicious dancing. From there, they should bring water-jars, either mounted upon the backs of elephants or covered with beautiful cloths, and enter [the temple].

Having caused the Śrī Bhagavān to enter, one should bathe him and worship him according to the procedure for enjoyment (*bhoga-vidhi*) and the ritual prescribed for consecration (*pratiṣṭhā*). One should honor the Śrī Bhagavān with dance, instrumental music, and song. Then, when the day of the procession (*yātrā*) arrives, having firmly placed the small image known as the *pratimā* in a chariot that is adorned with various kinds of garments, equipped with small bells, and decorated with jeweled garlands and banners, one should cause it to circumambulate the city on well-trained horses or by means of men.
The citizens, well-dressed and with bows in their hands, should perform a circumambulation in front of the gabled pavilion. Others should scatter garlands of flowers and offer hymns of praise.
Bards and reciters of auspicious verses should stand before them.
The king, accompanied by a fourfold army, should follow while playing musical instruments.
The city magistrate or the official in charge of that [district], mounted upon the back of an elephant, should follow the astrologer. He should observe the omens:
if the banner breaks without wind, one should predict the death of kings;
if the parasol breaks, there will be the destruction of the realm.
If there is even slight damage, the death of the king's wife occurs.
When the rope is cut, there is suffering for the fool.
In the case of the death of a tamed horse or a man, there is suffering for the country; in the case of the destruction of the Mātṛkā, there is suffering for the king's mother.

If the image breaks or falls, there will be the destruction of the world; if the entire gabled roof collapses, there will be the ruin of the kingdom along with its king; if musical instruments produce discordant sounds, there will be the arrival of a foreign army; if a cow or similar animal appears upon the banner, there will be fear of war;
and if it appears in a region where no one has asked for it, there will be fear of famine.
O children, whatever auspicious act one performs when the lunar mansion is auspicious becomes exactly of that same nature;
and for whichever person, on that day, such pleasure or pain occurs.
Such a year must also be known by him;
therefore, on that day, he should be well-fed, well-dressed, and highly distinguished among the citizens.

Having thus wandered through the city and identified Cihnāka, one should hold a great festival once the image has been installed. Starting from the second day, for as long as resources permit, one should daily provide wealth for the performances of actors, dancers, female dancers, wrestlers, magicians, and others.
During the performance, one should honor the audience with gifts such as garlands, betel, and ointments.

For the invisible beings who are spectators, one should scatter food offerings along with water, fruits, flowers, meat-cakes, fried cakes, and sweetmeats in the cardinal and intermediate directions of the stage and surrounding area.
One should utter: "May there be welfare for the spectators who have arrived.
And one should utter: "May the spectators who have arrived behold the future procession."
When an inauspicious sign arises, one should again properly undertake the journey according to this procedure in order to pacify it.
Whoever performs a pilgrimage to the abode of the gods according to this rite, [attains the fruit].
He obtains all his desires and goes to the world of Viṣṇu.
It bestows wealth, fame, and long life, and grants victory to kings.
The performance of the festival procession is proclaimed as that which brings benefit to the citizens.
For the sake of the satisfaction of the three Indras and for the welfare of the city.
O King, the people must perform the rites for the journey that bring victory.
It is declared to cause excessive rain and to destroy drought.
Furthermore, this act of pilgrimage to a temple of the deity should always be performed.
O King, every year, a king desiring victory [should perform this].

Thus ends the one hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "Description of the Rules for Pilgrimage," in the third section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. 117.
Vajra said:
Which specific form of Viṣṇu should a devotee worship, and with what desire?
Cut asunder this doubt of mine, for you indeed know everything. || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
One should worship the four-formed God, the bestower of all desires.
A man who desires the Dharma should always worship Aniruddha. ||2||
Likewise, one who desires wealth should worship the god Saṅkarṣaṇa.
O Indra among kings, even one who desires sensual pleasures should worship the Lord Pradyumna. ||3||
One who desires liberation should worship Vāsudeva, the Lord of the universe.
Likewise, O King, one who desires a son should worship Padmanābha. ||4||
Likewise, one who desires knowledge should worship the god Aśvaśiras.
But one whose desire for enjoyments has been fulfilled should worship the one who reclines upon enjoyments. ||5||
One who desires a stable position should worship [the deity] seated upon the coils of the serpent’s body.
A man desiring grain should always worship the god Matsya.
In the same way, one who desires freedom from disease should worship the deity Kūrma.
Or likewise Jñakāma, Haṃsa, Nṛsiṃha, or the all-pervading Vibhu. ||7||
Or, one who desires knowledge should worship either Vālmīki or Vyāsa.
Likewise, [he taught] Kapila for the sake of fully understanding the knowledge of Sāṃkhya.
One who desires prosperity should worship Varāha, the best among men and boars.
Likewise, one who desires victory in legal disputes, in battle, or in gambling [should worship] separately.
Likewise, one who desires the Dharma should worship both the Dharma and Brahmā.
One who desires the destruction of enemies should worship Mahādeva.
One should worship Rāma, the descendant of Bhṛgu, with the desire to fulfill one's vow.
Or rather, [he addressed] Rāma, the tiger among kings and son of Daśaratha.
O Great King, one who desires prosperity should worship Śrīsahāya.
Likewise, one who desires strength should worship the god Balabhadra.
To that very tiger among kings, for the successful accomplishment of agricultural works.
One should worship the God who grants all desires, who has assumed a form according to his will, because of his omnipotence and his bestowing of the fruits of all desires.
Free from desire, they worshipped the venerable Vāsudeva, the Lord of Gods, the ancient one.
That supreme place which exists is said to be the abode of the best of men, attained by their bodies according to their desire.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship for Various Desires," in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 118 ||
Vajra said:
Upon the occurrence of which action should one worship which particular body?
O great sage, tell me that by which one desiring the accomplishment of one's purpose may attain it.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On a sea voyage in a ship, one should worship the Lord Matsya.
Or likewise, O illustrious one, [one should offer] a boar when crossing a river.
A person should worship Aśvaśiras at the commencement of the study of the Vidyā.
Likewise, one should worship the god Trivikrama at the time of departure.
O King, when the time for marriage has arrived, one should worship Pradyumna.
And among all the conditioned phenomena (saṃskāra), one should worship Dattātreya. || 4 ||
At the commencement of a poetic work, however, one should pay homage to both Vālmīki and Vyāsa.
Likewise, during the consecration, one should worship both Mṛtyu and Vainya.
Necessarily, whether in legal disputes, in battle, or even in gambling, [one must act].
One should worship the divine Varāha at the commencement of agricultural work.
Or else, O Great King, [worship] the all-pervading Lord Saṅkarṣaṇa.

Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The entire world is indeed one; it is known as both Prakṛti and Puruṣa.
At the commencement of the bright fortnight of Caitra, fasting and with senses subdued, ||1||
One should worship Viṣṇu as the Supreme Person, whether on land or in water.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food. ||2||
A man should likewise recite the Pauruṣa Sūkta while remaining submerged within the water.
And likewise, a wise person should offer a handful of water to him as he passes away. ||3||
Likewise, O knower of dharma, O mighty-armed one, [he offered] flowers and fruits.
One should offer incense along with an oblation of food, and likewise recite that [mantra] according to one's ability.
Likewise, one should offer oblations with clarified butter and give gold to a twice-born man.
O Bhārgava, one should take food with milk at the time of night. || 5 ||
Having performed this for a year, remaining unwearied in his constant vow, [he attains the goal].
O Hero, by [observing this] for both fortnights, one is liberated from all sins.
Having attained grace from Vāsudeva—the Lord of all, the omnipresent, and the inconceivable—[he became free from fear].
From Lokeśvara, those perfected ones and renowned sages who go attain the state of liberation.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Pauruṣī Pratipad," in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Both the Puruṣa and Prakṛti are proclaimed to be the entire universe.
Thus, everything is proclaimed to be of the nature of Agni and Soma. ||1||
Vāsudeva and Lakṣmī—they alone are thus proclaimed.
And on the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having observed a fast and subdued his senses, ||2||
A person should worship the fire with the Pauruṣa Sūkta.
Those who offer perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food; (3)
And one should worship the goddess Lakṣmī, the bestower of boons, with water.
And with the Śrīsūkta, O knower of dharma, O lord of men, according to the proper rule.
One should give both gold and silver as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
A wise person should sustain his life with milk and ghee.
Having performed this vow for a year, he has fasted properly.
One is liberated from all sins and finds the means to liberation. || 5 ||
He obtains desires, or else various worlds, and the entire earth in its excellence.
He beheld forms both deformed and even most excellent, as well as supreme fame and preeminent sons.
Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Prakṛti and Puruṣa," in the third section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods, are celebrated as Nāsatyas.
O King, those two alone are proclaimed in the world as the lords of the sun and the stars.
Because they delight in traveling on horseback, the two Aśvins are so celebrated.
On the second day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having observed a fast and subdued his senses, || 2 ||
One who is self-restrained and pure should worship the two Aśvins, the physicians of the gods.
With perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food. || 3 ||
And having fashioned an image, a person should not worship one that is not real.
Then, one should especially offer a garland of lamps to those two during the night.
One should give both gold and silver as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
Closing both eyes, a person should meditate upon Viṣṇu.
He becomes possessed of blazing splendor and is born indeed with keen vision.
One should sustain one's life with curd mixed with ghee.
Having performed the Netra-vrata for twelve years, one shall become a renowned lord of the earth.
The destroyer of hosts of beautiful and lovely women, delighting in righteousness, he was the foremost among the best of kings.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirtieth chapter, titled "The Eye-Vow of Worship to the Nāsatyas," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara. || 130 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe this and another, the second [mantra], which grants all desires.
Having fasted upon which, a man obtains all his desired objects. || 1 ||
Having reached the second day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, a person—
At the end of the day, one should properly perform a bath in river water;
having drawn the orb of the crescent moon, one should worship it with white pigments.
With white flowers, fruits, and abundant quantities of excellent food.
Or with sugarcane, products of sugarcane, molasses, or salt.
At the end of the day, having worshipped the Lord of Gods and the Moon, ||4||
Having performed an oblation with clarified butter, one should eat at night while restraining one's speech.
Then, one should eat the green herb with oil only once. ||5||
Having duly observed this vow for a full year while remaining pure, a man—
One attains great good fortune and goes to the heavenly world. ||6||
O King, this is a purifier that destroys enemies, bestows good fortune, and removes disease.
O chief of the Yādava lineage, this vow has been proclaimed; it must be performed with diligence by a woman as well. ||7||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Second Day of the Waxing Moon," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O King, listen to me as I describe the second [tithi], Aśūnyaśayanā.
Having observed this fast, a woman never again falls into widowhood under any circumstances. || 1 ||
And a man never experiences separation from his wife.
That lunar day (tithi) on the second of the dark fortnight should be observed when it coincides with the Śravaṇa asterism.
Upon a well-spread bed, [one should worship] Viṣṇu and likewise the goddess Lakṣmī.
O Bhārgava, one should worship him with fruits, flowers, perfumes, and water-offerings (argha).
Then one should offer the food offering (naivedya), as well as a lamp and incense, according to one's capacity.
Then, having worshipped the Lord of Gods, one who is pure should mutter this mantra. ||4||
O bearer of the Śrīvatsa, O beloved of Śrī, O abode of Śrī, O Lord of Śrī, O Acyuta!
May my householder life not come to ruin; may it grant the fulfillment of dharma, artha, and kāma.
May the fires not perish; may the deities not perish.
May my ancestors not perish because of a separation between husband and wife caused by me.
O Lord, may you never be separated from prosperity, just as you are now.
Likewise, O Lord, may my connection with my wife not perish.
O Giver of Boons, may your bed never be empty of Lakṣmī, as it always is for you.
O Madhusūdana, let my bed likewise not be empty.
Having thus propitiated the Lord of Gods, one should eat at night while remaining restrained in speech.
And on the second day, one should indeed give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brāhmaṇa. ||9||
And when four months had passed while he lay upon his bed, O best of the twice-born.
O King, for three births, no destruction of his home shall occur.
And he is one whose bed is never empty, the accomplisher of dharma, action, and purpose.
A person becomes one whose sovereignty is unimpeded; there is no doubt in this matter. ||11||
Free from widowhood, fortunate, free from disease, devoted to her husband, dedicated to dharma, and virtuous.
Endowed with beauty and free from fear, such a woman shall be possessed of every virtue. ||12||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-second chapter, titled "The Narration of the Aśūnyaśayana-Dvitīyā Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the third day of the bright fortnight, having fasted and subdued his senses, he should [proceed].
One should draw three mandalas using separate colors for each.
A person should make the mandala white on the right side.
One should place red [color] in the middle and below, while white [is for] the north, specifically for Dhruva.
And among those mandalas, the three steps of Viṣṇu should be worshipped.
One should place the first foot on the ground and the second on the solar disc.
But the third, one who is restrained and pure, should worship in the god Dhruva.
Just as the marks of colors on a mandala, O twice-born one, are [adorned] with perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
The sacrificial mantra "tad viṣṇoḥ param" is thus prescribed.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, for a woman or a Śūdra, [the mantra] is "to Trivikrama."
One should offer into the fire unbroken grains, sesame seeds, and clarified butter—these three combined.
One should give copper, silver, and gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) according to one's ability.
And one should feed the most excellent Brahmin a meal consisting of the three sweets.
And one should sustain one's life for that day with the products of three cows.
Having performed this for three years, at the conclusion of the vow, one should indeed [offer] a three-year-old [animal].
But by giving a cow to a Brāhmaṇa, one shall obtain all desires.
On the earth, as well as in the atmosphere and in heaven, O best of men.
Her movement becomes unimpeded, O slayer of enemies.
For three thousand years, Sarvaga remained without moving.
He relinquishes that which is mental, vocal, and indeed physical. || 3.133.10 ||
O fortunate one, by that [means], a person is born free from all evil.
He becomes wealthy in his family, endowed with beauty and riches;
free from disease, he achieves all his goals and accomplishes the three aims of human life.
Having performed [this] for twelve years, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
There too, he eternally beheld the boon-granting, most excellent, ancient Person, who has Lakṣmī as his companion.
He beholds the Lord, who is unfailing, inconceivable, eternal, and the cause of the destruction of suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Trivikrama Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall tell you the second; listen to the Traivikrama vow.
The first quarter is indeed the earth, and the next is the intermediate space (antarikṣa). || 1 ||
And the third [world] of the god of gods, the wielder of the discus, is to be known as heaven.
Vahni is remembered as the lord of the earth (bhuvaḥ), and likewise the lord of the intermediate space (antarikṣa) beyond that.
Likewise, Sūrya is the lord of heaven, and that is the triple step of Viṣṇu.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, having observed a fast and subdued his senses, [he should worship].
Having bathed in well-water at dawn, a person should worship the fire.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food. || 4 ||
Then, having bathed in the river water when the sun had reached its meridian, [he performed his rites].
Having performed the worship of Vāyu, one should give barley meal (saktu) to a twice-born man.
And having bathed in the waters of a lake, one should worship the Sun in the evening.
And thereafter, being pure and restrained in speech, he should eat sacrificial food at night.
Thus, O King, having observed the vow for a year without sloth, he—
Having completed it in the month of Vaiśākha, one should give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
Copper, silver, and gold—these three metals, O Yādava.
A pair of garments with a turban, and also three other robes.
A pair of sandals, a yoke, and an umbrella—these three [should be offered] with devotion.
Having performed this Traivikrama vow for one year, a man [attains the fruit].
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
By means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and garlanded with networks of tiny bells.
With the lutes, drums, and other instruments played by the hosts of the king of gods;
When the one whose banner is Garuḍa is pleased, there is indeed food, long life, and sons.
O best among the upholders of Dharma, those three steps of his who had pervaded the three worlds—
O hero among men, by worshipping him, people obtain their desires and attain their desired destination.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fourth chapter, titled "The Narration of the Second Traivikrama Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O illustrious one, the Traivikrama vow has been explained to you.
O tiger among kings, listen as I describe the third to you. || 1 ||
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, a man who has properly observed a fast, [should proceed].
One should perform the worship of Bhuvana with incense, garlands, and unguents.
One should give lamps, various kinds of food, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
Bowlfuls filled with seeds and containing gold, according to one's ability.
Thus, the worship of the intermediate space is indeed prescribed as Āṣāḍhā.
In that case, a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consisting of a pair of garments should be given to the twice-born.
Furthermore, the worship of the Sun should be performed in the month of Śrāvaṇa, just as previously described.
One should cause an umbrella, a pair of sandals, and a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to be given there.
In this manner, after three months, the first breaking of the fast shall take place here.
And another [period] of three months, and then again another three months.
Then, O sinless one, after three months and another year, he [attained] this other [state].
The fourfold completion of the dharmas of one who is constant in the Dharma is to be understood. || 7 ||
Having performed the first breaking of the fast, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
O King, likewise, on the second day of breaking the fast, there is the fruit of an Atirātra sacrifice.
On the third breaking of the fast, the wise man shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice.
It is declared that at the fourth breaking of the fast, one obtains the fruit that results from the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By means of a celestial chariot, sun-colored and garlanded with networks of tiny bells.
[He traveled] by means of a divine vehicle yoked with swans, accompanied by the sounds of lutes, drums, and other instruments.
By that beautiful lover, who was enriched by a multitude of excellent apsarases.
He goes wherever he desires for a long time, without a doubt. || 11 ||
Having attained birth in the human state, one should achieve the state of the "threefold purity."
Knowledge, birth, and likewise action—no deliberation need be made regarding these. || 12 ||
And the three steps of that peerless Trivikrama, the Lord of the moving and the unmoving.
For one who worships him, all desires become fulfilled; there is indeed no doubt in this matter. || 13 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Third Traivikrama Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 135 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Yādava, I shall indeed describe the means of propitiating that deity.
O lord of men, learn that [account] of Viṣṇu, whose valor is immeasurable. || 1 ||
The Lord Hari, who possesses the forms of wind, sun, and moon, is the embodiment of the triple manifestation.
In this Jagatī [meter], the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is proclaimed as the moon and the sun. || 2 ||
And the Blessed One, Vāyu, is likewise the support of all and omnipresent.
This entire world, both moving and unmoving, consists of the five elements.
These two, the earth and likewise the sky, are the foundational supports.
Know, O knower of dharma, that the three elements are likewise always to be established [within it]. || 4 ||
The moon, the sun, and the wind, O twice-born one, belong to the entire world.
This world is pervaded by the elements through the relationship of container and contained.
And indeed, there is nothing whatsoever in this world that is devoid of the primary elements.
Therefore, O best of the Yadavas, this world is indeed pervaded by living beings.
Know Brahmā, and the earth, and the sky immediately following that.
Within the egg reside the gods: Vāyu, Arka, and Tuhiṇāṃśu.
They protect the entire world, including its gods, asuras, and humans.
In that very same way, all those remaining within the cosmic egg protect the three worlds.
In the very same way, those residing in the body protect the bodies of embodied beings.
By way of wind, bile, and phlegm, they are the winds, the sun, and the cool-rayed moon.
Just as the cosmic egg is proclaimed to be the support of the world, so too [is this].
Likewise, it is said that within the body of embodied beings, she resides as the skin.
In both the cosmic egg and the body of the embodied being, space is perceived in both cases.
Their bodies were like the cosmic egg; they were the wind, the sun, and the cool-rayed moon.
O protector of the earth, they maintain [the body] by means of the portions of wind, bile, and phlegm.
The body consists of wind, sun, and moon; therefore, Viṣṇu is the bearer of the three forms.
O Bhārgava, listen as I explain how his worship should be performed according to the rules.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Jyeṣṭha, a pure man shall remain without food.
One should perform the worship of the Trimūrti on the second lunar day according to the prescribed rite.
Having bathed in pure waters mixed with those from wells, rivers, and tanks, one becomes purified. || 13 ||
At dawn, one should worship Vāyu on a clean, auspicious spot that has been smeared with unguents.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food offerings. || 14 ||
One should perform the fire sacrifice (homa) with the primary grains, barley, and should give a garment to a twice-born man.
At midday, one should worship the Fire and likewise the Sun without weariness.
One should offer sesame seeds into the fire and give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
At the time of sunset, one should worship the moon in the water. || 15 ||
One should perform the oblation with clarified butter; silver is prescribed as the sacrificial fee.
Then that man, knower of dharma, should eat at night, avoiding oil.
Having performed this vow for a full year without sloth, [he attains his goal].
He attains the heavenly world for a thousand years. || 18 ||
Having attained human birth, he then becomes a king in a remote forest retreat.
Having observed the vow, O great king, for a full three years. || 19 ||
For five thousand years, he is honored in the heavenly world.
And having attained human birth, he becomes a righteous king.
A hero, a sovereign of a circle of kings, a warrior who strikes fear into the armies of enemy forces.
Free from disease, handsome, fortunate, and beloved by the people. || 21 ||
Having observed this unsurpassed vow for twelve years.
Then, at the conclusion of the vow, one should feed a thousand Brahmins.
One should offer food with the three sweets as a drink, and give a sacrificial fee according to one's ability.
Then, the observer of the vow attains heaven for a hundred years.
Then, having attained human birth, he becomes a king, a ruler of the earth.
The powerful Dharmarāja, beloved by the people, possesses a blazing discus. || 24 ||
Having attained another birth, he shall thereafter obtain the status of a Brahmin.
Then, having attained the status of a Brahmin, he finds the means to liberation. || 25 ||
O Viṣṇu of great majesty, I have thus described to you this means of propitiating the one who possesses the three bodies.
O Foremost of the World, he by whom you have been propitiated shall obtain his desired wishes, even if they be known only to the wise. || 26 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrīviṣṇu-trimūrti Vrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Henceforth, I shall describe to you the Viṣṇumūrti vow.
O Yādava, the form of the God of gods is twofold.
One is Ghorā and the other is Śivā; Ghorā becomes the purifying fire.
And Śiva is the lord of the waters, since the world consists of the nature of Agni and Soma.
The fierce [deities] are specified as being of two kinds, and the gentle ones are likewise of two kinds.
The fierce ones are Vahni and Sūrya; the gentle ones are Soma and Jaleśvara. || 3 ||
And their worship should be performed in due order, beginning from that very moment.
Then, O best of the twice-born, beginning from the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, ||4||
On the first day, the king, being supremely pure, should worship the Sun.
On the second day likewise [worship] Vahni, and on the third day Jalādhipa.
And on the fourth day, O best of men, he should worship the Moon according to the prescribed rule.
But having fashioned their forms, the wise one should worship them. ||6||
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
On the first day, one should perform a bath with *vacā* and *haridrā*.
O tiger among the Yadus, on the second day, an auspicious bath with *āmalaka* fruits is performed.
And on the third day with priyaṅgu seeds, and on the fourth with white mustard seeds. || 8 ||
And with wheat, sesame, grain, and barley, [he should worship] day by day in sequence.
O knower of dharma, a fire sacrifice (homa) must be performed; now hear also about the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
Saffron, red cloth, sandalwood, and a parasol.
And here, one should sustain one's life every day with milk.
O best of men, having performed this vow for one full year, it is complete.
One who has fulfilled all desires enjoys the fruit of being established in sacrifice.
And he goes to the heavenly world by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, he is born into a great family.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, a lord of the earth, and a conqueror of the host of enemies.
Established in righteousness, devoted to truth, disciplined, with senses conquered, he was beloved by all people. ||13||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Caturmūrti Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O best of messengers, [you who are like] Śakra, Kīnāśa, Varuṇa, and Dhanādhyakṣa. || 1 ||
Vāsudeva, the Lord of the Universe, is declared to be fourfold in nature.
Having fashioned their forms, however, the wise person should worship them. || 2 ||
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship the Lord of the Thirty-three Gods.
On the second day [he worships] the god Yama, and on the third, the Lord of Waters.
On the fourth day, one should perform a daily bath for the sake of the Lord of Wealth (Dhanādhyakṣa).
Having reached the region of the river, Devadṛś proceeded day by day in due order.
The oblation (homa) should be performed with barley, sesame seeds, likewise with clarified butter, and with sesame and rice.
Red, yellow, black, and white are the garments according to the sequence of the days.
Having performed this auspicious vow for a full year, a man—
One attains the world of the gods for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras endures.
Having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease, a lord of the earth, and a conqueror of the host of his enemies.
Delightful to people and fortunate by nature, he further attains the state of a Brahmin. || 7 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Caturmūrti Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Jvara within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
Viṣṇu, the earth, the sky, and Brahmā are his fourfold form. || 1 ||
Having fashioned their forms out of clay, one should then worship them.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food. ||2||
On the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship the god Viṣṇu.
O knower of dharma, [I remember] the earth and you, my grandfather, in the second and subsequent [kalpas].
The entire other ritual procedure shall be as previously stated in the vow.
Having performed this vow, a man shall attain the heavenly world.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, devoted to the Dharma, and endowed with wealth.
Endowed with wealth, beauty, and happiness, he was beloved by the people and had conquered all opposing factions.

Thus ends the one hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Third Fourfold Form," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another observance, the vow of the four forms.
O joy of the Yadus, [I possess] strength, knowledge, sovereignty, and power. || 1 ||
The fourfold form of that God of gods is renowned.
That which has been described as the nature of Dharma is indeed the very same as that of power.
O King, you have thus described to me the form of that knowledge as Narasiṃha.
Furthermore, O King, the sovereign power in the form of Rudra has been described to you by me.
The god Śaktivarāha is said to be the slayer of Madhu.
Thus has this been proclaimed from the mouth of you who bear four forms.
Its eastern face should be that of Balabhadra, and its [other] face that of Vāsudeva.
They know the southern face to be the deity Saṃkarṣaṇa, who is wisdom.
The western face is that of Īśvara; it is fierce and likewise the destroyer of sins.
The northern face, Varāha, is proclaimed to be Aniruddha.
Having fasted for three nights in the month of Caitra, one should first worship the face [of the deity].
Likewise, one should worship the one facing south during the month of Vaiśākha.
In Jyeṣṭha, the western face [is worshipped], and likewise in Āṣāḍha, the northern.
In the month of Caitra, one should give articles useful for the household to a twice-born man.
O best of the Yādavas, that which is useful for battle should indeed be given in the month of Vaiśākha. ||8||
That which is useful for sacrifice should be given to the eldest member of the twice-born caste;
likewise, that which is useful for sacrifice should be given in the month of Āṣāḍha as well.
Having performed this vow for a full four months, a man—
It is the settled conclusion that this occurs when the first meal-break has arrived.
Having performed this first fast-breaking meal, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Having enjoyed heaven for ten thousand years as described, [he returns].
And during the watches beginning with Saumya (the third), the second breaking of the fast shall take place.
Having performed the second breaking of the fast, one who is pure should feed the Brahmins.
The food consists primarily of cow's milk products, combined with grapes and sugar.
And when the third feeding of the twice-born has arrived, he attains the same world as the God.
And having enjoyed the worlds of heaven and Indra for the duration thus stated, he shall be happy, desiring all prosperity. || 13 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Four-Form Vow," in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
This should be performed by a man who is highly wise and desires knowledge. || 1 ||
Having performed his external ablutions and having completed the worship of the Ṛgveda, the man—
One should daily listen to the Ṛgveda for the duration of a month, remaining free from sloth.
O knower of dharma, from the month of Caitra onwards, that twice-born man shall always eat only at night.
For it was heard by that twice-born man on the final day of his elder brother's life.
A pair of garments, gold, and likewise a milch cow.
A bell-metal vessel filled with clarified butter, along with gold, constitutes the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).
The vow of the Yajurveda should take place during the months beginning with Āṣāḍha.
In the months beginning with Āśvina, there shall be the vow of the Sāmaveda.
Likewise, that which is called the Sarvavrata is prescribed for the months beginning with Pauṣa.
In all cases, everything prescribed in the vows of the Ṛgveda must be performed.
Having performed the worship of Vāsudeva, who is the soul of the Vedas, for twelve years, a man...
He who has reached that distinguished world of Viṣṇu goes to the world of Viṣṇu and abandons all suffering.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "Vedavrata," in the fifth section on the Fourfold Form, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 141 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, that of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha).
But for all souls, worship should be performed just as it is for the Teacher of the World.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, having fasted and subdued his senses, || 1 ||
On the fourth day, having performed the auspicious worship of Vāsudeva, [one should proceed].
One should give gold as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to a Brahmin who is a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin).
Likewise, having worshipped the god Saṅkarṣaṇa, the teacher of the world.
In the month of Vaiśākha, one should give a well-prepared bed to a householder.
Having worshipped the god Pradyumna according to the prescribed rites in the month of Jyeṣṭha.
Likewise, one should give fruits, roots, and products of the cow to one who dwells in the forest.
Likewise, having worshipped Aniruddha, the Teacher of the World, in the month of Āṣāḍha;
And one should give a gourd vessel to a twice-born man established in yoga.
Thus has the breaking of the fast been described; one who performs it is glorified in the heavenly world.
When the second fast-breaking meal arrives, one is glorified in the world of Śakra.
Then, upon the arrival of the third fast-breaking meal, he attains the same world as Keśava.
Thus, this supreme vow called Āśrama, which destroys all impurities, has been described by me to you.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vows of the Āśramas," in the section on the Fourfold Form within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 142 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
Hari is said to be fourfold in nature, and there are likewise four sacrificial fires.

Having observed a fast on the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna.
Having worshipped Vāsudeva, the fourfold self, with unwearied devotion.
To that best of the twice-born, one should give sixteen prasthas of sesame seeds.
Gold for gold, clothing, and even a balance of ghee.
Having thus performed this vow for a year without weariness, ||4||
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
And he goes to the heavenly world by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
A human being will possess radiant splendor, have a blazing digestive fire, and be beloved by women.
He conquers his enemies in battle and likewise becomes possessed of wealth.
Those four fires which have been designated are indeed Vāsudeva himself, described as being fourfold.
He who would honor a Brāhmaṇa who maintains the sacred fires—by him the gods themselves are honored.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Agni-vow," in the seventh section on the Fourfold Form, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
On the first day at the commencement of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform worship.
The twice-born man has performed all that is prescribed with white perfumes, garlands, and so forth.
On the second day, one should likewise worship Tretā with blood.
On the third day, the wise man should worship Dvāpara with that which has been drunk.
On the fourth day, one should worship the Tiṣya-yuga with Kṛṣṇa.
With white mustard seeds, saffron, and likewise with turmeric.
In that very manner, one should perform the *āmalaka* bath according to the sequence of days.
Likewise, one should offer oblations with white mustard seeds, unbroken grains, sesame seeds, and ghee.
Likewise, o Yādava, pearls, diamonds, and rubies [are produced]. || 5 ||
Likewise, one should give sapphire to the Brahmins day by day.
One should indeed sustain one's life with milk alone every single day.
Having observed this single vow for one year, he rejoices on the back of the celestial realm for a cycle of four yugas.
Having fully worshipped the God known as Yugamūrti, he rules the entire earth through the four ages.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vows of the Four Yugas," in the eighth section on the Four Forms (*caturmūrti-kalpa*), within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra in the third part of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other observance, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O Yādava, this occurs constantly during the four months beginning with Śrāvaṇa.
One should worship the full jars marked with the signs of the four oceans.
The wise should know Hari as fourfold in nature, having the ocean as his essence.
O Yādava, one should always perform one's bath in the waters of rivers.
And one should perform the fire sacrifice every day with cow's milk.
One should present those jars to the Brahmins every day.
O knower of dharma, [he should offer] these along with sacrificial gifts, with devotion and according to his capacity.
And one should always perform the consumption [of food] at night, avoiding oil entirely.
On the final day of the month of Kārttika, having fed the most excellent of the twice-born,
And by giving a cow to a Brahmin, one is glorified in the vault of heaven.
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled. ||5||
Having attained human birth, one becomes a lord of the earth after enjoying the world girdled by the oceans.
In that case as well, the king becomes devoted to righteousness, free from disease, and endowed with strength.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sāgara-vrata," in the section on the Four Forms of Viṣṇu within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
Garuḍa is the vehicle of Vāsudeva, and Tāla is that of Saṅkarṣaṇa.
Likewise, the emblem of Pradyumna is a crocodile with its mouth wide open.
