Yellow, blue, white, and red, O delighter of the Yadus.
But for them, their dwelling has been described; such a banner is likewise desired. ||3||
Whatever is the emblem of whichever deity, that is proclaimed as its very self (ātman).
Whatever kind of banner one has, such is one's garment. || 4 ||
In the month of Caitra, however, a person should worship Garuḍa every day.
The twice-born [should worship] with yellow perfumes, food offerings, garlands, garments, and so forth. ||5||
And likewise, in the month of Vaiśākha, one should always worship Tāla.
The twice-born [should worship] with blue perfumes, food offerings, garlands, garments, and so forth. ||6||
One should worship the god Ṛṣya according to the prescribed rite during the month of Āṣāḍha.
With blood, as well as perfumes, food offerings, garlands, garments, and so forth, the twice-born should likewise perform an external bath; thereafter, he should perform the worship of the fire.
And one who knows the Dharma should always likewise perform the satiation of Brahmins.
One should conduct one's livelihood in such a way that it is free from oil, as has been prescribed.
Likewise, he should sleep on the ground and remain a celibate student.
One should thus perform this vow constantly for four months.
One should honor the Brahmins according to one's ability on the final day of the month of Āṣāḍha.
O knower of dharma, one should give garments, wealth, and sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the brahmins.
O King, by performing this single fast-breaking meal, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Having performed the second breaking of the fast, one is honored in the world of Śakra.
Having performed the third breaking of the fast, one is glorified in the world of Brahmā.
Having performed six fasts, one is glorified in the world of Rudra.
Having performed twelve pāraṇas, one attains the world of Viṣṇu.
O foremost of Bhārgava’s lineage, having observed the Dhvaja-vow for twelve years, a man [attains his goal].
He attains union with the divine Janārdana, Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord. || 14 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dhvaja-vrata," in the Caturmūrti-kalpa of the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. 146.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now declare to you this other vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
And likewise Īśāna, Vahni, Virūpākṣa, and Samīraṇa. || 1 ||
O tiger among the Yadus, this fourfold manifestation of the divine form is to be known.
Having fashioned their forms, the wise man should worship them.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food.
In the bright fortnight of Caitra, O fortunate one, starting from the first day (pratipad) in due order.
One should perform the ritual bath with earth, cow’s urine, salt, and the essence of lotus stalks.
The oblation should likewise be performed with curd, sesame seeds, barley, and ghee.
Camphor and saffron, as well as agallochum and sandalwood.
O King, it should likewise be given to Brahmins according to the sequence of the days.
Likewise, for three days, one should eat only what is obtained unasked in the morning and evening.
Likewise, O best of men, one should eat for one day while observing celibacy.
Having thus performed the vow for one year, O best of men, [he attained his goal].
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled. || 7 ||
Having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease, a lord of the earth, and a conqueror of the faction of his enemies.
In another birth, he shall become a preeminent and chief among the twice-born, devoted to the Vedas and a performer of many sacrifices. ||8||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Divine Form," in the section on the Fourfold Form, within the Dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the Third Part of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 147 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
The fourfold self is proclaimed as the conch, the discus, the mace, and the lotus. || 1 ||
Vāsudeva is remembered as the conch, and Saṃkarṣaṇa likewise as the discus.
Pradyumna holds a mace and a lotus, and Aniruddha is the teacher of the world. ||2||
During the months beginning with Śrāvaṇa, one who eats only once a day should perform his ablutions outdoors.
One should perform their worship, month by month, in due order.
With perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food.
Then, at the end of the month of Kārttika, when the vow was likewise completed, ||4||
One should feed the Brahmins with devotion and give them a sacrificial fee according to one's capacity.
And likewise a bronze vessel containing ghee and gold. ||5||
Having observed the vow for four months, one attains the world of the Lord of the Thirty-three.
Having thus attained human birth here, he subsequently becomes a hero and a lord of the earth in this world. ||6||

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Weapon Vow," in the section on the Caturmūrti Vow within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now proclaim this other vow of yours, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
Having fasted for three nights, one should properly [perform this] on the day of the equinox in the spring season.
Having performed worship of Vāsudeva according to one's ability, O slayer of enemies.
Then, for three months, one should constantly worship Vāsudeva.
And for those three months, the wise one should subsist on fruit alone.
Then, having reached the autumn month, he arrived at the equinoctial day, O knower of dharma.
Having fasted for three nights and bathed, one should worship the beloved Pradyumna.
Having performed the fire sacrifice (homa), one should then eat after giving gifts according to one's ability.
But one should maintain one's life-sustenance with barley-gruel alone, O Mahāmati.
Having reached the conclusion of the vow on the equinoctial day of spring.
One should feed a Brahmin according to one's ability and give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the learned Brahmins.
Gold, silver, clothing, and a cow, O delighter of the Yadavas.
Having performed this vow, which is dear to Hari, for one year, it is called the "Vrata."
One attains the heavenly world for a long time, without a doubt.
From there, the twice-born attains the worlds of the Aśvins, and from there, the world of the Vasus.
And likewise for all the gods and the Aṅgirases, O twice-born one.
Then [the lineage] of the Rudras, the Sādhyas, the Bhṛgus, and likewise that of Savitṛ.
O knower of dharma, you are likewise the foremost among the Maruts and the cool-rayed moon.
And he attains the world of the gods, moving through the air at will like a bird.
He attains the world of Agni, as well as that of Śakra, the god, and likewise of Hara.
Having reached the world of the Grandfather (Brahmā), that person then proceeds to the realm of Viṣṇu.

Thus ends the one hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit-Eating Vow, the Vow Dear to Hari," within the *Caturmūrtivratakalpa* of the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you another vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O King, in that very auspicious vow previously described by me. ||1||
The wise person should perform worship of the infinite Viṣṇu in his own abode.
Having performed the worship of that [deity], as well as of the Earth, the Sky, and Brahmā; || 2 ||
One who has conquered the senses should perform [the rites] on the second day and subsequent days in the prescribed manner.
On the first day, the wise man should worship Ananta according to the prescribed ritual.
Having performed this vow for a full year, a man [should then proceed].
One attains the world of Viṣṇu for as long as the fourteen Indras endure.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, with senses conquered, devoted to truth, and disciplined.
Endowed with wealth, beauty, and happiness, he was beloved by the people and dear to women. || 5 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of Ananta," in the section on the Four Forms within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third part of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other vow, the Caturmūrti-vrata.
O King, all the hosts of gods were born from a portion of Vāsudeva.
By that superior portion, the Asuras were likewise produced as their destined counterparts.
And even there, Hari is traditionally remembered as being fourfold in his predominant aspects. || 2 ||
Nara, Nārāyaṇa, the horse, and the powerful Haṃsa.
The horse is known as Hari, and the swan is celebrated as Kṛṣṇa. || 3 ||
O Yādava, Hari, whose nature is fourfold, was born in the house of Dharma.
Likewise, among the Ādityas, he is joined with those known as Mitra and Varuṇa.
Know that those two alone, Hari and Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava, are the ones to be propitiated.
But among the Ādityas, Śakra and Viṣṇu, the two best of gods, were joined [to him].
Those very same Nara and Nārāyaṇa appeared once again among those who have attained perfection and those still seeking it.
On the fourth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should worship while observing a fast.
O lord of men, [worship] the Lord of Gods, who is fourfold in nature, according to your financial capacity.
Having performed this vow for a full twelve years, a man—
He does not fall into an evil rebirth and finds the means to liberation. ||7||
Then, having attained the state of partlessness, it reaches equality with the Supreme Person.
The Lord of All, of incomparable power, liberated from suffering, and the protector of the world. || 8 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Śrī Viṣṇu Vrata," within the Caturmūrti Vrata section of the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra in the third book of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
The vow of the four forms is completed.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Hereafter, I shall describe the worship of the fivefold form (Pañcamūrti).
Earth, water, fire, air, and space as well. || 1 ||
The five forms of the divine Vāsudeva have been described.
But on the fifth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, the wise man, having reached that time, [should act]. || 2 ||
Fasting, one should worship the fivefold Lord Hari.
The five mandalas should be executed separately with five different colors.
O Lord of the Earth, a circular mandala of white color should be prepared.
Likewise, the white [lotus] is associated with Varuṇa, while the red is held to belong to Agni.
That which is yellow belongs to Vāyu, and that which is black has Ākāśa as its deity.
One should worship them individually with perfumes and flowers of corresponding colors.
And with incense, lamps, and other offerings according to one's ability and as they may be obtained, O subduer of enemies.
With barley, or with other grains, sesame seeds, mustard seeds, and ghee. || 6 ||
One should offer oblations with the five mixed substances for all [the deities] individually.
Then, O King, either with their characteristic marks, or with mantras, or indeed by their names.
Having offered oblations preceded by the syllable *oṃ*, one should honor the Brahmins according to one's ability.
Having performed it in this manner for a year, then, when the year was complete...
Having given garments to the brahmins that were as bright as the color of the gods.
Now, he who performs this fivefold vow of the great elements (mahābhūta-vrata) [attains success].
One obtains, in due order, the five sacrifices that have been enumerated.
He is honored in the heavenly world for many thousands of years.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, endowed with strength, and a destroyer of hosts of enemies.
Endowed with learning, beauty, and virtue, he was beloved by the people and dear to women.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Five Forms and the Five Great Elements," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
I shall now describe to you this other observance, the vow of the five forms.
The year is known as Vahni, and likewise Parivatsara is Arka. || 1 ||
Iḍā was preceded by that, and Prajāpati followed after Soma.
And prior to that, the Great Lord Maheśvara, the God of gods, was likewise proclaimed. || 2 ||
For them, the arrangement of the mandala is performed in the same manner as previously described.
Sacrifice and worship should be performed, and likewise, the fire-oblation (homa) should be performed in that same manner.
With sesame, rice, barley, ghee, and white mustard seeds;
Or else, one should worship daily in sequence by means of their characteristic marks, mantras, or names.
Likewise, one should remain eating only at night for five days, as previously described.
One should undertake this vow during the year known as Saṃvatsara.
O Yadava, at the conclusion of the vow, five measures of gold must be given as a gift.
O Yādava, that which is to be given to those who know the four Vedas must be given according to the division of their Vedic branches.
Each one should be given as the fifth; likewise, it should be for one who knows the proper time.
For this vow which has been described by me to you yields the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
Moving through the air at will, he attains whatever world he desires.
"O knower of dharma, nothing has been achieved by him, even though he is being honored by gods and asuras."
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease and endowed with excellence of complexion, beauty, and strength.
The king, by whose majesty the hosts of enemies were bowed down, was like a supreme deity who had performed many sacrifices.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "Description of the Fruit of the Horse-Sacrifice in the Annual Worship within the Ritual of the Five Vows," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim to you this vow known as the Śrī-vrata.
On the third day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should perform a bath preceded by an oil massage.
Having dressed in white garments, O King, and adorned with white garlands and unguents, he should proceed.
He should subsist on a diet of ghee and boiled rice, and he should sleep upon the ground for that night.
And on the fourth day, one should likewise perform a bath by going outside.
And especially at a lotus pond; then, pure and wearing white garments, [he should proceed].
One should worship Lakṣmī in a lotus, whether it be artificial or natural.
And then, with white perfumes and garlands, as well as a lamp of ghee.
And with curd, fine rice, ginger, and jaggery.
With sugarcane, products of sugarcane, and abundant salt.
And according to one's own power, O Great King, by means of abundant sacrificial rites.
Then, being pure, one should offer lotuses into the fire while reciting the Śrīsūkta.
And in the absence of those, bilva fruits; and in the absence of those, likewise clarified butter.
One should cause the Brahmins to consume food consisting mostly of cow's milk products and abundant ghee. || 7 ||
And one should give a gold māṣaka as a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brāhmaṇas.
Then, without food, he should sleep according to the rule in a clean place.
Then, having reached the fifth day, in the forenoon, she entered the lotus pond in the water.
Having bathed, one should perform worship as before; likewise, [the Lord] is pleased.
Furthermore, one should first give a gold māṣaka to the twice-born.
Then, immediately thereafter, one should consume either lotus seeds or bilva fruits.
Then, the best of men, restraining his speech, should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya).
For this year he should eat the wood-apple fruit, and immediately thereafter [he may eat other food].
Having performed this vow for one year, O best of kings.
One obtains the vast fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
One should perform this vow even without the gift of gold. || 12 ||
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give a māsaka coin; one shall obtain the fruit of the Vajapeya sacrifice.
Having performed worship while observing a fast on the fifth day of the bright fortnight, || 13 ||
He constantly attains unsurpassed prosperity through the goddess Śrī.
One attains supreme strength, as well as beauty and health;
she is the foremost in the world, the giver of boons, the most excellent, the radiant one, all-pervading, O lord of men.
He who, endowed with faith, worships here, obtains all his desires at all times.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Lakṣmī-vrata," in the section on the Ritual of the Five Forms within the Dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third part of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, furthermore, I shall proclaim to you the vow of the five forms.
O mighty-armed one, [he holds] the conch, the discus, the mace, the lotus, and the earth.
Having prepared mandalas with perfumes, one should worship them five by five.
O King, beginning from the end of the bright fortnight of Caitra, starting from the fifth day.
Having fasted, bathed outside, and being pure, he should likewise wear white garments.
With perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and offerings of food. ||3||
Having performed the worship of all [the deities], one should offer oblations into the fire.
Likewise, ghee [should be offered] with the names of all the gods.
And on that occasion, one should feed the Brahmins a meal of sweet food.
Having performed this for a year, at the conclusion of the vow, [one should offer] five garments.
One who gives [a gift] to a knower of the Pañcarātra obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
And by [offering] five colors, O Indra among kings, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice. || 6 ||
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, endowed with strength, devoted to dharma, and disciplined.
Endowed with wealth, beauty, and happiness, he may even become a sovereign king of kings or a lord of men.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vows Concerning the Weapons and Other Implements" within the *Pañcamūrtivrata*, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe to you the worship of the sixfold form.
One should worship [him] constantly during the two months of spring, Madhu and Mādhava. || 1 ||
One should worship with fruits, flowers, and decoctions during every summer season.
O Great King, [he spoke] to him with sweet words, beneficial during the rainy season.
One should always worship Śarad with sour substances and Lavaṇa with salt.
And with *baṭuka* in the winter, and likewise with *tikta* in the cool season. ||3||
Likewise, he should subsist on food at night and avoid the flavors prescribed for the seasons.
And here one should feed the Brahmins a meal of savory juices as prescribed for the season.
Having observed this most purifying vow for one year, he performed it.
One obtains the merit of the horse sacrifice and attains the royal consecration. ||5||
One attains all desires; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
O best of men, one obtains the imperishable fruit of this vow.
Then, beginning from the sixth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, one who thus worships throughout the six seasons—
But one who has observed the fast as prescribed shall obtain this fruit in its entirety; thus it has been said. || 7 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Six Forms," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Henceforth, I shall describe to you the vow of the seven forms.
Then, beginning from the month of Caitra, starting from the first lunar day (pratipad) in due order. || 1 ||
For the Subhāsvaras, the Barhiṣads, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas;
And those who eat raw flesh, those who are invited, those who drink clarified butter, and those who are well-timed. || 2 ||
One should worship it every day, O King, with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
One should prepare kṛsara as the food offering and offer sesame seeds into the fire as oblations.
One should feed the Brahmins krisara and give sesame seeds as a sacrificial fee.
Likewise, O lord of men, he should remain eating only at night, subsisting on sacrificial food (haviṣya).
O best of men, having performed this vow for one year, [he attained his goal].
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a pala of silver to a brahmin.
By the performance of this vow, one shall attain the world of the Sun.
Being honored by the thirty gods, he became a bird capable of moving at will.
O lord of men, by performing this for an entire year, a person attains liberation from saṃsāra.
Having performed [this] for twelve years in that manner, one shall become a lord of the earth upon attaining human birth. ||7||

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow for the Ancestors Beginning with Subhāsura," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vyāsa within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 157 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, beginning from the month of Caitra, on each day of the dark fortnight, [one should practice].
One should perform the worship of the netherworld (pātāla) in sequence, beginning from the first lunar day (pratipad).
Likewise, the earth has golden soil, while Pātāla has blue clay.
[One should prepare] red earth, yellow earth, and also white and black clay. ||2||
With gold, perfumes, garlands, and abundant offerings of food.
By the offering of ghee lamps and by the satiation of the fire, || 3 ||
Having thus observed the vow of eating only at night for one year, he then—
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should offer a lamp in the houses of the twice-born.
But he, O king of kings, [offered] garments according to their respective colors.
Having performed this vow, a man shall become a sovereign lord among men. ||5||
Divine maidens obtain husbands by the hundreds of thousands.
They delight you, O Great King, just as the Iḍaviḍa bird does.
And having reached the world of men in due time, he shall become a king who crushes the hosts of his enemies.
Endowed with strength, beauty, and wealth, he was of great intelligence and the foremost in all the world.
Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of Vows for the Netherworlds," in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully describe the auspicious vow of the seven islands.
Then, beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, for seven days every day.
It is known by the names of Jambū, Śāka, Kuśa, Krauñca, and Śālmali islands.
One should worship Gomeda and Puṣkara daily in their proper sequence.
One should always perform the bath in this manner only outside [the house].
One should perform a fire-oblation with clarified butter and cause the seven grains to be given as a gift.
One should likewise eat only one meal at night, doing so only once [per day].
He should always sleep on the ground for three days dedicated to that deity. ||4||
When a full year has passed, one should give [an image] fashioned from silver.
Its extent was made like that of a continent by means of a hundred walls. || 5 ||
Having performed this vow for a full year, a man remains pure.
He attains the heavenly world until the dissolution of all beings.
Having attained human birth, he enjoys all the continents, ruling the earth after having conquered the faction of his enemies.
He was always being honored by the gods, the great seers, and the most eminent of brahmins.

Thus ends the one hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vows for the Seven Islands, beginning with Jambūdvīpa," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||159||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully declare to you the vow of the ocean.
Then, beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, for three days every day.
Salt water, milk, a stream of clarified butter, whey, and wine-water.
In the same manner, one should worship the sea of sugarcane juice (Ikṣusuroda) and the sweet sea (Svādūda). || 2 ||
One should perform the daily bath every single day outside of the house.
One should perform a fire-oblation with clarified butter and cause the seven types of grain to be given as a gift.
Eating only sacrificial food (haviṣya), he should observe this vow at night for one year.
And at the end of the year, one should likewise give a milch cow.
By the performance of this vow, [one conquers] the earth girdled by the seven oceans.
And for seven future births, the king enjoys the earth.
One who desires health should likewise observe this most excellent vow.
One who desires dharma, one who desires fame, and another who likewise desires prosperity.
This is supremely auspicious, most pure, increasing prosperity, and causing the growth of dharma.
This must be performed with diligence by men, especially by those who desire sovereignty.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vows of the Seven Oceans, Beginning with the Salt Ocean," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 160 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Now, therefore, I shall fully proclaim to you the auspicious Śailavrata.
Mahendra, Malaya, Sahya, Śuktimān, and also Ṛkṣavān. || 1 ||
The Vindhya and the Pāriyātra—these seven are the principal mountain ranges.
Starting from the beginning of the bright fortnight of Caitra, for seven days every day. ||2||
One should perform their worship and carry out the ritual bath outside.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and the excellence of food. || 3 ||
Likewise, an oblation with barley should be performed, and one should give sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
One should eat barley-food at night and observe this vow for a year.
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should give twenty vessels of barley.
To that preeminent brahmin, the reciter, he gave gold and a cow.
By practicing this [rite] for a full year, one [conquers] the entire ocean-girdled earth.
O King, having brought his enemies under control, the monarch enjoys the earth.
And having enjoyed pleasures in the third heaven, O King, one attains human birth as has been described.
O lord of men, one indeed attains everything that I have described, as well as seven future births.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Saptaśailavrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Henceforth, I shall proclaim to you the auspicious vow of the world.
As for the seven Vyāhṛtis that are proclaimed throughout the three worlds: || 1 ||
One should perform one's bath daily outside, always remaining free from sloth.
Then, beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, for seven days in succession.
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, clarified butter, and water infused with kuśa grass.
And one should likewise perform the fast for a single night in this same sequence.
An oblation with sesame seeds should be performed day after day using the Mahāvyāhṛtis.
And at the end of the year, one should likewise give a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) to the Brahmins.
A garment of great gold, a bronze vessel, and a milch cow.
Having observed this vow for a year, O best of men.
O Lord of Men, the illustrious one may move through all worlds at his own will.
Until the end of the kalpa, he shall become a king at the beginning of the kalpa.
That universal monarch, worthy of worship by the best of kings, possessed a majesty exceeding even that of the gods and asuras.
For ten million years, Sampāti, who brings delight to the entire earth, protected it.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Seven Worlds and the Seven Vyāhṛtis," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, every day for seven days.
One should worship Hlādinī, Hrādinī, and Pāvanī. || 1 ||
[He visited] Sītā, Rāma, as well as the Sindhu and the Bhāgīrathī, in due order.
Then he should perform his external ablutions and should always eat only at night.
One should offer milk into the water, reciting their names day after day.
And a water-vessel filled with milk should be given to the twice-born.
He should subsist on milk alone and remain in that state for seven days.
Having performed this for a year, when the year is complete, the man—
Thereafter, one should give a pala of silver to each of the twice-born.
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of Phālguna, in due order.
To that world does a man attain, where there is a mire of milk-rice.
There are divine rivers flowing with milk, which bestow the fruits of all desires.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, that high-souled one attains human birth and becomes free from disease.
Endowed with beauty, virtue, and wealth, whether he be a king or a preeminent brahmin; ||7||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the River Vow," in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, every day for seven days.
Suprabhā, Kāñcanākṣī, Viśālā, and the Mānasa lake. || 1 ||
That river with its triple roar, with its beautiful reeds, and likewise with its pure water.
One should always worship with devotion and perform an external bath.
And for each of them, one should perform a fire-oblation daily with curd, reciting their names.
And here one should feed the Brahmins with food mixed with curd.
Likewise, one should eat rice with ghee only once at night.
Having performed this for a year, when the year is complete, the man—
During the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, however, one should perform it every day according to the sequence of the days.
One should give a set of seven garments to an excellent twice-born man who has bathed at a sacred ford.
Having performed the vow in this manner for one year, he should recite the Sārasvata [mantra].
Having dwelt there for a very long time, he is then born as a human being.
Then, he may be a king who has conquered the faction of his enemies, or a preeminent brahmin who performs many sacrifices.
Endowed with beauty, virtue, and wealth, and possessed of learning, he shall be beloved by the people. ||7||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Sārasvata Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, for seven days every day.
Marīci, Atri, Aṅgiras, Pulastya, Pulaha, and Kratu. || 1 ||
And one should worship the highly fortunate Vasiṣṭha according to the sequence of the days.
With fruits, flowers, and cow's milk produced in their respective seasons, each separately.
One should perform the ritual bath every day outdoors and subsist on food only at night.
One should perform the fire sacrifice with the Mahāvyāhṛtis, using fruits, roots, and products of the cow.
And water-pots filled with milk should be given to the twice-born.
Having performed this for a year, at the conclusion of the vow, [he should give it] to one who has maintained the sacred fires.
One should give a black antelope skin, O King, just as previously instructed by me.
Having performed this vow, a man finds the means to liberation. || 5 ||
Having attained the means to liberation, one attains liberation without doubt.
He reaches the world of the sages, or that of the god Viṣṇu, or even that of Īśvara.
O one of great majesty, this is also due to the incomparable grandfather having observed his vow.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Seven Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, one should [proceed].
O best of kings, one should perform the worship of the Maruts on the seventh day.
O King, one should have the sevenfold circle constructed with seven tiers.
Likewise, a row upon row should be made, provided with seven mandalas.
Mandalas should be prepared with perfumes, each marked individually with their respective names and symbols.
O one of great strength, you are the single light, the double light, and the triple light.
And likewise, O King, according to the sequence of one, two, three, and four powers.
O best of kings, one should first arrange them in rows according to the prescribed rule.
Indra, Gati, Dṛśya, and then Pratiśakṛt; |||
Mita, Samita, and the mighty Amita. || 5 ||
Likewise, on the second row, one should place these same gods.
Ṛtajit, Satyajit, and the valiant Suṣeṇa. || 6 ||
Atimitra, Amitra, and likewise Purumitra.
Likewise, on the third row, one should place these following deities.
He is the Truth, the one who possesses truth, the supporter, the ordainer, Varuṇa, and the steadfast.
O King, one should place the *vidhāraṇa* on the fourth line.
Such is he, like him, and of this very measure is Amitāśana.
Kīrtita, Prasādṛkṣa, and the highly illustrious Śarabha were also proclaimed.
O lord of men, one should place seven deities in the fifth row.
The bearer of the earth, whose roar is terrifying, he is exceedingly swift and capable of enduring all things.
And on the sixth row, one should install the seven deities in their proper sequence.
Dyuti, Vasu, Anādhṛṣya, Vāsa, Kāma, Jaya, and Virāj. || 11 ||
And likewise, on the seventh row, one should place seven kings.
But the first row, O best of kings, should be white.
The second has the luster of a lotus petal; the third resembles blood.
The fourth should be yellow in color, and the fifth resembles a parrot.
The sixth is like the sky, and the seventh is black in color.
O King, garlands and ointments should be given to them that are appropriate to their respective colors.
There, forty-nine lamps indeed should be offered.
One should present the food offering (naivedya) to each of the deities individually.
And one should offer clarified butter into the fire, reciting each name individually.
And here one should feed Brāhmaṇas, equal in number to the gods.
O best of men, having observed this vow for one year, [he attained success].
Likewise, one should give a garment together with gold and a cow.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should present it to a Brahmin learned in the Purāṇas.
But for this vow, O Indra among kings, a Brahmin who knows the ritual rules must perform it correctly.
O best of men, one who desires health should observe this vow.
Whether desiring a son, desiring wealth, or again, desiring riches. || 19 ||
For this indeed bestows all desires; it is purifying and a destroyer of sins.
It is declared to be auspicious, bestowing heaven, and the most excellent among all vows.
By performing this vow for a long time, one enjoys heaven for a long duration.
Having attained human birth, he would likewise fall from heaven before long. || 21 ||
Endowed with wealth, beauty, and strength, he was beloved by the people and dear to women.
He possesses a body free from disease, has destroyed the faction of his enemies, is eloquent, and likewise upholds the sacred scriptures in this world. || 22 ||
Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of Marudvrata," in the [section on] Māgha-vrata within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 166 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having fasted properly on the sixth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, one should [proceed].
On the seventh [lunar day], one should perform the worship of the God of gods, the Lord of Light.
Having performed his external bath, a man should smear [the ground] with cow dung.
O King, one should properly smear the sacrificial ground with white clay.
There, one should draw an eight-petaled lotus using pigments.
There, upon the pericarp, one should place the god of gods, Vibhāvasu.
O King, the deity should place two [syllables] on the eastern petal and two on the northern petal.
And one should place the two Gandharvas, Ṛtu and Kārika, upon the southeastern leaf.
And likewise, one should place a pair of apsarases upon the petal in the south.
O Great King, one should place two Rākṣasas upon the leaf of the Nairṛtaka tree. || 5 ||
The two great nāgas, descendants of Kadrū, are the guardians of the western waters.
Likewise, O best of kings, there are two Yātudhānas in the northwest.
And one should likewise place two sages on the northern petal.
O best of men, one should place a single planet upon the petal in the northeast.
Their worship should be performed with perfumes, garlands, and ointments.
O subduer of enemies, with incense, lamps, and food offerings, each distinct from the others.
Having thus performed the worship of all [the deities] immediately thereafter, [one should proceed].
One should perform a fire-oblation with clarified butter for the Sun, one hundred and eight times.
Or else, O lord of men, one should give eight of each to others in that same manner.
Likewise, one should feed a single brahmin for each of all their names.
And a sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given according to one's ability to those very persons, O best of the Yadus.
Having performed this vow in this manner for a year, O best of men.
To the Brahmin versed in the Purāṇas, at the conclusion of his vow, [he should give] a milch cow.
And then, O best of the Yadus, one should give gold according to the prescribed rule.
And this vow, which grants all desires, was indeed proclaimed by the Self-Existent One.
By performing this vow, one shall attain the world of the Sun.
Then, he performs this great vow for twelve years.
Having pierced through the solar orb, the king shall attain union with Viṣṇu. ||14||
This vow destroys sin; it is auspicious, brings fame, and destroys enemies.
O King, it bestows heaven and likewise grants liberation, both in this world and in the next.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Sūryavrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Saṃvarta within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Vajra said:
O Brahmin, in whichever sacrifice they follow the Lord Ravi, [they attain his world].
Whosoever they were, beginning with the gods—please deign to tell me that.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O king of kings, Dhātṛ and Aryaman are the two deities in the spring season.
Tumburu and Nārada were two excellent Gandharvas, skilled singers.
Kṛtasthalā and Apsaras, as well as Puñjikasthalā;
Likewise, Hotā and Prahotā, as well as the two preeminent jewels that destroy demons. ||3||
The serpent Vāsuki and both those [serpents] with ears like those of a bull.
Likewise, Rathakṛtsna and Rathaujas were the two foremost among the Yātudhānas.
And Mitra and Pulaha—these two were likewise the best of sages.
And it follows the white [moon] just as the planet [Jupiter] does in the spring. || 5 ||
Learn now of those by whom the god Ravi is followed during the summer heat.
And the two gods Mitra and Varuṇa dwell [there] during the summer.
The sages Atri and Vasiṣṭha, and the two nāgas Rambha and Takṣaka.
Menakā and Sahajanyā, and the two Gandharvas Hāhā and Hūhū.
Both Rathasvanapramāṇa and Rathakṛt were there as well.
The man-eater and the slayer—these two are known as Yātudhānas.
And likewise, the planet Mars follows [the sun] during the summer heat.
Learn from me by which [rays] they follow the god Ravi during the rainy season.
Indra, Vivasvat, Aṅgiras, and Bhṛgu as well.
Likewise, the serpent Elapatra and the naga Śaṅkhapāla.
And Śuci, Sena, Ugrasena, as well as Vrāta and Aruṇa.
And the two Apsarases, Pramlocā and Nimlocantī, were both there.
Likewise, O lord of men, the Yātudhāna, the serpent, and the tiger [are also destroyed].
But during the rainy season, the planet who is the priest of the gods approaches him.
Hear further from me, O lord of men, concerning the autumn season.
Parjanya, Pūṣan, Bharadvāja, and Gautama; || 13 ||
And the Gandharva Citrasena, as well as Vasuruci indeed.
Viśvācī and Ghṛtācī—thus there were two Apsarases. || 14 ||
And the elephant Airāvata, and the famous Dhananjaya.
And Senajit and Suṣeṇa, two Rākṣasas of terrible prowess. || 15 ||
And likewise, the two Yātudhānas, Vāta and Udvāta, were possessed of great strength.
The planet Saturn likewise follows the sun in this manner. || 16 ||
After this, O King, I shall describe to you the winter season.
Aṃśa and Bhaga—these two—and Kaśyapa and Kratu indeed. || 17 ||
And the serpent Mahāpadma, as well as the snake Karkoṭaka.
And Citrasena the Gandharva, and the exceedingly powerful Ūrṇāyu. || 18 ||
The Apsaras Pūrvacitti and the Gandharvī Urvaśī likewise.
Tārkṣya and Ariṣṭanemi were two Rākṣasas of terrible prowess.
Likewise, there were two exceedingly powerful Yātudhānas, fierce like flashes of lightning.
And the planet Mercury, O King, likewise follows the sun.
Henceforth, O knower of dharma, listen as I speak concerning the winter season.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Viṣṇu, Jamadagni, and likewise Viśvāmitra; ||21||
Likewise, both Kambala and Aśvatara, the two Nāgas who are the sons of Kadrū.
And also the Apsaras Tilottamā, and the goddess Rambhā, who is enchanting.
Kāraṇī, Śitiśa, and the highly illustrious Satyajit.
And indeed, he was accompanied by Brahmā, as well as by the Rakṣas and Yajña. ||23||
The Gandharva Dhṛtarāṣṭra, and another named Sūryavarcas.
And the moon, the king of planets, follows after the sun. ||24||
For in this way, O King, they perform the pursuit during the cold season.
For these groups, numbering seven and twelve, are indeed conceited regarding their respective positions. || 25 ||
In the same way, a group of six likewise follows the sun.
These nourish the sun, the supreme light, with their own splendor.
And with words composed in verse, the sages offer praise to you.
And the Gandharvas and Apsaras attend upon him with songs and dances. || 27 ||
And the Vidyāgrāmaṇīs also take possession here.
The serpents indeed carry the Sun, and the Yātudhāna follows after him. || 28 ||
And the planet, having surrounded it, leads it to its setting according to the prescribed rule.
According to the power and according to the austerity of these very gods. || 29 ||
Just as the sun is according to the capacity of beings, so too is he established for them by his splendor.
By its splendor, it destroys the inauspicious karma of living beings.
In summer, winter, and the rainy season, that maker of day brings forth [heat].
Dharma, snow, rain, day, along with night; || 31 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Attendants of the Sun," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharma*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the seventh day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, O lord of men.
On ground smeared with cow dung, one should prepare a mandala using clay.
There, an eight-petaled lotus should be drawn with beautiful colors.
Having observed a fast, a person should worship the Sun-god in the midst of that [rite].
And likewise Aruṇa, Dantāka, Māṭhara, and Dama.
And Yamunā, Yama, Kāla, and the second Manu as well. || 3 ||
Likewise, Śanaiścara, the Queen (Śani’s consort), Chāyā, and Revanta.
The seven meters, the rain, the sky, and Piṅgala as well. || 4 ||
Or one may worship the aforementioned deities upon the filaments or the petals.
O King, the worship of the directions and time should be performed outside the lotus.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
And when the vow is completed, the horse should be given to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice according to their strength, they then attained the worlds of Purandara.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, O King, one attains union with the Sun.

Thus ends the one hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "Praise of the Worship on the Seventh Day," in the *Saptavrata-kalpa* within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O lord of men, in the dark fortnight of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having observed a fast on the seventh lunar day, one should worship the Sun-god upon a lotus.
Whether in an image or on a sacred spot, one should worship with white flowers according to the prescribed rite.
With red sandalwood, as well as with small cakes and kṛsara porridge. ||2||
At the conclusion of the vow, one who desires the destruction of enemies should give two red garments to an eminent brahmin.
One who desires good fortune likewise attains a kingdom, and at the end, the worlds of the Sun.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Raktasaptamī Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
And whatever man performs this rite every month, |||
One should perform this pair of seventh-day rites until the year has passed.
He obtains the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice and goes to the world of the Sun.
He uplifts his family, O King, and enjoys all desires. || 2 ||
Having performed the shaving of the head, one should worship the Sun-god.
The Sun becomes pleased with him, and he obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice. || 3 ||
With cakes mixed with jaggery and likewise combined with salt, [one should offer] with devotion.
Having worshipped [the deity] with gold, one obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
He who, eating only at night, worships the Sun during the forenoon;
One attains desired objects of longing and goes to the world of the Sun.
He who always worships the Sun at sunrise, [attains the highest state].
He attains his desired objects and goes to the world of the Sun.
In whatever manner one worships the Sun, all desires become fulfilled.
O hero among men, health is likewise the foremost thing, as is the world of the sun for all that exists. (7)

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Sun-Worship," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Varuṇa, Dhruva, Soma, Āpa, Anila, and Anala;
Pratyūṣa and Prabhāsa are proclaimed as the eight Vasus. || 1 ||
This Vāsudeva, consisting of eightfold nature, exists through both manifestation and dissolution.
O lord of men, he who observes a fast and worships on the eighth day [shall attain great merit].
O Yādava, beginning from the month of Caitra, during the bright fortnight...
Or else, O lord of men, [perform it] duly within mandalas or before images.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and the excellence of food.
O Indra among kings, by means of bathing outdoors as well as sleeping on the ground; || 4 ||
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise devoutly give a cow to a Brahmin.
Having performed this vow, a man attains all his desires. || 5 ||
One attains the state of Puṇḍarīka and uplifts one's own lineage.
Having reached the world of the Vasus, he rejoices like an immortal.
Having attained human birth, he becomes free from disease, with senses conquered, devoted to truth, and disciplined.
He shall be endowed with wealth and grain, beloved by women, and likewise well-dressed.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of Suvrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, O lord of men, beginning from the eighth day of the moon in the bright fortnight, [one should perform the rite].
One should worship the three-eyed God of gods while observing a fast.
Whether in a linga, or in an image, or in a lotus, or on a flat surface.
By means of an ablution with ghee and milk, and by various kinds of bathing; || 2 ||
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and the excellence of food.
By means of song, dance, instrumental music, and the propitiation of the fire.
And by worshipping the brahmins according to the rules, O best of men.
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise give a milch cow.
One obtains the fruit of the white lotus and goes to the heavenly world.
And likewise, having worshipped Maheśvara on the eighth days of the dark fortnight, || 5 ||
One obtains the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Having performed [the vow] on two eighth days in that manner for a year, a man—
Having duly obtained the fruit of the horse sacrifice and enjoyed the pleasures in the world of the Lord of the Gods.
Then, having attained the worlds of Maheśvara, he attains union (sāyujya) with him before long.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Maheśvara-Aṣṭamī Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Himavān, Hemakūṭa, Niṣadha, and Nīla;
And Śveta, Śṛṅgavān, Meru, Mālyavat, and Gandhamādana. || 1 ||
On the ninth day, a person should worship these nine mountain kings.
The Northern Kurus are meritorious, as is the delightful Hairaṇvatī region.
Bhadrāśva, Ketumāla, and likewise Ilāvṛta.
Harivarṣa, Kimpuruṣavarṣa, and Bhāratavarṣa as well. || 3 ||
Likewise, O King, these are to be honored according to their respective positions.
O King, starting from the ninth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, verse 4.
O knower of dharma, [he should do so] while fasting, with offerings of perfumes, garlands, and excellent food.
At the conclusion of his vow, a man [should offer] silver representing the shape of Jambūdvīpa.
One should give the weight of a tulā; indeed, one attains all desires.
He obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Having attained human birth, he shall become a universal monarch, a king who delights the hosts of gods.
Having ruled the earth for a long time, he attains the worlds and even the objects of desire beyond that.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Parvatāṣṭamī Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the ninth day, however, one should worship Bhadrakālī while observing a fast.
O Great King, beginning from the month of Kārttika, this occurs in sequence during the bright fortnight.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and the excellence of food.
At the end of the year, having performed worship at the conclusion of the vow, one should give [the gift] to a Brāhmaṇa.
By giving a pair of garments, a person shall obtain their desired wish.
One afflicted by disease is freed from disease; one who is bound is released from bondage.
And one who is occupied with the affairs of the king is released from great fear.
He has no fear of thieves, nor ever any fear from the wilderness.
One obtains sons, wealth as desired, excellent women, and various kinds of base metals and goods.
By performing worship according to the prescribed rites for Bhavānī, one obtains all desires exactly as one wishes.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "Description of the Worship of Bhadrakālī," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Kratu, Dakṣa, Ripu, Satya, Kāla, Kāma, and likewise Dhvani.
Kulavān, Manuja, Viśva, and Rocamāna—these are your ten [sons]. || 1 ||
The Viśvedevas are thus enumerated; the all-pervading Keśava is the tenfold self.
O lord of men, his worship should be performed during the bright fortnight.
O best of kings, beginning from the eighth day of the month of Kārtika...
And whether in the principal mandalas or in the images, O Yādava.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should give gold to a twice-born man according to one's ability.
Having observed this desired vow for one year, he attains their worlds for a very long time.
Having dwelt there in that world and attained human status, he shall become either a king or an eminent Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Worship of the Viśvedevas on the Tenth Day," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
For the self, life-span, mind, skill, exhilaration, and likewise vital breath;
Haviṣmān, Gatīṣṭa, Ṛta, and Satya—these are your ten [sons]. ||1||
On the tenth day, a person should worship the deity named Aṅgiras.
Fasting during the dark fortnight, a man should perform [the rite] according to the previously mentioned procedure. ||2||
Having observed this vow for a year, one attains those desired worlds and remains there for a very long time.
Having dwelt there in that world and attained the state of a human being, O Brāhmaṇa, he shall become either a king or a preeminent Brāhmaṇa.

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Aṅgiras Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the tenth day of the bright fortnight, a man should likewise observe a fast.
O subduer of enemies, starting from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, this should be performed daily.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
One should offer oblations of clarified butter into the fire and honor the Brāhmaṇas there;
at the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise give a milch cow as a gift.
This vow has been prescribed as bestowing the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Likewise, having performed this vow for a year during the dark fortnight, one attains the same result.
He obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and extracts his own merit.
O best of men, having performed this vow during both fortnights, [one attains the fruit].
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices;
one attains the heavenly world and uplifts one's own lineage.
If his mind is fixed on the Dharma, he will undoubtedly attain the Dharma.
Wherever one may be born, there one should be devoted to dharma.
O King, he who is devoted to dharma is the foremost among them because of that.
It bestows health, longevity, fame, and a secure position, while destroying all evil.
This must be performed by men in the proper manner, for the Blessed Lord Viṣṇu, together with his Dharma, is worthy of worship. ||8||

Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Religious Vows," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Mārkaṇḍeya said: Likewise, one should worship Aṅgāraka, Sūrya, Nirṛti, and Vāyu.
Havana, Īśvara, Mṛtyu, Kapālin, and then Kiṅkiṇa. || 1 ||
And there, with eleven parts, [he fashioned] the gods who are the lords of the three worlds.
On the eleventh day, fasting, he should likewise worship Soma with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food.
Then, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it shall continue for as long as a year.
And at the end of the year, one should likewise give a milch cow.
Having observed this desired vow for a year, O King, a man indeed attains auspiciousness.
Having sported for a very long time together with Rudra, she then attained all the delights of love that were pleasing to her mind.
Thus ends the one hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rudra Vow," in the Māgha-vrata-saṃhitā of the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||179||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Bhuvana, Bhānu, Sujanya, and likewise Sujana;
Kratu, Sarva, Mūrdhan, Tyāja, and likewise Vyamnaka. || 1 ||
Prasava, Āpyaya, and Dakṣa, as well as Dvādaśaka.
The twelve gods worthy of sacrifice are designated as the Bhṛgus. || 2 ||
One should always perform their worship specifically on the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī).
Starting from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, it should always be performed during the dark fortnight.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
And at the end of the year, one should give a milch cow to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having observed this desired vow for one year, one attains the very same world as theirs.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, that person shall become either a king or an eminent twice-born man.
Thus ends the one hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Bhṛgu-vrata," in the third section of the Māheśvara-khaṇḍa of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara-purāṇa. || 180 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Mind, thought, as well as vital breath, man, and the heroic vehicle.
Citi, Hayas, Naya, Haṃsa, and likewise Nārāyaṇa. || 1 ||
Vibhu and Prabhu—these are proclaimed as the twelve Sādhyas.
One should worship them during the bright fortnight, beginning from the twelfth day of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa.
Having observed this desired vow for one year, one attains the very same world as theirs.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, O lord of men, he shall become either a king or a preeminent brahmin.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Sādhya Vow," in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa*, [as recorded] in the Mādhava-vamśa-saṃhitā. || 181 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Dhātṛ, Mitra, Aryaman, Pūṣan, Śakra, Īśa, Varuṇa, and Bhaga.
Tvaṣṭṛ, Vivasvat, Savitṛ, and Viṣṇu likewise constitute the twelve.
Having fasted during the bright fortnight, one should worship the twelve Ādityas.
Then, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, [one should worship] with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, and food.
Having given gold at the conclusion of his vow, O hero among men, a person attains the worlds of the Sun.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, has conquered the senses, and is endowed with wealth. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Kāmadeva Vrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Great King, having fasted on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, [one should proceed].
O Lord, one should worship Kāmadeva starting from the month of Vaiśākha, with perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food offerings.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise give perfumes and a pair of garments to a Brahmin.
Having observed this vow for a year, a person reaches that desired world and remains there for a very long time.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, endowed with happiness, and possesses beauty and a symmetrical form.
Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Kāmadeva Vow," in the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa, in the Māheśvarakhaṇḍa, in the Brahmottarakhaṇḍa. 183.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Great King, having fasted on the thirteenth day of the bright fortnight, [one should...]
Starting from the month of Phālguna, a person should worship [it] constantly. || 1 ||
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should present gold to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa. || 2 ||
Having performed this desired vow for a year, O King, and having likewise dwelt among the Yakṣas for a very long time;
Having attained human birth, one shall be endowed with wealth, possessed of good fortune, and likewise free from disease. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Dhanavrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
O Yādava, beginning from the fourteenth day of the bright fortnight in the month of Jyeṣṭha, [the rite should be performed].
Having fasted and subdued his senses, one should worship the god Vāyu. ||1||
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and the excellence of food.
At the end of the year, a pair of garments should be given to a twice-born man.
O King, having observed this vow for a year and attained the world of the Maruts, a man enjoys pleasures for a very long time; then, returning to the human state, he becomes free from disease.
Thus ends the eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vāyu-vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight, one should worship Virūpākṣa.
Then, beginning from the month of Pauṣa, the vow lasts for one year.
Through perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and the excellence of food.
O scorcher of foes, at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a camel to a twice-born man.
Having performed this desired vow for one year, he incurs no fear from the rākṣasas.
O King, he attains his desires, becomes free from disease, and does not experience any fear whatsoever.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Virūpākṣa Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
And at whatever river there may be, on the fourteenth day of the dark fortnight.
At a time when the sun has not yet risen, one should worship the god Yama.
O Yādava, [he saw] Dhūmra, Ūrṇa, Citragupta, and the nooses of Kāla.
He who knows the dharma [attains] both death and heaven through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, and food.
Then one should offer oblations of sesame seeds with the verse beginning "yamo dadhāra."
Likewise, for a woman or a Śūdra, the injunction is that they should say "namo yamāya."
O best of men, one should feed the Brahmins with kṛsara as food according to one's ability.
Likewise, at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a milch cow to a Brahmin.
O King, having performed this desired vow for a year, a man does not go to hell.
Upon the exhaustion of his life, he goes to heaven, and having returned to the human state, he shall be endowed with righteousness.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Yamavrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Then, O lord of men, beginning from the bright fortnight of the month of Phālguna, [he performed the rites].
One should worship Maheśvara on the fourteenth lunar day while observing a fast.
With perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food.
At the conclusion of the vow, one should likewise give a cow; thus, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having observed this very vow for a year during the bright fortnight, [one attains the desired fruit].
One obtains the Puṇḍarīka [merit] and uplifts one's own lineage. || 3 ||
Having performed these two fourteenth-day rites for a year, a man—
By worshipping with such devotion month after month, one shall attain all desires.
O King, having attained the desires of Maheśvara and having dwelt there for a very long time, he remained.
He attains union with that Maheśvara, the Lord of all, who is without equal.

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Maheśvara Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
The Prabhāsvaras, the Barhiṣads, and likewise the Agniṣvāttas.
The flesh-eaters, the invited ones, the ghee-drinkers, and those who observe auspicious times; || 1 ||
O King, the hosts of ancestors are to be honored constantly through fasting.
Then, O lord of men, beginning from the first day of the bright fortnight of Caitra until the fifteenth day, ||2||
One should perform the śrāddha on that day for as long as the year lasts.
Through the excellence of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and food. || 3 ||
And at the end of the year, one should likewise give a milch cow.
To a Brahmin who was devoted to his ancestors, O illustrious one, [he gave it] with devotion.
Having performed this desired vow for a year, he likewise attains their world.
Having dwelt there for a very long time, O King, foremost among men, one attains liberation at the proper time. (5)

Thus ends the one hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow for the Ancestors," in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
O Yādava, on the fifteenth day of the dark fortnight beginning from Caitra...
Having performed the worship of the fire with perfumes, garlands, and an abundance of food.
Then, O lord of men, one should perform an oblation with sesame seeds in the name of Agni.
And at the end of the year, one should give gold to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having observed this desired vow for a year, one obtains constant wealth and fame.
O foremost among men, [grant] devotion to the Dharma, supreme beauty, and desired objects of pleasure.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vahni-vrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 190 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the occasion of the new moon, O best of men, he should remain fasting.
One should worship two lotuses, representing the moon and the sun situated in a single zodiac sign. || 1 ||
The sun is in the eight-petaled lotus, and likewise, the moon is in the sixteen-petaled one.
O Yādava, one should worship the sun with all-red [pigments] and the moon with white.
O highly fortunate one, one should perform the fire-oblation with garlands and other offerings, as well as with sesame seeds and rice.
Combined with ghee and milk, [one should offer] according to the rule by means of the names of those two kings. || 3 ||
At the conclusion of the vow, one should present gold to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa.
And silver, O highly fortunate one, for one who desires prosperity for oneself. || 4 ||
Having observed this desired vow with devotion and having offered abundant lamps according to the prescribed rite, one should proceed.
Having reached the supreme eye, his splendor increases; endowed with wealth, he shall abide in the celestial realms and other such places.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Moon-Vow," in the third section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 191 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Starting from the month of Kārttika, [one should worship] the one whose mark is the full moon.
O King, one should always worship [the deity] in the stomach and should subsist on food only at night. || 1 ||
Having prepared a salt circle and anointed it with sandalwood paste,
There, one should worship Soma together with the ten lunar mansions.
One should worship [the deity] conjoined with the asterisms Kṛttikā and Rohiṇī during the month of Kārttika.
O King, it is likewise in the month of Saumya, accompanied by the asterisms Saumya and Ārdrā.
O Yādava, it is joined with the Puṣya constellation in the month of Pauṣa.
O King, listen: when Maghā is conjoined with the serpent [Śeṣa] in the month of Māgha, and in Phālguna as well.
One should worship the Lord together with those [deities] belonging to Aryaman, Bhaga, and Savitṛ.
The month of Caitra is joined with Citrā and Svātī; now hear concerning Vaiśākha, O King. || 5 ||
And one should likewise worship [the deity] together with Viśākhā and Maitra.
In the month of Jyeṣṭha, [the festival] is joined with Jyeṣṭhā and Mūla; immediately thereafter, it begins with Āṣāḍhā.
In the month of Śrāvaṇa, it was joined with the asterism Śravaṇā and accompanied by Śraviṣṭhā.
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, [one should worship] the constellation Revatī (Pauṣṇa) conjoined with Ājāhirbudhnya.
Likewise, one should worship the Lord during the month of Āśvayuja when it is joined with the asterisms Aśvinī and Bharaṇī.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and excellent food. ||8||
With jaggery, with fine rice, with salt, and with ghee.
With sugarcane, products of sugarcane, milk, and milk-rice. ||9||
And noble women who are not widows, possessing auspicious characteristics such as those, are worthy of worship.
Immediately after that, a self-controlled man should eat sacrificial food (haviṣya).
But at the conclusion of the Brahmins' vow, [he gave] that which was dyed with great silver.
And according to one's capacity, a woman or a man should offer clothing. || 11 ||
A man shall be endowed with beauty, good fortune, charm, and wealth.
By performing this vow, one goes to the heavenly world.
He who, while fasting, should perform this unsurpassed vow, [attains the highest state].
A human being obtains the fruit of a thousand horse-sacrifices. || 13 ||
And he obtains in an especially eminent manner whatever has been declared regarding good fortune and other such qualities.
One undoubtedly attains all the desires longed for by the mind. || 14 ||
He will be as pleasing to people as the moon, and likewise, there will be the acquisition of wealth and the like through prosperity.
And likewise, O King, having attained human birth, he shall become equal to Śakra in power.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Full Moon of the Lunar Mansions," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 192 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
On the full moon day of Kārttika, [he beheld] the full orb of the cool-rayed moon.
One should worship upon the sixteen petals of the lotus and in its pericarp. || 1 ||
There, one should worship the twenty-eight lunar mansions upon the filaments.
One should likewise worship the lunar-day deities upon the leaves, as well as Jyotsnā.
By means of perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and the excellence of food.
With jaggery, with fine rice, with curd, and with salt. || 3 ||
And with cakes, O illustrious one, as well as with fruits produced in their season.
And at the conclusion of the vow, one should give a pair of garments to a twice-born man.
And for the Brahmani, O highly fortunate one, it was colored with great silver.

Both the astrologer and the time-announcer should be honored according to the prescribed rite and to the best of one's ability. Then, observing a fast or eating only at night, one should perform this vow.
Or, O knower of dharma, one may eat only at night, or likewise subsist on sacrificial oblations.
It bestows good fortune, increases beauty, grants loveliness, and provides the enjoyment of love with women.
O lord of men, a man should perform his duty with diligence; likewise, O one of undaunted spirit, so should women.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Full-Moon Day Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, beginning from the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, a person [should worship] within the lunar orb.
Having observed a fast and performed worship, one obtains the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Having observed this desired vow for one year, he attains the world of the Moon.
O King, having dwelt there for a very long time, he then attains union with Him.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Candra-vrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara. || 194 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Then, beginning from Proṣṭhapada, when the moon was full.
Having worshipped the god Varuṇa with an abundance of perfumes, garlands, and food, || 1 ||
Having given a water-cow to a twice-born man at the conclusion of the vow, however, [one attains the fruit].
Equipped with an umbrella and sandals, and adorned with a pair of garments.
O King, that man reaches the world of Varuṇa and dwells there for a very long time.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, endowed with beauty, and likewise possessed of wealth.

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Varuṇa Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 195 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In the bright fortnight of the month of Āśvayuja, on the full moon day, a pure man—
The king, having observed a fast, should likewise worship the god.
Śacī, Airāvata, the thunderbolt, and Mātali, O lord of men.
With perfumes, garlands, prostrations, incense, lamps, and an abundance of food. || 2 ||
Having given gold at the end of the year, he attains the world of Purandara.
Having attained human birth, one shall become either a king honored by lords of men or a preeminent among the twice-born. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Śakra-vrata," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having observed the fast on the fourteenth day or the full moon day, that best of men—
Thereafter, one should drink the five products of the cow (pañcagavya) and likewise subsist on sacrificial food (haviṣya). || 1 ||
Having performed it in that manner for a year, one is liberated from the sin of a month.
Therefore, with every effort, one should perform this practice month after month. ||2||
Having reached the world of the lords of men for one year, O King, that best of the twice-born dwells there for a very long time.
Having attained human birth, one shall become either a king honored by the lords of men or a preeminent among the twice-born. || 3 ||

Thus ends the one hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Brahmakūrca," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having fasted on the fourteenth day, one should worship the god Hari, who is the embodiment of Yoga.
If one worships on the full moon day, he shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
One who has become Brahman on the new moon day and likewise on the full moon day.
He obtains the merit of the Rājasūya sacrifice and uplifts his own lineage. || 2 ||
One should worship Him who has become Brahman on the new moon day and on the full moon day.
By attending upon Keśava, who has become yoga, one shall attain greatness.
He always experiences extreme joy at the end of each month and fortnight.
The supreme deity Hari was worshipped with devotion by him who observed a fast.
This is known as the Great Vow, which destroys all impurities.
Having performed this for a year, one is glorified upon the back of the celestial vault.
This vow is proclaimed as the pacifier of all sins.
