Therefore, one attains desire according to one's wish; there is no doubt in this matter.
There is the Māheśvara [rite], the group of Mothers, and likewise the worship of the fire there. || 99 ||
O King, by wearing a single garment, one obtains whatever desire one longs for.
In that manner, a person should worship the pentad connected with Tumburu.
One attains victory everywhere; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 101 ||
Likewise, under the asterism Kṛttikā, a man, having worshipped those who attend upon Skanda, [attains his desires].
One attains great health, or always obtains whatever is desired by the mind. ||102||
One should worship that which is connected with Nṛsiṃha when the moon is full.
A man, having worshipped the group of Mothers, shall obtain all his desires. ||103||
Or, O King, by [worshipping] a single mother, one obtains all desired objects.
By honoring the lords of the forest, one obtains the merit of [offering] forest-produce. || 104 ||
Whether they be Daityas or Dānavas, or others who belong to their side.
Having performed their worship on the fourteenth day, one shall become happy. || 105 ||
Or at the proper time of action or at the auspicious moment, one should worship the deity according to the rules.
Therefore, one attains desire and finds the highest state. || 106 ||
Then, starting from the month of Caitra, a person should always act according to what has been stated.
Having worshipped the desired deity as prescribed, one enjoys the fruit thereof.
O knower of dharma, within a year, whether it be on a particular lunar mansion or a lunar day, [the fruit is attained].
Or, O knower of all dharmas, one who is fasting and composed in mind during a planetary eclipse [attains success]. || 108 ||
In a year, or in a solstice, in a season, in a month, or in its fortnight.
Eating only at night, he should constantly perform worship of its owner at all times.
For that length of time, O illustrious one, he shall therefore obtain his desire. || 109 ||
O noble one, beginning from the month of Caitra, if it pleases you, worship the Lord Rocana.
O moon of the Yadu dynasty, by pleasing Roceśa, he effortlessly attains that supreme desire.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "Description of the Fasting on Specific Lunar Days and the Worship of Deities," in the Māgha section of the Third Part of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
Vajra said:
O Blessed One, I wish to hear about the Roca mountains individually.
What should be done by one who has observed the fast, and what would be the fruit thereof? || 1 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Likewise, listen now as I relate this historical account.
Then follows the conversation between Dhanādhyakṣa and Aṣṭāvakra.
In former times, Aṣṭāvakra, who was learned in the Dharma, sought the hand of a maiden in marriage.
And she was the daughter of the munificent sage, the foremost of the Bhṛgus, named Suprabhā.
And that sage spoke to the sage who was endowed with beauty and wealth.
If the nature of women has been understood by you, O best among those who know the Dharma.
Therefore, I shall give you that maiden with eyes like those of a young fawn.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
O best of Brahmins, the true nature of women was not understood by me.
And from where was that known by me? Tell that to me as I ask you.
Bhārgava said:
Look toward the northern direction; she will tell it to you according to the truth.
O illustrious one, go quickly and without delay to the nature of a woman.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed, that righteous-souled one set out toward the northern direction.
Then, from Gaṅgādvāra, the eminent sage proceeded by stages with haste.
Sacred fords, rivers, mountains, and cities as well. ||8||
Having leaped over the abode of the Giver of Wealth, the one of great asceticism reached his destination.
On Kailāsa, the best of mountains, which is enriched with the fulfillment of all desires.
There he saw the illustrious Lord of Wealth seated.
The hero was seated upon an excellent throne, his chest adorned by the weight of a heavy necklace.
On his left side, he was resplendent with a well-arranged crown.
With two variegated earrings, as well as with armlets and bracelets; || 11 ||
He who holds a mace, possesses a massive body, and has one tawny eye.
And likewise, it was resplendent with the two treasures, Śaṅkha and Padma.
And by highly fortunate yakṣas of terrifying form and prowess.
Then by the hero Dīrghabhadra and also by Pūrṇabhadra.
Then by the hero Maṇibhadra and also by Yakṣabhadra.
By Dīrghabāhu, Mahābāhu, Padmakiñjalka, and Sṛñjaya. || 14 ||
By Svabhadra, Supārśva, and likewise by Maṇidhara.
And by other Yakṣas as well, O knower of Dharma, who possess great strength and prowess. || 15 ||
And by Gandharvas of various guises, who are great beings of immense power.
Citrāṅgada, Citraratha, Citrasena, and then Tumburu. || 16 ||
Pūrṇāyu, Anagha, and likewise the lord Śāliśiras;
Śṛṅgārakarṇa was exceedingly powerful, formidable, and possessed of terrifying prowess. || 17 ||
These and other Gandharvas, as well as auspicious Apsarases, [were there].
Urvaśī, Menakā, Rambhā, Miśrakeśī, and indeed Alambuṣā. 18.
Viśvācī, Ghṛtācī, Pañcacūḍā, and Manoramā.
And with these and thousands of other celestial women.
He saw the Lord of Wealth surrounded on all sides.
He was honored by the Lord of Wealth with water for the feet, the arghya offering, water for sipping, and other such rites.
Seated upon an excellent throne, O King, he praised the Lord Dhanada.
Aṣṭāvakra said:
Homage be to you, O Lord of Wealth; homage be to you, O Lord of Sacrifice. || 21 ||
O mighty-armed one, O being of great courage, O king of kings with the splendor of an immortal!
O inconceivable one praised by the assembly of sages, O you who wear the crescent moon upon your crest, O bestower of boons! || 22 ||
O tawny-eyed one, O large-necked one, O Lord of Gods, O you who are carried by men!
O Gadādhara, you of broad shoulders, whose splendor is equal to the radiance of the sun. || 23 ||
You are eternally the companion of Śarva, and likewise, you are an incarnation (aṃśa) of Viṣṇu.
Furthermore, they were struck down by you in the battle between the gods and the asuras.
Many heroic Dānavas possessed great strength and prowess.
You alone, O king of Yakṣas, sustain all the worlds.
The Lord, who is ever compassionate toward his devotees, is the sovereign of the northern quarter.
In this world, you are the bridge of Dharma; everything is established in you. || 26 ||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Thus addressed by the Lord of Wealth, the great sage replied.
O Lord of Wealth, I desire to hear from you about the great fruit of the Dharma.
Vaiśravaṇa said:
The worship of the Brahmins, of one's own self, and of the deity according to one's inclination.
O Brahmin, listen as I proclaim that dharma which yields great fruit. || 28 ||
O Brahmin, during all the auspicious conjunctions (rocas), one should remain fasting and with senses subdued.
Having performed the worship of the deity as prescribed, one enjoys the fruit as stated. || 29 ||
Beginning from the bright fortnight of Caitra, one should observe this unsurpassed vow.
For a year, one should take as much as desired, remaining unwearied throughout the year.
O best of sages, being composed in mind, he remained thus for thirty years and one month.
Eating only at night for one year, he should worship the deity Rocanā.
O highly fortunate one, by doing this daily, one shall obtain all desires.
He who shall perform the unsurpassed Rocavrata during the month of Āṣāḍha, || 32 ||
The twice-born man should eat only at night and take his meal at a single time every day.
One should avoid drinking water at any time other than the time for eating. || 33 ||
Starting from the Brāhma-loka up to the Pauruṣa-loka.
But when the human year has arrived, having performed the satiation of the Brahmins, || 34 ||
Having given garments, gold, and likewise silver to the brahmins.
O best of the twice-born, he attains the heavenly world for a long time.
And having attained birth as a human, he is born endowed with a beautiful form.
He is forever free from disease, powerful, and a conqueror of enemies, even when they are strong.
And he obtains preeminent women and likewise birth in an excellent family.
One attains great good fortune as well as supreme beauty. || 37 ||
One should cultivate friendship with the virtuous, as well as knowledge and the supreme goal in the Dharma.
He also [obtains] the principal vehicles and whatever else he desires. || 38 ||
O Brahmin, what you have said regarding the month of Roca for one who eats only at night is fruitful, O best of gods.
Henceforth, I shall tell you, if it pleases you, the distinct fruits of one who has correctly observed the fast.

Thus ends the one hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of the Month-long Fast during the *Rocya* [months]," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
Vaiśravaṇa said:
Having worshipped Brahmā in the Brahma-sacrifice, one attains the world of Brahmā.
One obtains the merit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice at Prājāpatya, and one reaches Prajāpati himself. || 1 ||
Likewise, one who delights in heaven attains heaven, the celestial world.
Likewise, Cakraroc gave the Vaiṣṇava discus, Sudarśana.
Having fashioned a twelve-spoked wheel with fragrant pigments, a man—
Having worshipped [the deity] at the end of the year, one should present a golden [image].
To the divine Vāsudeva and to the second, the Brāhmaṇa.
He conquers all enemies, both external and internal.
His wheel shall likewise be peerless and all-pervading.
He does not experience the suffering of hell and goes instead to the heavenly world. || 5 ||
Likewise, having worshipped the Lord of the Forest at the Vānaspatya and Rocya [stages], || 6 ||
A person obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice in the form of a garden.
And he likewise finds fruit-bearing wood everywhere.
If there is no food, one should likewise worship Vāsudeva with food.
But a person who stays in the middle of the field obtains abundant food. || 8 ||
Likewise, there is satisfaction in the world beyond, and similarly in the heavenly realm.
Having honored the day on that unblemished day, the person [should proceed]. || 9 ||
Having offered [the oblation] to Vāsudeva, he [worships] the lord, the all-pervading Saṅkarṣaṇa.
One enjoys health, beauty, charm, and good fortune.
O Kālarocanā, a man who knows the Dharma, having properly worshipped Kāla, [attains his goal].
He attains mindfulness at the time of death, and having died, he reaches the supreme goal.
One should worship Agni in the southeast; one shall attain all the worlds.
All fire-rites of his succeed without a doubt. ||12||
By worshipping the waters, O Lord, one obtains jewels as well as lotuses.
All water-related rites will succeed for him; of this there is no doubt. || 13 ||
Having worshipped the Sun during the Saura [period], one shall attain freedom from disease.
By worshipping the moon as the moon, one shall obtain supreme bliss;
by worshipping the cow as the cow, the fragrant mother of the worlds, one shall attain the world of the gods.
O knower of dharma, he likewise attains cattle and that very world. ||15||
Having reached Rocabha through destiny, he worshipped that very destiny.
He attains long life wherever he is born. ||16||
Having worshipped Viṣṇu in a Vaiṣṇava shrine, one attains the world of Viṣṇu.
Having worshipped Rudra in the Raudra [region], one attains that world. ||17||
By worshipping Kumāra, a man obtains sons in his youth.
Having performed the worship of the ancestors with a concentrated mind in the Pitṛloka, ||18||
One obtains one's desired worship and goes to the world of the ancestors.
By worshipping the god Varuṇa in the Vāruṇa [region], one obtains horses. || 19 ||
And having likewise worshipped the infinite mountain Ananta, he honored the great earth.
One obtains infinite fruit from well-performed action.
Having worshipped Vāyu in the north-western direction, one shall obtain profit in trade.
Furthermore, by worshipping Yama in the southern direction, one incurs no fear of hell.
And having worshipped the goddess Sarasvatī with the Sārasvata hymn, O twice-born one.
One obtains whatever knowledge one desires, and by means of it, one becomes eloquent. ||22||
Having worshipped Śrī in Śrīroca, one obtains beautiful prosperity.
And likewise, it pleases me that a man should worship me. || 23 ||
For wherever he is born, he indeed becomes a possessor of wealth.
Likewise, O Śailarocī, by worshipping Śaila, one shall become happy. || 24 ||
Having worshipped the earth with great splendor, one attains the unsurpassed earth.
Having performed the worship of the Vedas, he remained concentrated upon the splendor of the Vedas.
A man obtains the Vedas, and a lord of men also obtains the sacrifices.
Likewise, one who worships Puruṣa at Pauruṣa, Roce, and Jala [attains success]. || 26 ||
He attains all desires and finds the means to liberation.
Deficient in form, deficient in touch, deficient in smell, and deficient in taste.
By worshipping the ancient Person who is beyond sound, one proceeds upon the path to liberation. || 27 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of the Prati-rocaka," in the third section of the Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Having heard this vow of Rocā and having eaten in the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), [he departed].
Having heard the singing and the instrumental music, and having seen the captivating dance, || 1 ||
Having stayed there for one night, honored by the Lord of Wealth (Kubera), he departed.
That righteous twice-born man ascended the Himalaya mountain.
In a certain mountain region, he beheld a beautiful house.
Resembling a mass of moonbeams, it was endowed with the fulfillment of all desires.
Then, in that house, he saw an elderly woman who was beautiful in form.
Adorned with all ornaments and surrounded by many [attendants]. || 4 ||
And by young, excellent women, all beautifully attired.
And she honored him in due order with water for the feet and other offerings.
And having honored him with fragrant oil, the Yādava bathed him.
And likewise with breezes pleasant to the touch and various fragrances.
And he anointed his limbs with fragrant sandalwood paste.
And he likewise honored him with garments, ornaments, and garlands.
And he fed them with food that was enriched with all desirable things.
And he gave him betel-leaf that was fragrant and very charming. || 8 ||
It had a white upper cover, was variegated, well-spread, and possessed supreme splendor.
In a variegated house, he gave him a most enchanting bed.
In that supreme state, the beautiful woman fell asleep.
Having dismissed all those women, whose eyes were like those of young fawns.
Then, under the pretext of cold, he rose from his bed at the dead of night.
The woman of excellent complexion went to the bed of Aṣṭāvakra.
Seeing her lying upon the bed, he said, "What is this?"
"O lady of lovely smiles, this is not befitting of your age."
I have remained unbroken in my celibacy and have avoided the wives of others.
Having disregarded me at your own will, what is this that you seek to do?
Diti said:
O twice-born one, it is not only women who are fickle in their youth.
Even at the end of our lives, impelled by desire, we indulge in restlessness.
I believe, O best of the twice-born, that you have not heard of the character of women.
These women do not take delight in age, nor in beauty, nor in lineage, nor in learning. (15)
They are attached only occasionally to virtue, dress, wealth, or valor.
"Women desire a man according to their availability," so says the Śruti. || 16 ||
For those women whose protection is great are guarded by hunchbacks and dwarfs.
Or even by means of servants, O Bhārgava, they here entice a man. (17)
Fire is not satiated by wood, nor is the great ocean by rivers.
Neither by all living beings nor by men, O fair-eyed ones, can Death be overcome.
Smiling, women destroy a family with mere playfulness.
For women, O best of the Bhṛgus, are by their very nature difficult to find as sources of pleasure. (19)
There is no privacy, there is no leisure, and there is no one to invite [one].
O knower of dharma, it is by this that the virtue of fidelity arises in women.
O highly fortunate one, you have been sent to my presence by that great-souled one.
Thus have we observed and heard regarding the character of women here in this world.
Knowing this, you should not feel any loathing toward women.
For women alone are the root of dharma, artha, and kāma. || 22 ||
Fire, food, and water are indeed the causes of sustenance for human beings.
They are said to be the slayers themselves, and women should be understood to be likewise. || 23 ||
Just as there is no sustenance in the world without fire, food, and water,
so too the life of a householder cannot exist in any way without women.
Therefore, they should be guarded through wisdom, neither by severity nor by mildness.
Women are the root of misfortunes and the means for achieving the three goals of life.
One should not place trust in them, but should guard them like a precious gem.
Those who are engaged in household duties should be protected by one who desires prosperity.
Having heard this, on the second day, he was honored by that woman.
From there she went to the abode of the Giver of Wealth (Kubera), and from there also to her father-in-law's house. || 27 ||
Then, having approached her father-in-law, she reported everything to him.
And he questioned that brahmin after hearing of the conduct of women.
Tell me this: has the inclination to enter [the path] arisen in your mind, or has it not?
Having heard this reply, Aṣṭāvakra spoke these words to the sage.
And this path is not secure, nor does any other path exist.
Therefore, O knower of dharma, give your own daughter to me for the sake of my wife.
Having heard this, the sage Bhārgava gave his daughter to him.
On an auspicious lunar day, at a favorable time of day and under a propitious constellation and moment (muhūrta), [he should perform the rite]. || 31 ||
Having obtained that dark-eyed wife, who is the very root of the three aims of life.
He attained supreme satisfaction and rejoiced with her. ||32||
Then that great-souled one protected her, constantly keeping her engaged in household duties.
And she, being established in dharma and supremely virtuous, gratified that best of the twice-born.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Dialogue between Aṣṭāvakra and Dik," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Tell me of some vow that destroys all impurities.
O Brahmin, it is the best among vows, a purifier, and an increaser of merit.
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
But having attained manly vigor, fasting and with senses subdued, || 2 ||
Having bathed with the Pauruṣa Sūkta, he should remain with a restrained mind.
Having performed the libation with that very [water], O best of men, one should perform the recitation of the mantra.
In the center of an eight-petaled lotus is Haṃsa Janārdana.
And a person should honor and worship him with the Pauruṣa Sūkta. || 4 ||
Then, immediately thereafter, [he should worship] further with flowers, incenses, and fruits.
Then, O King, with a lamp, and after that with an offering of food (naivedya). || 5 ||
And then one should worship the fire with the Pauruṣa Sūkta.
Then, at the conclusion of the rite, a milch cow should be given as a gift.
Having performed this most purifying vow for one year, he—
One obtains all desires, both those that are divine and those that are human.
One obtains the merit of the horse sacrifice and attains the fruit of the royal consecration.
After enjoying worldly pleasures, he thereafter attains liberation without a doubt.
This is supremely auspicious, most purifying, increasing prosperity, and increasing righteousness.
The supreme vow known as the Haṃsa-vrata, which removes sin in the world of men, should be performed by a person.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Haṃsa Vow," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 225 ||
Vajra said:
What was done by Viṣṇu, the god of gods, in the form of a swan?
O great sage Mārkaṇḍeya, sever this doubt of mine. ||1||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
In former times, O King, during the Kṛta age, all living beings were established in knowledge.
O scion of the Yadu lineage, at that time, people were devoted to knowledge.
Thus, sovereignty came to him of its own accord, as did the hosts of gods.
Likewise, at the end of the Kṛta Yuga, they began to take possession [of property]. ||3||
From that grasping arose greed, and from greed arose hatred.
The knowledge of those overcome by passion and hatred disappeared.
Likewise, when knowledge was lost in the world, Dharma met its destruction.
But seeing the world perishing when the Dharma had been destroyed, Janārdana [acted].
Having become equal to a swan in color, he wandered over this earth.
He has beautiful wings, moves like a god, possesses a fine beak, and has long, extended eyes.
Then he saw the sages residing in a certain place.
Meditating with deluded understanding, they are intent on what ought to be done.
Having seen them, he inquired after their welfare and well-being.
They said to him: "O twice-born one, when our knowledge has perished, how can there be well-being for us? (8)
Then that Haṃsa, the king of birds, spoke to all those sages.
I shall reveal that knowledge; listen to it, O best of beings.
Having heard these auspicious words spoken by the high-souled Haṃsa, [he was filled with joy].
The high-souled ones said to Haṃsa: "O best of the twice-born, become our protector! (3.226.10)
Through the destruction of ignorance, may the entire world in its totality perish for me no more.
"O great bird, first of all, tell us about yourself."
For we, whose wisdom has fallen away, do not know you, O one of great splendor.
The Swan spoke to those twice-born ones: "O best of the twice-born, I am Viṣṇu."
Having then recognized him as Viṣṇu, they quickly worshipped him.
And they spoke thus of the knowledge as it was declared by him, O Yādava.
And likewise, fearing its destruction, they imparted it secretly to their disciples.
From that time forward, however, only a few in this world have been possessors of knowledge.
Having done this, Viṣṇu, in the form of a swan, destroyed that knowledge and bestowed it upon the foremost of the brahmins.
O hero among men, once that knowledge was attained, all the foremost of the brahmins on earth were freed from sorrow.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of the Haṃsa," in the Haṃsagītā within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||226||
Vajra said:
What was said by that swan to the sages of purified souls?
Cut through this doubt of mine, O enhancer of the Bhṛgu lineage! ||1||
Mārkaṇḍeya said:
Much was said by that swan concerning the sages of purified souls.
Therefore, I shall say something; listen to me as I speak it. || 2 ||
The sages said:
O best of the twice-born, tell me the dharma of the social classes and the stages of life.
Likewise, what may be eaten and what may not be eaten, as well as purity and impurity; ||3||
The swan said:
Sacrificing, officiating at sacrifices, giving gifts, and receiving distinguished gifts.
Teaching and studying are proclaimed as the duties of a Brahmin. || 4 ||
Giving, study, sacrifice, cattle-rearing, and trade;
And non-miserliness, O knower of dharma; for dharma is considered to be common to all.
In the direct order of the castes, the offspring shall belong to the same caste as the mother.
All those born in the inverse order of castes are despised by the noble ones.
The Sūta, the Vaidehaka, and the Cāṇḍāla, O best of the twice-born.
The sons of a Brāhmaṇī woman born from the wombs of Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras are thus to be known. || 7 ||
The Māgadha and the Pukkasa are the two sons of a Kṣatriya woman born from Vaiśya and Śūdra fathers respectively.
And the son of a Śūdra born of a Vaiśya woman is proclaimed as an Āyogava. || 8 ||
Others, arising from a mixture [of lineages], cannot be described because of that very confusion.
Their marriage is with equals, and not with those who are superior or inferior.
The duty of the Sūtas is the management of horses and chariots; that of the Māgadhas is the performance of praise.
A Vaideha becomes a Tantrijīva, and for Pukkasas, the state of a hunter.
The crafts of the Āyogava, as well as his entering the arena for performance, [are his duties].
There shall be no contact with Caṇḍālas, as well as the state of widowhood. || 11 ||
For those who have been slain in battle for the sake of cows and Brahmins, or even for the sake of women and children, or for the sake of the whole [world].
If those performing tasks for the sake of their master attain success, there is indeed no doubt in this matter. || 12 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of the Social Classes," in the *Haṃsagītā* within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Having initiated the disciple, the teacher should first instruct him in the rules of purification.
Proper conduct, the fire-ritual, and likewise the twilight worship; || 1 ||
Having risen at dawn with a disciplined mind, bathed, and offered oblations into the fire;
Having approached the teacher, he should perform a respectful salutation with self-restraint. || 2 ||
Once permitted by the teacher, he should then engage in study.
Then he should practice the life of a mendicant among Brāhmaṇas according to the prescribed rule.
One should not beg for alms within the family of the guru; one should eat only with his permission.
Free from egoism, he should perform with devotion whatever work of his guru is beneficial and pleasing. || 4 ||
Honey, meat, collyrium, the ancestral rite (śrāddha), dancing, singing, and rashness;
One should avoid violence, slandering others, and ornamentation.
One who is self-restrained should always carry a girdle, an antelope skin, and a staff.
Having cast those that are ruined into the water, one should likewise preserve the others as well.
He should always sleep on the ground, remain celibate, and be composed in mind.
A wise man, observing such a vow, should undertake the acquisition of the Vedas.
Having given his word to the guru, he should bathe with his permission.
Or else, O twice-born ones, they may dwell in the teacher's household until liberation from the body.

Thus, at the conclusion of his vows, having bestowed the sacrificial fee upon the preceptor as prescribed, the eminent twice-born, possessing perfected knowledge, shall duly enter the householder stage; for it is ordained that the journey to the second world begins from there.

Thus ends the two hundred and twenty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Vow of the Religious Student," in the *Haṃsagītā* within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Haṃsa said:
Then, remaining in the householder stage of life and having established the sacred fires, he who knows the Dharma—
Having performed the marriage according to the prescribed rites and through righteous means, he acquired wealth. || 1 ||
There, one should pursue the three aims of life and worship with various sacrifices.
One should observe the rules of conduct and likewise engage in the study of the Vedas.
One should perform the formal abandonment (utsarga) of the Vedic meters at the end of the bright fortnight of the month of Śrāvaṇa.
The commencement of Vedic study (upākarma) is prescribed under the asterism Rohiṇī in the month of Pauṣa.
After performing the ritual of suspension (utsarga), one should never study the Veda at any time.
Even there, the study of the scriptures is prescribed for the twice-born.
Effort must be made in honoring guests; this duty should be performed by householders at all times.
No other dharma exists for him; O brahmins, this dharma is declared to be his supreme one.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Yoga of Auspicious Omens in the Song of the Swan to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third book of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
The sages said:
What are those faults that, though they suppress the sins of men, lead to their destruction?

The swan said:

The study of the scriptures and likewise service to the elderly.

Thus ends the two hundred and thirty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Knowledge," within the *Haṃsagītā* in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Through evil, a person becomes a vessel for all sufferings.

The wretched, the blind, the miserable, the protectorless, as well as very young children. || 4 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fortieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Manifestation of Sin," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
A man who follows after desires perishes along with those desires.
But he who is solely devoted to sensual desires is soon deprived of his prosperity.
A man who follows his desires does not long abide by the Dharma and its purpose.
Therefore, a man should not indulge in sensual desire that is devoid of virtue and purpose.
When sensual pleasure is pursued, the destruction of both dharma and artha is certain.
One blinded by desire understands only that which ought to be done.
But regarding another's wife or an unapproachable woman, he does not perceive the precipice.

When dharma has perished and likewise when wealth and sensual pleasure are indulged in, O twice-born one.
A fall into hell is certain; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
For a man who pursues desire while it is joined with righteousness and purpose is never truly overcome by desires.
Consequently, the wise man experiences separation [from his goals]; therefore, he should constantly devote himself to that which is joined with dharma and artha.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Deeds of Desire," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 241 ||
The swan said:
The wise should never, under any circumstances, allow themselves excessive joy.
A man who is excessively delighted understands nothing at all regarding his duty.
Having obtained prosperity that is as fickle as lightning, the wise man should abandon all elation.
For many have been seen in this world who, though suspended by prosperity, have perished. || 2 ||
Whether in prosperity or in adversity, a wise person should not abandon their true nature.
O twice-born ones, all prosperities are indeed fickle by their very nature.
What wise man would trust them, just as one would not trust courtesans?
Through association with them, a human being falls into delusion.
All accumulations end in exhaustion; all elevations end in a fall.
Unions end in separation, for life ends in death.
Wisdom is not for the acquisition of wealth, nor is dullness for the sake of lack of prosperity.
The wise man understands the history and the various states of the world, but no one else does.
But the wise man, having understood her to be thoroughly fickle, should abandon all joy upon obtaining her.
One should not experience sorrow at the destruction of prosperity; what is destined to happen will happen, for there is no escaping it.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Excessive Joy," within the Haṃsagītā, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. ||242||
The swan said:

And likewise, a person certainly performs improper deeds through pride.
For one seized by the grasping of pride, there is no liberation whatsoever.
Lust, anger, and greed are the destroyers of all living beings.
But when a man is seized by pride, O best of the twice-born, [vices] enter him.
And one who is overcome by pride likewise falls into hell.
O best of men, he is without foundation; therefore, one should avoid him.
There is no enemy equal to pride for a man; through pride, a living being goes to destruction in this world.
Therefore, pride should indeed always be avoided by the wise, for it is the path to hell.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fault of Pride," in the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Arrogance, which has been abandoned by the virtuous, should be avoided with great effort.
For many faults arise from this, which cause ruin in both worlds. || 1 ||
Intoxicated, he does not recognize his duty and even treats his teachers with contempt.
O Brahmins, for the intoxicated man, the gate to hell is perpetually open.
The intoxicated man knows no fear, even of death, which is most loathsome.
Intoxicated and fallen into delusion, he does not perceive anything at all. || 3 ||
Among all forms of intoxication, it should be known that intoxication from drinking is the lowest.
A person overcome by that is not superior to one who is dead. || 4 ||
Indeed, there is no fault equal to ignorance, and its cause here is supreme intoxication.
Therefore, a person should, with diligent effort, completely avoid drinking, which is the cause of intoxication. ||5||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Pride," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
The greedy man does not recognize faults; the greedy man does not perceive evil.
A man possessed by greed likewise falls under the power of calamities. || 1 ||
The hair of one who grows old decays; the nails of one who grows old decay.
The teeth decay as one grows old, but craving alone does not decay.
O best of the twice-born, this pit of craving is unfathomable and unprecedented.
Though it is constantly being filled, it is dug out even more by that [thirst]. || 3 ||
No one at any time is ever able to fill it.
Even all beings who have taken refuge in contentment are not able to fill it. || 4 ||
Whatever rice and barley, gold, cattle, and women there are upon the earth—
Thinking that "this is not enough for even one person," one should attain tranquility.
That which is difficult for the wicked-minded to abandon, and which does not decay even as one decays.
For one who abandons that craving which is a life-ending disease, there is happiness.
For the greedy man there is no kinsman, nor son, nor teacher; for the greedy man there are no higher worlds, nor even the way of worldly life.
All the faults of the greedy person have been declared by the hosts of gods to cause suffering in both worlds.

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Greed," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Anger alone is the supreme enemy; anger alone is the cause of destruction.
A person overcome by anger may even destroy himself. || 1 ||
He does not distinguish between what is beneficial and what is harmful, nor likewise between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
A man possessed by anger does not [distinguish] anyone else, even his own friend, O twice-born ones. || 2 ||
Out of anger he insults his gurus, for people do not bow down before him.
Association with harmful things arises from that; therefore, one should abandon anger.
Anger is the root of all misfortunes and indeed the gateway to hell.
One should avoid with every effort that which is a terrible abode of calamities.
How can he who has been conquered by anger defeat another?
Know that when anger is conquered, the three worlds, including all things moving and stationary, are conquered.
When anger, which causes harm, is considered to be one's brilliance;
Therefore, having recognized the fault in anger, anger has been conquered by the great-souled ones.
Sacrifices, gifts, austerity, the purifying power of sacred fords, and likewise the Vedas—these too are [means of purification].
For a man overcome by anger, false [views] arise; therefore, one should avoid that [anger]. || 7 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Anger," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Among all sins, atheism is the greatest transgression.
O best of the twice-born, there is indeed no sin greater than atheism.
Having performed actions that ought not to be done, a man, under the influence of those very deeds, [suffers].
Endowed with remorse, one quickly casts off evil. || 2 ||
But that lowest of men who, with the thought that they are his duties, performs what ought not to be done;
O twice-born ones, how indeed does his turning away from them come about?
Likewise, the root of nihilism is immersion in false scriptures.
Therefore, one who understands this should avoid it with every effort. ||4||
For every human being in this world is bound to the next world.
Even in that case, what indeed would be the worldly basis for one who is independent?
But those men in the world who are atheists regarding the next world, O twice-born ones, [are as follows].
For they are cooked in hell for a long time; of this there is no doubt. ||6||
O best of Brahmins, it is declared that atheism alone is the destruction of a person in this world.
Therefore, those who desire happiness should strive with effort to avoid a state of nihilism. ||7||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Fault of Atheism," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
In this world, there is nothing that destroys more than the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra).
By means of egoism, hundreds of kings have met their destruction.
Likewise, thousands of Brahmins have been ruined by their sense of egoism.
Puffed up with egoism, they do not distinguish between what is worthy of respect and what is not, nor between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
Likewise, one who is possessed by egoism does not attain knowledge in this world.
And likewise, one whose business has failed does not consult with the wise. || 3 ||
Likewise, one who is full of pride, though appearing wise, does not listen to others.
There is no medicine other than falling; out of pride, there is no renown here.
Likewise by those superior in strength, by heroes, and similarly by the gurus.
Even when death is imminent, the wise man remains discerning regarding death. || 5 ||
He practices censurable actions that serve as the causes [of his downfall].
He reviles those who are wise, even as they stand still or speak.
For those who act with egoism and are censured by the world, their destination is certainly ordained to be hell.
Therefore, a wise person should always avoid pride, which invariably leads only to destruction. //7//

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Ego," in the *Haṃsagītā* within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
The deities do not accept that which is given by one who is devoid of purity.
And those desirous of knowledge, the knowers of dharma, and the deities who long for purity. || 1 ||
And by yakṣas, as well as by rākṣasas and piśācas who roam at night.
And by the ḍākinīs; for one who knows the Dharma but is devoid of purity is overcome. || 2 ||
O twice-born ones, when one approaches someone devoid of purity, whom does he himself blame?
For one who is free from disease yet impure is overcome by everyone. || 3 ||
In that way, misfortunes increase, and even those who are capable meet their end.
O twice-born ones, the enemies of one who is devoid of purity attain supreme growth.
O twice-born ones, there is purity regarding women, purity regarding wealth, and also purity of speech.
He who possesses these purifications is proclaimed to be pure.
He who is pure in purpose is truly pure; he is not pure merely by means of water or clay.
Furthermore, purity greater than that is proclaimed to be non-violence (ahiṃsā). || 6 ||
Those devoid of purity go to hell; those devoid of purity bring about misfortunes.
Those who are devoid of purity become objects of reproach; therefore, impurity must be completely avoided. || 7 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and forty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of Purity," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
O twice-born ones, men who are devoid of proper conduct become short-lived.
And likewise, one who is devoid of proper conduct is overcome by Rākṣasas.
By yakṣas, piśācas, gandharvas, and likewise by other night-stalkers.
The hosts of attendants of the gods were likewise [separated] individually by the ḍākinīs. ||2||
The deities do not accept what has been given by one who is devoid of proper conduct.
And the Pitṛs, O highly fortunate one, as well as the sages whose wealth is their asceticism. || 3 ||
Even if a man is endowed with all auspicious marks, if he is devoid of proper conduct, [he is of no account].
In that way, one does not attain knowledge, nor does one obtain anything desired.
A person devoid of proper conduct falls into hell. || 4 ||
The Vedas do not purify one who is devoid of right conduct, even if they have been studied along with the six auxiliary sciences.
But indeed, every religious act performed by one devoid of proper conduct becomes futile in this world. || 5 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fiftieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Improper Conduct in the Songs of the Haṃsa to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
One should always avoid falsehood; falsehood is the supreme sin.
For there is nothing superior to untruth as a door to the destruction of the self. || 1 ||
All expressed meanings are bound to speech; they are rooted in speech and have issued forth from speech.
Therefore, one who desires his own welfare should not steal speech.
Untruth should never be spoken, especially when giving testimony.
For one who speaks falsehood when giving testimony sinks into hell along with his ancestors. || 3 ||
One kills five by lying about cattle; one kills ten by lying about cows.
One kills a hundred horses by lying; one kills a thousand men by lying. || 4 ||
By speaking untruth for the sake of gold, one destroys both those already born and those yet to be born.
It destroys every falsehood regarding land; therefore, one should never speak a lie concerning land.
They say that women are like the earth in their waters, in their enjoyment, and in sexual intercourse.
And likewise among lotuses, gems, and all things made of stone.
Having considered all these faults in speaking untruth, [one should refrain from it].
One should speak everything exactly as it was heard and exactly as it was seen, straightforwardly.
Naked, shaven-headed, and carrying a skull-bowl, he was a beggar tormented by hunger and thirst.
A blind man should not go to an enemy's house, nor should he speak false testimony.
Speaking falsehood in testimony, one is bound tightly with the nooses of Varuṇa.
They settle into that same class; therefore, one should speak the truth in testimony.
Whatever sin has been spoken of by me regarding a twice-born man who gives false testimony, [that shall be his].
One immediately incurs even greater [sin] by making a false accusation.
Just as [one might act] out of anger, fear, greed, or ignorance, O best of the twice-born;
He who speaks untruth to the virtuous certainly goes to hell. || 11 ||
Headlong into blind darkness, the sinner shall fall into hell.
He who, when questioned regarding the determination of the true Dharma, should speak falsely in response to the question; || 12 ||
Like a blind man, he devours fish along with their bones, without any discrimination.
He who, having entered the assembly, speaks of a deficiency in meaning or of that which is not perceived [by others]. ||13||
In fraudulent weighing and measuring, as well as in the adulteration of liquids;
In the misappropriation of entrusted deposits and the disclosure of secrets; || 14 ||
And he who imagines death [to result] from honey or meat commits a sin.
Or even for a twice-born man, [this occurs] through liquor, and especially through greed. || 15 ||
Or likewise in the case of killing a cow or a Brahmin, as well as in the killing of one's teacher or father.
In approaching the wife of a friend, or in showing the wife of one's guru; || 16 ||
And in the exposition of weapons, as well as in the destruction of weapons.
In misappropriating the sustenance provided by one's master, and in fleeing from battle; ||17||
Abandoning one who has sought refuge, and approaching a woman by day;
There is sin for one who goes to a female servant, and likewise for one who commits treason against the king. || 18 ||
And likewise, the śrāddha offered by one who gives unequally among the row, as well as that offered to a friend.
Of one who gives his daughter for a bride-price, and of a seller of hair; || 19 ||
Whatever sin belongs to a Brahmin, and that which arises from the sale of living beings;
[The same fate awaits] one who eats at a funeral rite (śrāddha) for raw food, and one who officiates at a sacrifice for those unworthy to sacrifice.
They are false in their governance of the kingdom and are stealers of the property of others.
A twice-born man who is a member of the assembly incurs all these sins. || 21 ||
If he should speak otherwise than that, the member of the court should always speak what is consistent with the Dharma.
This very same sin is to be understood as belonging to false witnesses. || 22 ||
But one who performs fraudulent acts sinks into hell together with his ancestors.
For ten thousand years and ten hundred years. ||23||
For ten times that duration, one who speaks falsely in an assembly [suffers].
But a king who acts out of passion and hatred, even in his worldly affairs, [is ruined]. || 24 ||
Then he certainly dwells in hell for a period ten times that length.
But when these words of dharma have been spoken, one is immediately liberated from sin.
A king incurs hell by transgressing a truthful statement.
In cases where the death penalty has been prescribed for Śūdras, Vaiśyas, Kṣatriyas, or Brāhmaṇas, one shall undergo that same punishment. || 26 ||
In that case, a falsehood must be spoken, for it is superior to the truth.
And [he worshipped] Sarasvatī with oblations of sacrificial porridge (caru) dedicated to the deities of speech and with sacrifices. ||27||
Or one should offer clarified butter into the fire with the Kūṣmāṇḍa mantras according to the prescribed rule.
Or he should offer it with the verse beginning "ud u tyam," which is dedicated to Varuṇa, or with a verse whose deity is Speech. ||28||
Performing the supreme expiation for that falsehood, he fell under its power.
Many prosper in happiness when that [tree] has been struck down by the wise.
"When his slaughter is at hand, he must speak the truth as it is"—such is the sacred revelation (śruti). || 29 ||
O Brahmins, a word spoken in jest does not cause harm, nor does one spoken to women, nor at the time of marriage.
In a life-threatening emergency, or when all one's wealth is being seized, they say that five kinds of falsehoods are not sinful. (3.251.30)

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Untruth in the Songs of the Swan to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa.
The swan said:
Indeed, among all evils, violence is said here to be the supreme.
Violence is the strength of the wicked; violence is the destroyer of both worlds.
Not even an insect or a moth should ever be killed under any circumstances.
A person incurs great suffering by killing living beings. || 2 ||
If one encounters an assassin approaching, whether he be a man or even a beast.
Having killed him by means of a stratagem, one is not afflicted by sin. || 3 ||
Whether it be a teacher, a child, an elder, or even a person worthy of respect;
One should indeed kill an approaching assassin without hesitation.
One should slay an assassin who comes upon him in battle, even if he has reached the further shore of the Vedanta.
One may strike back at one who seeks to kill; by that, no sin is incurred.
There is no sin whatsoever in striking an enemy who has been struck down in battle.
If he is captured after being defeated or slain, there is sin in that very act.
That man who, being capable of conquering in battle, subsequently causes himself to fall, [is a fool].
He goes to a terrible hell for many hundreds of years.
And he was liberated from the suffering of hell after many hundreds of years.
Those men who are slayers of humans are poured into raw wombs.
As many hairs as there are on the animal's body, for that many times shall one undergo death here.
One who slaughters animals in vain obtains no atonement either in this world or after death.
Even by killing an insect, or even by cutting a blade of grass, a person [incurs sin].
O knowers of dharma, a man goes to hell by his own action.
Violence against women, violence against wealth, and violence against living beings are all terrible.
Violence is said to be of three kinds, and it is avoided by wise men. || 11 ||
But one who is non-violent should, with effort, avoid the wife of another.
Likewise, one should carefully return another's property even when it has been left in a secluded place. || 12 ||
Therefore, one must certainly not commit violence against living beings, for it brings about fear.
Having deprived a living being of its life-breaths, even a single one, he was likewise merciless.
For once liberated from hell, one does not increase in any happiness whatsoever.
The night on which a woman is wedded, and likewise the night she is defeated at dice; || 14 ||
The night that he was deprived of his kingdom, and the night that he was deprived of all his possessions.
And separated from beloved kinsmen, he experiences suffering throughout the night.
And the suffering that comes from being defeated in a legal proceeding due to false witnesses.
O twice-born ones, one incurs all that suffering even by killing just a single [creature]. (16)
There is nothing more sinful in the world than men who eat meat.
External flesh arises from grass, wood, or even from stone.
A person should completely avoid that which arises from the terrible slaughter of living beings.
If there were no eater, likewise there would be no killer. (18)
For this reason, the eater is more blameworthy than even the killer.
For as many living beings as have eaten one's flesh here in this world, [one must suffer for each].
Those very wombs of yours are certainly not so many that they must be traversed.
But for those living beings, O best of the twice-born, by whom that meat was eaten, [the same fate awaits].
His flesh shall certainly be eaten by them in birth after birth.
"He who eats my flesh here, he shall be eaten by me for his flesh in the next world. (21)
The wise declare this to be the "meat-ness" (essence) of meat.
And the origin of meat, as well as the slaughter and bondage of embodied beings.
Having carefully considered this, one should desist from the eating of all meat.
The one who consents, the one who dismembers, the one who kills, and the one who buys or sells [the meat]. || 23 ||
The preparer, the server, the eaters, and the destroyers [all share in the karmic result].
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another. || 24 ||
Indeed, there exists no one else in the world who is a greater evildoer than he.
A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, eat unprepared animals using mantras.
Having resorted to the eternal rule, one should eat [the food] consecrated by mantras.
For that violence which is ordained by the Vedas is not considered violence. (25)
Herbs, animals, trees, as well as crawling creatures and birds;
Having met their end for the sake of sacrifice, they attain exalted states once again.
At the honey-mixture offering, at a sacrifice, and at rites for the ancestors and the gods.
For animals are to be sacrificed only here, and never elsewhere. || 28 ||
Knowing the true meaning of reality, the twice-born slaughter animals for these purposes.
They cause both themselves and the sacrificial animals to attain the highest state. || 29 ||
Animals were created by the Self-Existent One in the beginning for the purpose of sacrifice.
And sacrifices are for all beings; therefore, in a sacrifice, killing is non-killing.
But a man who eats meat in vain, O Brahmins, goes to a most terrible hell.
The destruction of a living being is indeed censurable; therefore, meat must be completely avoided. || 31 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Violence," within the *Haṃsagītā* of the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
Tell us, O best of the twice-born, how a man [is affected] by sinful action.
O knower of dharma, O great-minded lord of birds, what does one obtain? || 1 ||
The Swan said:
O Brahmins, having committed evil, a man falls into hell.
And having been released from hell, he likewise goes to the womb of an animal.
Through the defects of actions born of the body, a person goes to the state of being stationary.
Through verbal [sins] one attains the state of birds or wild animals; through mental [sins], the state of those born of the lowest castes.
The destinies of human beings—whether superior, inferior, or middling—are born of their karma.
They are taught to be threefold, characterized by ten marks.
Coveting the property of others and harboring evil thoughts in the mind.
And false attachment, as well as the threefold mental action. (5)
Harsh speech, falsehood, and slander in every form;
And idle chatter; thus, that which consists of speech is fourfold.
Taking what is not given and violence contrary to the prescribed rules.
And serving another's wife is recorded as the threefold bodily [sin]. || 7 ||
Therefore, O Brahmins, one should practice even a single one of these ten characteristics.
When, having obtained human birth through unrighteousness, one becomes miserable; || 8 ||
In this world, some [suffer] due to their own misdeeds, while others likewise due to those committed in the past.
Evil-minded men undergo a transformation of their appearance.
A killer of a Brahmin shall suffer from consumption; one who violates the Guru's bed shall have a skin disease.
One with black teeth, a drinker of liquor, one with deformed nails, and a stealer of gold. || 3.253.10 ||
A stealer of clothing becomes afflicted with vitiligo; a stealer of horses becomes lame.
In that same way, one who steals all vehicles should be known as being like a cripple. || 11 ||
Furthermore, that lowest of men who has stolen a cow is born in the world below.
A thief of grain has an extra limb; a stealer of speech is mute. || 12 ||
One who reviles one's guru, master, or twice-born brahmins, as well as those who revile the Vedas;
Having heard it, that lowest of men becomes dull-witted and deaf. || 13 ||
Likewise, one who steals food becomes chronically ill.
Likewise, one who is afflicted by disease [is purified] even by depriving a single living being of its life.
Those who steal clothing or food, as well as those who remain naked or hungry, [are likewise reborn as such].
And thus, overcome by indigestion, he becomes dull-witted. || 15 ||
O best of the twice-born, he who offers oblations into a fire that is not kindled [commits a fault].
Likewise, one who steals gems becomes a leper, the lowest of men. || 16 ||
The slanderer has a putrid nose, and the informer has a putrid mouth.
And such a person is born in this world as a eunuch who transgresses against his wife. || 17 ||
Or if he gives her to another man, his wife shall likewise become such.
Likewise, one who steals a woman becomes afflicted with leprosy, even if he is a knower of dharma.
One who engages in sexual intercourse with a non-vaginal opening incurs the disease of the genitals.
And having gone to Gāṃ, O best of the twice-born, one shall attain Liṅganāśa.
One who insults those worthy of worship becomes bald; one who strikes those worthy of worship becomes a person with a withered arm.
And that evil-minded person who does not grant the path to one who deserves the path. || 3.253.20 ||
One of poor intellect becomes lame by giving a seat to one who is worthy of a seat.
One who is ill-famed, constantly self-restrained, envious, and deceitful is born [as such]. || 21 ||
One who steals a lamp becomes blind, and one who extinguishes it becomes one-eyed.
Having performed an action with knowledge obtained from fate, the one of evil mind—
He is born with eyes like bubbles, or else he is afflicted with eye diseases.
Having seen another's wife naked with a wicked eye, a man [commits an offense].
He attains the state of being blind from birth in the next world; of this there is no doubt. || 23 ||
Having lived as one of superior caste, [to fall] through an action unworthy of that caste.
He enters the very womb of that [being]; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 24 ||
In the same way, if one of a higher caste survives by means of his own occupation, [he remains pure].
Likewise, that evil-minded one becomes blind and of low caste in this world. || 25 ||
If a twice-born man should ever meet his death while the food of another remains in his stomach, [he incurs that sin].
He attains the very womb of that [being] through his own performed action. || 26 ||
Likewise, by eating at a funeral rite for the uncooked (āmaśrāddha), a man is born deformed.
He indeed becomes deformed by selling what ought not to be sold. || 27 ||
Having thus superseded his wife without cause, he commits an offense.
He meets with defeat both in legal dispute and likewise in battle. || 28 ||
Having thus performed the root-rite for the purpose of subjugation.
He becomes hateful in this world; of this there is no doubt. || 29 ||
And he becomes one who has spilled his seed, afflicted with diseases of the male organ.
Likewise, in this world, the one who marries before his elder brother is afflicted with all manner of diseases.
One who officiates at the sacrifice of those unworthy to sacrifice becomes a sinful person who causes the intermixture of castes.
He is born as a fool who sells the Vedas and also as a gambler. || 31 ||
Likewise, knowledge becomes useless for one who sells what ought not to be sold.
In this world, one who eats delicious food alone becomes a source of thirst for others.
But the wandering mendicant who acts out of desire is constantly miserable.
Likewise, the man who delights in violence and eats meat shall have a short lifespan. || 33 ||
But an atheist shall be poor and deprived of all enjoyments.
But one who is given over to excessive pride is born into a contemptible family. || 34 ||
Of those who are despised and devoid of consciousness, such as the Śvapākas, Pukkasas, and others.
They are born into those families as those who show respect and deference to their teachers and elders. || 35 ||
One who delights constantly in causing distress to others is born with many afflictions.
O twice-born ones, a living being who engages in promiscuous sexual intercourse indeed becomes a eunuch.
A man of evil conduct meets with a contemptible death.
In this world, death occurs in a pit, or from poison, whether stationary or mobile. (37)
From fanged creatures, from clawed beasts, from outcasts, and likewise from Brahmins.
And likewise from the collapse of houses, as well as by trees and horses falling upon them. || 38 ||
From the breaking of a boat, from being consumed by fire, and likewise from the act of hanging oneself;
And death from cattle is to be known in this world as the lot of the evildoer. || 39 ||
Having encountered any one of these deaths, he shall go to hell.
And those men who perform auspicious deeds are joined with all nine of these as well.
In this world, one who has been beaten is beaten again, and likewise, one who is bound is bound once more.
The slayer incurs death; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 41 ||
Whatever one practices for another, that very thing arises for oneself. || 42 ||
One incurs whatever harm another suffers when that same action is performed [by oneself].
For him as well, such an affliction is to be known in birth after birth. (43)
Therefore, with every effort, one should avoid the affliction of evil.
Listen to the essence of all dharma, and having heard it, let it be firmly grasped.
One should not do to others what is disagreeable to oneself. || 44 ||
One should not engage in the act of harming others for the sake of acquiring wealth, as it produces a multitude of faults.
For a fault born from the injury of others cannot be destroyed even in the abode of the gods.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Sinful Actions," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Knowledge brings happiness in the world; knowledge is considered the supreme eye.
Through knowledge a person attains dharma, and through knowledge he attains wealth. || 1 ||
Through knowledge one obtains desire, and through knowledge one attains liberation.
Therefore, with every effort, one should apply oneself to the cultivation of knowledge. || 2 ||
Through knowledge, one attains everything that one desires in the mind.
Likewise, constant study of the scriptures is the sole cause of knowledge. || 3 ||
Service to teachers and gurus, as well as attendance upon the elderly.
Freedom from laziness, absence of meanness, and avoidance of sleeping during the day. || 4 ||
Knowledge is this supreme kinsman; knowledge is the guide of the path.
Likewise, one is liberated from the afflictions that bind one to saṃsāra through knowledge. ||5||
Through knowledge a person knows; from knowledge one attains detachment.
Through knowledge one attains that, having gone to which, one does not grieve.
Having understood this, O you of undaunted spirit, a person should always exert effort toward knowledge.
Having attained knowledge, those of great majesty become happy, freed from suffering. || 7 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Knowledge," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Effort should always be made in the Dharma; the Dharma alone brings happiness.
By means of Dharma, the entire triple world, including all that is moving and unmoving, is sustained. || 1 ||
They say it is called *dharma* because of its upholding; *dharma* sustains all living beings.
When dharma is practiced, one obtains the desires wished for by the mind. || 2 ||
In this world, one thus obtains through righteousness the wealth desired by the mind.
Having cast off the dead body upon the earth like a piece of wood or a clod of earth.
Relatives depart with averted faces, but Dharma alone follows after one.
Even when a single day has passed devoid of dharma, [it brings great loss].
It is fitting that he should lament for a long time, like one who has been robbed by bandits.
One should practice dharma by force alone, since life is impermanent. || 5 ||
O twice-born ones, there is not even the slightest happiness for one who is devoid of dharma.
By means of dharma, the gods attained godhood, and likewise the sages attained the state of sageship.
The entire world was obtained through Dharma and was created by Brahmā.
He by whom all this was created—Hari indeed abides as that Dharma.
There is no destruction of dharma once it has been performed; therefore, dharma must be practiced by a person.
O best of the twice-born, when one acts in accordance with dharma, there is no fear for men, neither in this world nor in the next.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Dharma," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Service to the guru should be known as the supreme cause of dharma.
Through service to the teacher, a person fully attains knowledge. || 1 ||
Through knowledge one attains that state, having gone to which one does not grieve.
Three kinds of men search the earth for flowers of gold.
One who is brave, learned, and knows how to serve.
Although devoid of all religious merit, he was devoted to the service of his teacher.
Even a most cruel man attains the heavenly world.
Whether it be one's mother, father, or even one's elder brother. ||4||
Or that man who serves his guru or the one who bestows knowledge.
One attains the heavenly world for as long as the reign of fourteen Indras.
Whatever merit a twice-born man obtains through service to his teacher, [he obtains that same merit by studying this work].
A Śūdra, by serving the twice-born, enjoys that very same fruit. ||6||
That virtuous woman who serves her husband with vigilance attains supreme merit.
In the world of men, it is declared that the highest merit for subjects comes from service to the lord of the earth. ||7||

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Service to the Guru," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
The practice of self-study must always be performed by one who possesses true knowledge.
Through the private recitation of the Veda, one obtains whatever one desires in the mind. || 1 ||
With milk, honey, curd, and meat, respectively.
One should likewise recite the Ṛgveda, Yajurveda, Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaveda.
One should perform the libation for the ancestors with clarified butter mixed with the Vedic auxiliary sciences.
Reciting even the Upavedas, he satisfies them with the cooked rice.
Likewise, a man [should act] according to his own will, without regard for all formal positions.
He who studies the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāñcarātra, and likewise the Pāśupata [scriptures].
In that same way, one satisfies the ancestors with milk mixed with honey.
The dialogues, the Purāṇas, the Nārāśaṃsī hymns, and the Gāthās. ||5||
And constantly reciting hymns of praise, with curd as well as honey.
Therefore, a twice-born man should practice the study of his own Veda with every effort.
In this world, the study of the Vedas alone is the purifying austerity; in this world, the study of the Vedas alone is likewise the sacrifice.
The man who is devoted to the private recitation of sacred texts goes to heaven, or even attains his desired liberation. ||7||

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Vedic Study," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*, [the dialogue between] Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra. || 257 ||
The swan said:
A twice-born man who is fully devoted to the practice of celibacy attains heaven.
Celibacy is the supreme abode; celibacy is the supreme austerity.
Celibacy is the supreme sacrifice; celibacy is the supreme glory.
Endowed with celibacy, one shall attain all desires.
One may turn a non-deity into a deity, and even a deity into a non-deity.
In the same way, a human being may create other worlds through the practice of celibacy.
Likewise, one should cause even previously committed [sins] to perish very quickly.
By means of celibacy, a human being attains whatever he desires. || 4 ||
O best of the twice-born, that power which belongs to the Prajāpatis to create progeny—
O twice-born ones, she is to be known through the practice of celibacy even by the sages.
Many thousands of those who practice celibacy from their youth.
They have gone to heaven, O Brahmins, without having established the continuity of their lineage.
He who has not fallen away from the holy life (brahmacarya) goes to heaven, even if he is destitute of a son.
For those who have fallen away and are deprived of their offspring, no destination in the worlds is prescribed.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Celibacy," within the *Haṃsagītā* in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
But that man who has fallen from the holy life (brahmacarya) is devoid of progeny.
Even for one who has performed well-heated austerities, no higher destination exists in this world. || 1 ||
Through a son one conquers the worlds; through a grandson one attains immortality.
Likewise, through his son's grandson, he attains the realm of the Sun.
O best of the twice-born, one attains the world of the gods by means of a daughter.
In the same way, through a daughter's son, a man goes to the worlds of Prajāpati.
Because a son saves his father from the hell named Punnāma, [he is called "son"].
Therefore, he was called "Putra" by Svayambhū himself.
In this world, no distinction is found between a son and a daughter.
For even a daughter's son rescues him in the hereafter, just like a grandson.
Therefore, he shall be the destroyer of the lineage; he goes certainly to hell.
Surrounded by sons and grandsons, he is glorified in the world of the gods.
O best of the twice-born, a man who possesses a lineage shall likewise be endowed with supreme fame.
Endowed with fame, that preeminent man who possesses progeny then proceeds to heaven.

Thus ends the two hundred and fifty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Progeny," within the *Haṃsagītā* in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
A person preeminent in fame is honored in heaven for a long time.
Fame is declared to be the body of an embodied being, even after death. || 1 ||
A person does not recognize one endowed with fame, neither in this world nor in the next.
Endowed with fame in this world, they become supreme vessels for spiritual welfare.
The sound of meritorious action touches both heaven and earth.
As long as that sound exists, so long is it called "person. || 3 ||
At that very moment, he likewise [created] worlds that were inexhaustible and yielded all desires.
A person enjoys this eternally, both in heaven and here on earth. || 4 ||
That man whose reputation is ill-famed goes indeed to hell.
As long as he remains in the worlds, his fame as a knower of Dharma is sung.
For that long he enjoys unsurpassed divine pleasures in heaven.
Virtuous fame in the world of merit never brings about evil.
Since it is proclaimed for a human being, one should therefore practice merit.
Those eminent men who are endowed with fame go to the heights of heaven for a very long time.
Those joined with ill-repute go to hell; therefore, reputation is the most important thing for a person. || 7 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixtieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Fame," within the *Haṃsagītā* in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
A living being endowed with fame shall become a vessel for the highest good.
Endowed with glory, a living being attains the third heaven. || 1 ||
A person endowed with fame becomes a worthy recipient of prosperity.
A living being endowed with fame attains all desires. || 2 ||
He alone is a man of renown in this world who is indeed endowed with glory.
For whom the great fame of their virtuous gathering is sung. || 3 ||
Their fame and merit are likewise sung even upon the heights of heaven.
For that which the deities know, there is a certain attainment in the heavenly realm.
Likewise, he who hears his own fame being proclaimed by the virtuous.
The man who knows the Dharma attains a happiness even greater than that of heaven. || 5 ||
Fame is the splendor of a person; it is his supreme ornament.
For one devoid of fame in this world, ornamentation is merely a mark of disgrace.
Fame is the foremost thing for a person in this world; those who prioritize fame go to the third heaven.
And for those endowed with fame in both worlds, their desires become fulfilled exactly as they are wished for in the mind. || 7 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Fame," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
By sacrifice the gods live, and likewise the ancestors by sacrifice.
All subjects are dependent upon the gods, and the gods are dependent upon sacrifice.
For the Blessed Viṣṇu is the sacrifice, in whom everything is established.
"Beasts were created for the sake of sacrifice, as were the gods and likewise the medicinal herbs. (2)
Human beings were created by the Self-existent One himself for the sake of sacrifice.
And sacrifice leads to the prosperity of all; therefore, one should be devoted to sacrifice.
The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins.
The wise know that whatever wealth belongs to those whose nature is sacrifice is the property of the gods.
Of herbs and animals, the sacrifice alone is the ultimate refuge.
Together with his kinsmen and his family, he is glorified upon the vault of heaven.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, animals sprinkled with water at a sacrifice and medicinal herbs are the same.
Those who have been employed in sacrifice rejoice in the third heaven; there is no doubt about this.
Through sacrifice, the great-souled person, being perfectly fashioned in heaven by the thirty gods, [attains immortality].
Those of great majesty attain happiness; therefore, one should worship with sacrifices through diligent effort.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Sacrifice," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Virtue is preeminent in this world; upon it everything is established.
Through ethical discipline, one obtains everything whatsoever that one desires in the mind. || 1 ||
Actions performed by one who is devoid of moral discipline become fruitless.
Therefore, a discerning person should be possessed of virtuous conduct. || 2 ||
Through virtue, the King of Gods, Śakra, attained sovereignty over the deities.
By means of ethical discipline, even Dharmarāja attained the status of Dharmarāja. ||3||
By means of his virtue, the god Varuṇa attained the sovereignty of kings.
And through his virtue, even Kubera attained the status of the lord of wealth. || 4 ||
Through morality, O best of men, one attains happiness and heaven.
Through virtue one attains that state, having gone to which one does not grieve. || 5 ||
Having attained moral discipline, a preeminent person obtains all primary desires.
Therefore, a person should always diligently cultivate virtuous conduct, for it is the perpetual bestower of happiness. (6)

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Virtuous Conduct," within the *Haṃsa-gītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
A person endowed with self-restraint shall attain all desires.
Therefore, one who possesses discernment should practice self-restraint with every effort. || 1 ||
The conquest of the senses in this world is designated as self-control (dama).
O best of the twice-born, no ritual actions whatsoever are effective for one who has not mastered the inner sound (nāda).
One who has not mastered the internal sound (nāda) does not attain perfection, nor does one who has not mastered the internal sound attain the desired goal.
One who does not master the sound (nāda) does not attain prosperity; indeed, one who does not master the sound attains nothing at all.
If even one sense-organ among the five senses of a mortal man is defective, [he fails].
Then his wisdom flows away, like water from a leather bag or a vessel. || 4 ||
Having abandoned the goals of human endeavor, he is constantly intent upon his own self-interest.
A wise man should strive for his own welfare regarding those very senses.
Through attachment to the senses, one goes to a terrible state.
Having conquered those very [senses], a man shall obtain all his desires. || 6 ||
The self-controlled man goes to the celestial realm; the self-controlled man proceeds upon the path to liberation.
For one who is self-controlled, there is indeed no suffering whatsoever; the self-controlled man attains all desires.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Self-Restraint," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Truth alone is the supreme Brahman; truth alone is the supreme austerity.
Truth alone is the supreme sacrifice; truth alone is the supreme sacred learning. || 1 ||
Truth awakens within the Vedas; liberation is the fruit of the tree of truth.
Austerity, fame, merit, and the worship of ancestors, gods, and sages; ||2||
The primary ritual and knowledge—all is established in truth.
Truth, sacrifices, the Vedas, and the goddess Sarasvatī—[these are the protectors]. (3)
Likewise, the practice of vows, truth, the syllable Om, and indeed truth itself.
By truth the wind blows; by truth the sun shines. || 4 ||
By truth the fire burns, and by truth one goes to heaven.
And by means of truth, Parjanya casts down water upon the surface of the earth.
It is the fulfillment of all the Vedas and the immersion in all sacred fords.
And one speaks the truth in the world; whether things be equal or not equal.
A thousand horse-sacrifices and truth were placed upon a scale.
Indeed, truth alone excels even a thousand horse-sacrifices.
By truth the gods are pleased, as are the ancestors and the brahmins.
