They say truth is the supreme dharma; therefore, one should not violate the truth.
The sages are devoted to truth, established in truth, and are the best among the thirty gods.
In heaven, those devoted to truth always rejoice like the gods.
And they approach in celestial chariots crowded with throngs of Apsarases.
Truth must always be spoken, for there is nothing superior to truth. 3.265.10
In the deep, stainless, and pure lake of truth, whose waters are clear.
One should bathe in the mental sacred ford; that bath is remembered as the supreme.
Whether for one's own sake, for the sake of another, for the sake of a son, or for the sake of an enemy.
Those men who do not speak untruth are destined for heaven. || 12 ||
That which is ultimately beneficial to living beings—that is truth; such is the firm conviction.
Whatever is beneficial for living beings should be spoken by one who possesses discernment.
The sun and the moon, wind and fire, heaven, earth, water, the heart, and Yama;
Day and night, the two auspicious twilights, and Dharma know the conduct of a man. || 14 ||
That is no assembly where there are no elders, and they are not elders who do not speak according to dharma.
That is not dharma where truth is absent; that is not truth which is permeated by deceit.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of Truth," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
For there is nothing superior to austerity; by means of austerity, they know the Great.
O best of the twice-born, that power which belongs to the Prajāpatis for creating progeny— || 1 ||
Through austerity, the sages attained both the practice of giving and knowledge itself.
Many people rejoice in heaven by virtue of their ascetic penance.
Through austerity heaven is attained; through austerity fame is attained.
Through austerity, one attains great longevity as well as abundant enjoyments. (3)
Knowledge, discernment, faith, good fortune, and supreme beauty.
Everything whatsoever that is desired by the mind is attained through austerity. || 4 ||
Elixirs, mantras, sciences, and likewise medicinal herbs.
O best of the twice-born, those who have not performed rigorous austerities do not attain perfection.
Whatever purpose a person may have in mind when he performs ascetic penance, it is that very purpose which he attains.
Therefore, a human being obtains everything from that, both in this world and in the next.
The killer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and the violator of the guru’s bed.
Through austerity a living being is liberated; indeed, one is liberated from everything.
By means of well-performed austerity alone, a human being attains liberation.
By Śakra, Vaivasvata, Ambhas, Padhanādhipa, and Hutāśana. || 8 ||
Likewise, a most exalted station was attained by Rudra, Arka, and Rātripa.
And there is no such happiness in the world that can exist without austerity.
Those who know the Dharma understand that all happiness comes through austerity alone.
Of eighty-eight thousand sages whose vital energy is drawn upward.
Through austerity, the twice-born rejoice in heaven together with the thirty gods.
But a person, having observed his own undertakings to be fruitless, [becomes despondent]. || 11 ||
One should practice austerity with diligence, for what has not been sown does not sprout.
Insects, moths, beasts, birds, and likewise the twice-born; || 12 ||
And even immobile beings go to heaven by the power of austerity.
Whatever is difficult to cross, whatever is difficult to attain, whatever is difficult to traverse, and whatever is difficult to perform.
Everything is to be accomplished through austerity, for austerity is indeed difficult to surpass.
Even when an action has been performed, if there should be a lack of lightness in the mind... (14)
One should perform austerity in that regard until it becomes a source of satisfaction.
Whatever sin people commit through their thoughts, words, or deeds, ||15||
Those whose wealth is austerity quickly dispel all that by means of austerity alone.
For a Brahmin purified by austerity alone, O dwellers of heaven.
And because of truth, they accept desires and cause them to increase.
O twice-born ones, [he is] Brahmā, the lord of creatures, the god, and likewise Mahādeva. || 17 ||
They constantly perform austerities that are most difficult to endure.
He to whom this entire world belongs, and who is the imperishable one (Acyuta) who consists of everything.
And he who is the Creator and who is victorious in this world is Viṣṇu, the Supreme Lord.
O highly fortunate ones, she constantly performs ascetic penance that is difficult to practice. ||19||
But the Blessed Vāsudeva is said here to be the supreme austerity.
Through austerity, a man attains the eight classes of gods in this world.
And through asceticism, one may even become capable of creating the three worlds.
And he becomes capable of wielding divine weapons as well. || 21 ||
O best of the twice-born, there exists nothing whatsoever in the world of the gods or on earth that is not possessed by that Puruṣa.
O noble ones, there is no attainment for one who lacks supreme excellence in austerity.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-sixth chapter, titled "The Praise of Austerities," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
They say this world is under control; it hangs from the arms of the brave.
Moreover, among all those who are brave, valor alone is what distinguishes them. ||1||
For the sake of a Brahmin, for the sake of a cow, for the sake of one's master, or for the sake of a friend.
Those who take refuge in these two, when they are brought forth, go to the back of the celestial vault.
When the loss of wealth has occurred, and when the ruin of one's wife has arrived.
And by fighting for the protection of oneself, one shall go to heaven. || 3 ||
For Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and Brāhmaṇas, battle alone is the ultimate recourse when it comes to protecting oneself during a national upheaval. (4)
When the loss of one's wife has occurred, or when there is a confusion regarding sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇā), [one should perform this].
But a Brahmin may take up arms when a state of social confusion has arisen.
A Brahmin may, however, adopt a livelihood according to the dharma of a Kshatriya, or he may not.
He should not retreat from battle; that is his duty and his welfare at such a time.
And [he saw] Tṛṇamukha, his only son, saying, "I am yours."
One who protects women and children, who is timid, and intent on flight.
One who has cast aside his weapons, one who is in distress, and one who is engaged in combat with another.
The leader, the driver of the leader, and the observer of the battle. ||8||
The best of the twice-born must not be slain by one who understands the dharma of war.
One standing in a chariot should not engage in combat with a man on foot. ||9||
Desiring battle with one who is equal, or likewise with one who is superior.
A man who kills one who is lowly, or even one who has killed him, falls into hell.
Or that man who, having not armored himself, would arm me.
He goes swiftly to hell, even by means of his well-performed deeds.
This dharma of battle has been declared; now learn its fruit from this.
For him, there shall indeed be the attainment of Dharma, the attainment of wealth, and the attainment of fame.
That hero who fights in battle, crushing the enemy host.
For him, there were virtue, wealth, and pleasure, as well as sacrifices accompanied by abundant sacrificial fees.
Having performed sacrifices such as the Agniṣṭoma with abundant sacrificial fees, he—
One does not obtain that fruit which is obtained in battle.
When blood flows from his limbs upon the field of battle, [he becomes invincible].
Together with that very [person], his sin departs from the body. ||15||
And he endures the supreme suffering of having wounds inflicted upon him.
Whatever a hero attains through austerity, there is nothing superior to that. || 16 ||
Whatever blows one may receive in battle, however, may by the turn of fate—
O knowers of dharma, even he who fights in battle is honored in heaven. || 17 ||
Just as one reaps the fruit by slaying those superior to oneself in battle.
For he who, having slain his enemy face-to-face, mounts that very vehicle [of the foe]. ||18||
Thus fighting on the field of battle, he conquers like Viṣṇu’s stride.
But he who, having slain the commander-in-chief, mounts his vehicle; || 19 ||
By that deed, one obtains the merit of four horse-sacrifices.
Whatever weapons pierce his skin in battle, [they all turn back]. // 3.267.20 //
He obtains as many worlds as there are, which are inexhaustible and yield all desires.
Wherever the hero was slain, having been struck down by his enemies.
One obtains inexhaustible worlds and liberation, free from wretchedness.
The master takes away the merit of those who have fled after being struck down. || 22 ||
And then she takes upon herself all the misdeeds of her husband.
O twice-born ones, a man fleeing in such a manner indeed attains [the same]. || 23 ||
At every step, the man of evil conduct reaps the fruit of killing a cow.
While living, he attains prosperity, and when dead, the man reaches heaven.
O Brahmins, glory exists in both ways; there is no pointlessness in battle.
O twice-born ones, as long as the hero advances facing his enemies... (25)
At every step, one shall obtain the fruit of sacrifice in successive order.
He should strike down the enemy while he is unbroken, and protect him once he is broken. || 26 ||
In that which abides, they flee; he who stands firm therein attains the supreme goal.
He who fights after having abandoned his life-breaths—whether facing upward, across, or downward—[attains the highest state]. || 27 ||
And when his enemies have been slain, he shall fall in battle; he does not return from heaven.
The body of one who has entered battle is marked by his enemies.
Having offered up one's own self as the sacrificial post, that sacrifice possesses infinite sacrificial fees.
O best of the twice-born, his kinsmen shall not be subject to impurity on his account.
The ancestral rite (śrāddha), the consecration by fire (agnisaṃskāra), and likewise the water-offering (udakakriyā).
But they are of no use for one who has died while facing the enemy in battle.
Those who know the Dharma perform these for his sake, along with their own kinsmen, in order to discharge their debt to him.
His body was marked with the signs of arrows, spears, double-edged swords, and javelins.
O hero, the celestial maidens delight him, and he delights them.
Thousands of excellent apsarases [attended] the hero slain in battle. || 32 ||
They ran forward in haste, each crying out, "He is my husband! He is mine!"
Of one who was slain while facing the enemy in battle, having fallen and not retreated. || 33 ||
Whatever wealth is taken away by others, that indeed yields the fruit of a human sacrifice.
However, it is possible for men who are prosperous to perform hundreds of sacrifices here.
O Brahmins, it is indeed extremely difficult to sacrifice one's own body in battle.
That which the Brahmins, seeking heaven, attain through multitudes of sacrifices, austerity, and the accumulation of virtuous qualities.
In an instant, casting off their own bodies in the great battle, they go to that very same destination.
All the Vedas along with their six auxiliary limbs, as well as Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and dwelling in the forest.
He alone who would sacrifice his own body on the field of battle shall attain these qualities by extension.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Qualities of a Hero," in the *Haṃsagītā* within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Non-violence is declared here to be the supreme dharma among all dharmas.
Through non-violence, one obtains whatever is desired by the mind.
Violence toward women, violence toward wealth, and likewise violence toward living beings.
By avoiding the threefold violence, one attains the world of Brahmā.
Civility, beauty, charm, and even the highest good fortune.
Wealth, grain, as well as health, dharma, knowledge, and likewise women. || 3 ||
Sovereignty, abundant enjoyments, and even the desired status of a Brahmin—these he attained.
And indeed, the eight qualities as well, and long life itself. ||4||
Those who practice non-violence attain whatever else is difficult to obtain.
Likewise, a living being who is non-violent should become one who abstains from meat.
He who might perform the horse sacrifice every month for a hundred years—
And he who would not eat meats—whether they be equal or unequal [in quality]—[should practice this].
He always sacrifices with a sacrificial session and always bestows gifts.
One is always an ascetic by virtue of abstaining from honey and meat. ||7||
Indeed, all the Vedas and all gifts together could not accomplish that.
He who, having tasted meat broth, should renounce all meats; || 8 ||
For it is indeed difficult for one who knows the taste of flavors to completely renounce meat.
This fourfold vow is the most excellent for living beings who fear death.
Then, in this world, it happens for living beings who desire life.
He is trustworthy and approachable, for he does not take pleasure in violence.
Just as life is dear to oneself, so too is it dear to all living beings.
Those great-souled ones who know the self should proceed by way of analogy with themselves. || 11 ||
Non-violence is the supreme dharma, and truth alone is so, O best of the twice-born.
Whatever man eats meat, whether out of greed or even out of delusion, [is a sinner]. || 12 ||
He should be considered merciless, having abandoned all dharmas.
He who desires to increase his own flesh with the flesh of another. || 13 ||
Wherever he is born, he dwells in a state of agitation.
The buyer destroys it with his wealth; the eater destroys it with his enjoyment. || 14 ||
The executioner [commits it] through killing and binding; thus, this slaughter is threefold.
But he who, having eaten meat, later desists from it; || 15 ||
Even for him, there is very great merit in that he turns away from evil.
Or by Rākṣasas, or Piśācas, or Ḍākinīs, or night-stalking spirits. || 16 ||
Likewise, he who completely abstains from meat shall not be overcome by others.
And the sky-dwellers perceive whether he is alive or dead.
O tiger among the twice-born, he who avoids meat from behind [the sacrificial animal] shall [attain merit].
Likewise, he who completely abstains from meat shall not be overcome by others.
Even at the scent of the smoke from a funeral pyre, the night-stalkers [flee] even from one who is dead.
Those who eat raw flesh perish; he who completely avoids meat [is saved]. ||19||
From weapons, fire, kings, and thieves, as well as from water and poison.
No fear exists for him, nor anything else whatsoever.
They do not attain those worlds which belong to those who abstain from meat.
He is the one who wields the staff, he is the valiant, he is the performer of sacrifice, and he is the one who practices austerity.
He who completely abstains from meat attains all the worlds.
For him, nothing whatsoever shall be difficult to obtain in either of the two worlds.
And likewise, one who abstains from meat shall possess the power to grant boons and to utter curses. || 22 ||
Having ascended a celestial chariot resembling the moon, that hero among men was accompanied by divine damsels.
Having enjoyed pleasures for a very long time in heaven, he indeed attains the worlds of the Grandfather (Brahmā).

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Faults of Violence," within the *Haṃsagītā* in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Forgiveness is dharma; forgiveness is truth; forgiveness is purity; forgiveness is strength.
Forgiveness is sacrifice; forgiveness is charity; and forgiveness is the highest austerity. (1)
He who endures being dragged away or even beaten by others [is a true ascetic].
Therefore, he takes away one's good deeds and bestows upon one their evil deeds. || 2 ||
O best of the twice-born, he who possesses forgiveness is a righteous soul by virtue of that very forgiveness.
He consumes the one who reviles him and goes to the heavenly world. || 3 ||
There is one fault among those who are patient; a second is not to be found.
When people consider one who is endowed with patience to be weak. || 4 ||
O best of the twice-born, that fault of his should also be understood as a great virtue.
Therefore, through the undertaking of merit and the surrendering of misdeeds, || 5 ||
A patient man who has died attains the world of Brahmā.
By means of a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans.
O Brahmins, he attains the principal desires both in heaven and here on earth for millions of years.
Therefore, a man should always be patient, enduring all things and devoted to forbearance.

Thus ends the two hundred and sixty-ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Virtue of Forgiveness," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
O best of the twice-born, compassion is the supreme dharma in this world.
Therefore, a man should indeed be self-possessed and grateful.
And for the slayer of a Brahmin, the drinker of liquor, the thief, and likewise for one who has broken his vow.
A means of atonement has been prescribed, O King, but for the ungrateful, there is no atonement.
Those lowest of men who are ungrateful are not liberated from hell.
They remain terrible until the dissolution of all beings; there is no need for further deliberation on this point.
For they are born in the animal realm and dwell in a state of suffering.
In such a time of fear, men find no protection anywhere.
A person is truly great only to the extent that what has been done for them does not go to waste.
The grateful person attains heaven; the grateful person finds greatness.
Whether it be a lord or a servant, a brahmin or even a teacher.
He who does not abandon one who has fallen into distress is honored in heaven.
He who, having served one who was prosperous, abandons him when he has become poor;
He is the most cruel man in the world, a vessel for hell.
A man should not abandon a servant in his own home merely because his youth has passed.
But if one abandons a person who has become incapable due to old age, one shall fall into hell.
An elephant, a horse, an old cow, or even one that has been tamed.
He who would abandon it is a person of very wicked intellect and falls into hell. || 9 ||
They do not care for the cattle once they have been bound, whether with fodder or water.
O tigers among the twice-born, those men have gone to hell exactly as they deserved.
Like an animal seized by an incurable disease within one's own home.
O best of the twice-born, one should not abandon this person who requires treatment as long as one lives.
By abandoning it, a human being certainly attains hell.
But that lowest of men who, having served a prosperous master, [deserts him].
If one subsequently abandons what has not prospered, one certainly goes to hell. || 12 ||
That man who incurs suffering from serving a master of inferior means, [is as follows].
O twice-born ones, that austerity of his is declared to lead indeed to the world of Brahmā. || 13 ||
In this world, the grateful man is one who shares everything with all beings.
The grateful person attains everything whatsoever that he desires in his mind.
One's mother, father, son, the person for whom one performs sacrifices, and likewise the officiating priest.
A master, a teacher, a servant, a kinsman, and even a domestic animal—[one should not eat their leftovers]. || 15 ||
O best of the twice-born, one should never, even in thought, abandon one's wife.
But by abandoning these, one certainly falls into hell. ||16||
Likewise, one should not abandon the sacred fire, nor should one extinguish the fire.
Likewise, O Brahmins, by abandoning the worship of the deities, one falls into hell. ||17||
If a person should find rest in the shade of such a tree, [he attains merit].
Therefore, remembering gratitude, one should not harm even a leaf.
One who is grateful attains prosperity, and likewise, one who is grateful gains renown.
One who is grateful attains heaven, or even the world of Brahmā. ||19||
The entire earth is supported by those high-souled ones who are grateful.
Only the grateful person performs sacrifice; the grateful person practices austerity.
He should likewise be a performer of sacrifices, a giver, a hero, and grateful.
One who is grateful will certainly sacrifice his very life for the sake of a friend. || 21 ||
O best of the twice-born, that world of Brahmā which cannot be reached through austerity even with great hardship—
For a grateful man attains that world of Brahman quickly; there is indeed no doubt about this. || 22 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Quality of Gratitude," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Proper conduct generates heaven; proper conduct increases one's fame.
And likewise, right conduct leads to long life, brings prosperity, and bestows happiness upon the world. || 1 ||
Even if he is devoid of all auspicious marks, that man who possesses right conduct [is truly noble].
The supreme person is to be known by all the characteristics and their defining marks. ||2||
Threefold is the conduct in the world that should be practiced by the wise.
And likewise, the conduct of the virtuous, as proclaimed by the Śruti and Smṛti, is another [source of dharma].
O best of the twice-born, happiness and wealth arise from right conduct.
One endowed with right conduct goes to heaven; indeed, it is only through right conduct that one becomes free from disease.
Only one who possesses good conduct may live long; only one who possesses good conduct enjoys prosperity.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-first chapter, titled "The Description of Conduct in the Songs of the Swan to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
The swan said:
The gods praise purity, and likewise the Brahman-sages praise purity.
That which is given by one endowed with purity, that the denizens of heaven consume. ||1||
Or one may partake of the fruit of purity through all dharmas whatsoever.
Only a person possessed of purity attains the desired state of existence. || 2 ||
Purity of the body is said to be achieved with water and clay, but purity through non-greed cleanses the mind.
The man whose mind is pure attains the world of the Grandfather (Brahmā).

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-second chapter, titled "The Description of Purity," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Following sacred fords is purification; following sacred fords is austerity.
Purified by the waters of sacred fords, men go to heaven without a doubt.
By traveling on the road, a person shall obtain the merit of visiting sacred fords.
But one whose sins have been exhausted by that path attains the third heaven.
It ordains that for evildoers, there is no pacification of their sins without austerity.
It ordains that which is proclaimed as being equal to freedom from sin.
Sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
Those foremost among the upholders of the Dharma cannot be attained by one who is poor.
O twice-born ones, the fruit of sacrifice can be obtained in another way by those who are poor.
Having visited the sacred fords (tīrthas), one should thereafter become devoted to those sacred fords.
He whose hands, feet, and mind are well-restrained.
Possessing knowledge, austerity, and renown, he enjoys the fruit of the sacred ford.
It is the pacification of the evils of the wicked, and likewise the increase of the Dharma for the virtuous.
A sacred ford (tīrtha) that has been frequented by the wise should be served; therefore, one should be devoted to sacred fords.
Those who maintain the sacred fires, possess wealth, and are devoted to visiting holy fords;
For them, the attainment of the fruit of the Yakṣas occurs even without the accumulation of wealth.
Of all the social classes indeed, and of those residing in all the stages of life.
A sacred ford (tīrtha) should be known as bestowing fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
He who, having gone elsewhere for another purpose, performs a ritual bath at a sacred ford (tīrtha).
For him, there is no fruit from pilgrimage, nor does he obtain the fruit of bathing therefrom.
Through the suffering of the journey, the fruit of a pilgrimage to sacred sites shall be attained.
Wandering to sacred fords on foot is said here to be the supreme austerity.
By performing that very act with a vehicle, one obtains the fruit of merely bathing there.
Just as other men perform a pilgrimage to sacred fords according to their ability, so too does that man.
And likewise, by means of a vehicle or a seat, his fruit is fourfold.
Having visited the sacred fords, the enjoyer of the field (the soul) has conquered his senses. ||13||
O best of Brahmins, one obtains the fruit [of that merit]; from a sacred ford (tīrtha), it becomes tenfold.
But one who is deprived of an umbrella and sandals shall likewise obtain a hundredfold [the merit]. || 14 ||
Deprived of an umbrella and sandals, subsisting on alms, and having his senses subdued.
One is swiftly liberated from the terrible sins born of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka). || 15 ||
Alms are not the cooking of another, nor is alms the act of receiving.
Alms-food is equal to the drinking of Soma; therefore, one should practice the collection of alms.
In this world, there are two kinds of ascetics: those who act according to their own will and those who are censured.
But those sacred fords beginning with Puṣkara, which are most great by their own power; || 17 ||
By the power of those sacred fords, the acceptance [of gifts] was performed by the ancestors.
Those sacred fords beginning with Kaṇva’s hermitage [attained their status] through the power of Kaṇva and the others. || 18 ||
These have been declared in the world as meritorious, destroyers of sin, and bestowers of the increase of merit.
The service of these two kinds of holy places should be known as yielding great fruit. || 19 ||
Those best of the twice-born who are devoted to visiting sacred fords, being freed from sin, attain heaven.
Having dwelt there for a very long time in happiness, they attain happiness in the world of humans.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Pilgrimage Sites," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Sacrifices require many implements and an extensive array of various materials.
Those foremost among the upholders of the Dharma cannot be attained by one who is poor.
Furthermore, O twice-born ones, even the poor are able to obtain the fruit of sacrifice.
Therefore, a person should observe the fast, being constantly devoted to fasting.
As long as one observes a month-long fast, for that long it is called austerity here.
From this point forward, the practice of fasting unto death (anāśaka) is proclaimed for the twice-born.
Eating only at the sixth mealtime is said here to be the supreme austerity for a Śūdra.
For those born of mixed castes, one day is prescribed.
After the sixth mealtime, a Śūdra may perform ascetic penance as he might at any time.
Then it should be known that there will be loss in the kingdom and great calamity for the king. || 5 ||
A Śūdra, however, eating at the sixth mealtime, should perform austerity according to his capacity.
Or, according to his capacity, a twice-born man may practice likewise for a period shorter than a month-long fast.
There is no sacred ford equal to the Gaṅgā; there is no goal equal to Kṛṣṇa.
There is no recitation equal to the Gāyatrī, and no oblation equal to that performed with the Vyāhṛtis. || 7 ||
Likewise, there is attainment while within the water through the Aghamarṣaṇa rite, which destroys sin.
There is no merit equal to non-violence, and nothing superior to the gift of procreation. (8)
In the same way, O twice-born ones, there is no austerity higher than fasting.
For those purified by fasts, there is long-lasting and uninterrupted happiness hereafter.
Devoted to fasting and ascetic practices, they have gone to the heavenly world.
They rejoice together in the world of the thirty-three gods, just like the hosts of deities.
It pacifies the evils of the wicked and grants the desired objects of the virtuous.
Fasting is prescribed specifically as that which has the deity as its refuge. || 11 ||
The gods, with faces brightened by grace, [favor] those who are devoted to fasting.
They are born according to their own desire; no deliberation need be made in this matter. || 12 ||
Then, having taken refuge in Vāsudeva, a person who has properly observed the fast, [attains the goal].
Ananta, the self-restrained Hari, attains infinite fruit.
Furthermore, by those Brahmins who have observed the fast while taking refuge in Vāsudeva, [the merit is attained].
Even now they do not turn back, like rivers flowing into the oceans.
Those men who have observed the fast according to the prescribed rules, having reached heaven, rejoice exceedingly.
Accompanied by celestial nymphs, men in this world become free from all suffering. || 15 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Fasting in the Haṃsa-gītā to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara Purāṇa. || 274 ||
The swan said:
The fruit resulting from following the sacred fords is obtained when one is endowed with mental concentration.
O Brahmins, one who has fasted properly likewise attains that which is most great. ||1||
All of these indeed are effective for a person in all undertakings.
Whatever a person performs with a purified mind, ||2||
That does not yield much fruit for him, either in this world or after death.
For the mind is the supreme element; one should always strive for its purity.
A living being endowed with purity of mind does not fall into hell.
He attains the world of the gods, or else the supreme state. ||4||
O givers of honor, he whose faults have been removed dwells together with virtues.
Fasting is to be understood as the [purification] of the mind, not the emaciation of the body. ||5||
In the stainless, most blissful, pure, and great lake that is the family of truth.
One should bathe in the mental sacred ford; for that sacred ford is indeed unsurpassed.
In this regard, O infallible ones, they cite this ancient verse:
Yama Vaivasvata is the god who dwells within your heart.
If you have no dispute with yourself, then do not go to the Gaṅgā, nor to the Kurus.
One should constantly perform actions that bestow lightness of mind.
Indeed, all his merits become even more abundant. ||8||
Whatever a mortal practices while endowed with purity of mind, [that alone becomes his].
The mind alone proclaims the preliminary signs of a human being. ||9||
The mind alone discerns the gravity or lightness of an action.
Truthfulness is purity, self-restraint is purity, and physical cleanliness is indeed purity as well.
All purifications belong to him whose mind is always pure.
For one devoid of purity of mind, all forms of external purification are useless. ||11||
But that artificial [faith] cannot be produced by those who are free from nihilism.
He whose mind is always free from defects and dependent upon virtuous qualities. || 12 ||
He alone sacrifices with sacrifices; he alone performs austerities.
He alone obtains everything whatsoever that he desires with his mind.
Therefore, among all forms of purity, purity of mind is remembered as the supreme. ||13||
The self is a river with virtue for its banks, excellent fords, truth for its water, fortitude for its shores, and compassion for its waves.
In that [tirtha], one of meritorious deeds who has bathed is purified; for the self is indeed the eternal enjoyment, the true tirtha. ||14||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Purity of Mind," within the *Haṃsa-gītā* addressed to the sages, in the third section of the *Māgha-saṃhitā* of the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Whatever one may perform with a mind endowed with faith, [that alone becomes fruitful].
For him, that [gift] becomes exceedingly fruitful in both worlds. || 1 ||
This person consists of faith; whatever his faith is, that indeed he is.
Men who have faith in the gods and who sacrifice to the gods are called "gods. ||2||
The Pitṛs are those who have faith in the Pitṛs, and the Daityas are the sons of Diti who have faith in her.
Likewise, those who have faith in evil and are themselves wicked should be known as those destined for hell. || 3 ||
Therefore, having established faith, the practitioner of dharma should practice dharma.
In this Dharma which has many doors, there is no action that is fruitless.
A man, having established himself in a state of faith and being endowed with devotion, [should act]. || 4 ||
One should constantly perform meritorious deeds and avoid sinful ones.
The merit of that which is performed by relying upon faith yields abundant fruit. ||85||
For faith is indeed the supreme purifier in the world; it is said that faith is the very body of a person.
And men, having established themselves in faith and performed meritorious deeds, attain a meritorious destination.

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of Faith," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
The daily, the occasional, the optional, that which is an auxiliary to ritual acts, and that which removes impurities.
Likewise, the ritual bath is the sixth; thus the sixfold bath is proclaimed. ||1||
The daily (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites should be performed with hot water and water from other sources.
And the third is bathing with others, which is said to remove impurities.
Having extracted five lumps of earth, one should bathe in the water of another.
Otherwise, a man who has bathed is tainted by a portion of his evil deeds. || 3 ||
A man who has bathed attains purity, but he does not obtain the full fruit of the bath.
Having extracted five lumps [of earth], even one who has bathed in the water of another [is purified]. || 4 ||
One who bathes with water heated by fire does not obtain the fruit arising from bathing.
Having bathed, one attains purity and becomes fit for ritual action. ||5||
Therefore, [one should perform this] at meritorious sacred sites, in oceans, and in lakes.
And likewise in divine rivers as well as in mountain springs.
One should perform a bath for the sake of dharma; by that, one is glorified in heaven.
Likewise, when there is lack of water or laziness, both the obligatory (nitya) and occasional (naimittika) rites [are suspended]. || 7 ||
One should perform the removal of impurities and the third bath.
One attains mere purification through heated water and other [purifying] waters. || 8 ||
The vulnerabilities of a sleeping man leak away during the night.
Therefore, having risen at dawn, one should always perform the ritual bath.
One who performs religious rites while devoid of ritual bathing incurs the failure of those actions.
Therefore, a wise person should perform the daily bath by whatever means possible.
Having bathed, he should perform the libation for the gods together with the ancestors.
One becomes a true bathed person when one's soul is righteous; otherwise, one is not said to be bathed.
Having bathed during a period of birth-impurity or death-impurity, one should not perform the rite of libation (tarpaṇa).
A wise man should perform the libation for the deceased for a single dead person.
Having bathed, one attains purity; indeed, bathing is the supreme means of bringing satisfaction.
Through bathing, one also dispels both external and internal defects.
This bath pacifies evil dreams and destroys all that is inauspicious.
It is the foremost producer of auspiciousness and the supreme purifier of the mind.
The best of men who bathes daily does not experience the suffering of hell.
Bathing increases the digestive fire; bathing increases good fortune.
This bath is the pacifier of misfortune; this bath is the destroyer of evil deeds.
Thus, the human being becomes bathed and capable of performing ritual acts. || 16 ||
One who has bathed without [washing] the head is not proclaimed to have truly bathed.
If one is unable to bathe in the morning when the time for the meal has arrived, [one should perform the bath at that time]. || 17 ||
One should regularly perform the ritual bath, which reveals the path to heaven.
O best of the twice-born, having bathed one's head, one should perform rites for the gods and the ancestors.
One should not perform rites for the gods or the ancestors without having bathed.
Even without the water of sacred fords, in rites pertaining to the gods and the ancestors. ||19||
One should always perform bathing, which is the supreme means for purifying the body.
By bathing alone, one obtains the supreme merit that one who has bathed at a sacred ford (tīrtha) attains.
The merit from water drawn from the ground is greater than that from water already on the ground; therefore, the merit from spring water is even greater than that.
And from that [lake] comes the water of the mountain stream; and from the mountain stream, the water of the lake. || 21 ||
Therefore, one should not accept even from a crane that which is to be taken from a virtuous person.
And the water of the Jāhnavī is said to be more meritorious than all of those.
Having bathed their limbs in the Ganges and enjoyed divine pleasures in heaven for a long time, they eventually attain human birth.
In this world, those who are devoted to the Dharma become happy, prosperous, endowed with fame, and free from suffering. ||23||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of Bathing," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Recitation is proclaimed in the world as that which brings about success for the twice-born.
O best of the twice-born, one attains perfection through recitation, especially so.
A Brahmin shall indeed attain perfection through recitation alone; there is no doubt in this matter.
Whether he performs [the rites] or does not perform them elsewhere, one who is friendly is called a Brāhmaṇa. || 2 ||
Seated comfortably on a wooden seat or even on a seat of kusha grass.
One should perform the recitation while composed in meditation, or even when standing up.
Facing either the east or the north, or even facing the sun.
O best of the twice-born, with darbha grass in hand, he understood the certainty of dharma.
Having understood the seer of the mantra, as well as its meter and deity;
One should perform the application and the recitation while meditating upon the deity of the mantra.
It should not be performed too hurriedly, nor indeed too slowly.
O best of the twice-born, one should pronounce all the syllables clearly at the time of recitation.
The wise one should indeed repeat the mantra according to his ability, remaining free from sloth.
But self-recitation (svādhyāya) is performed aloud; that which is muttered (japya) is said to be whispered. || 7 ||
But that which is recited mentally is likewise remembered as having much greater fruit than that.
O best of the twice-born, a rosary should indeed be made from rudrākṣa beads.
Or with lotus seeds, O highly fortunate ones, or else with putrajīvaka berries.
With pearls, coral, gold, or crystal. ||9||
Or, O Brahmins, with a cord of Kuśa grass that is well-knotted and intact.
Or one should likewise perform the counting correctly by means of the joints of the fingers.
Having done this, the twice-born must certainly perform the recitation of the mantra-deity.
Having propitiated him, one obtains whatever one desires with the mind.
Having attained perfection through recitation, one shall reach the world of Brahman.
By means of recitation one is liberated from evil; by means of recitation one shall go to the third heaven.
One attains liberation through recitation; therefore, one should be devoted to recitation.
One who desires no desires shall certainly attain liberation through the recitation [of mantras]. ||13||
One who desires objects of desire obtains whatever desire he wishes for in his mind.
All the perfected sages, O best of the twice-born, attained success through recitation alone.
The recitation is the supreme purifier for the twice-born; by means of recitation, one abandons all evil.
By means of recitation one obtains the desired worlds; by means of recitation the twice-born attains liberation. || 15 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-eighth chapter, titled "Description of the Mantras to be Recited," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
Having performed the recitation of the mantra while submerged in water, O best of the twice-born.
One obtains imperishable fruit and is liberated from all sins. || 1 ||
The mantra should be recited within the water while meditating upon the deity of the mantra.
It liberates a person from sin, even from that born of the great transgressions (mahāpātaka).
Then, having shaken off their sins by means of the inner water, the twice-born indeed go to the eternal heaven.
Then, by a person submerged in water, the recitation of the mantra must be performed with effort. || 3 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and seventy-ninth chapter, titled "Description of the Mantra to be Recited While Underwater from the Haṃsa-gītā to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
The Swan said:
O twice-born ones, [one should practice] exhalation (recaka), inhalation (pūraka), and likewise retention (kumbhaka).
Prāṇāyāma, which yields great fruit, should be understood as having three stages. || 1 ||
But he who should practice the study of mantras while holding his breath, [attains success].
O best of Brahmins, that which is performed with the mind is proclaimed as recaka.
Holding his breath, he neither took nor released it.
That is designated as pūraka, which destroys all impurities.
One should likewise perform meditation on the deity of the mantra as well as breath control (prāṇāyāma).
For the twice-born, there is no austerity superior to breath control (prāṇāyāma).
From cessation (nirodha) wind is born, and from that, fire is produced.
Then, by those three, the water in the body of that man is purified.
From the tips of his hair to the tips of his nails, he will perform supreme austerity upon himself.
But he who, O best of the twice-born, should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) without sloth— || 6 ||
O twice-born ones, one does not obtain that merit by merely visiting sacred fords.
One cannot attain [this] through sacrifice or through such hardships as breath-control (prāṇāyāma) and the like. ||7||
The Brahmins, devoted to the practice of breath control, have washed away all their impurities.
They attain the third heaven or the liberation desired by their minds. ||8||
Even those sins arising from the great transgressions (mahāpātaka) are destroyed by breath control (prāṇāyāma).
Therefore, those who know the Dharma should perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) even for terrible sins.
This is the supreme austerity of the twice-born; it removes sin and causes the increase of merit.
Or it bestows liberation upon the Supreme Persons; therefore, one should practice it with diligent effort.

Thus ends the two hundred and eightieth chapter, titled "The Description of Prāṇāyāma," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
The withdrawal of the mind that has been directed toward sense objects.
Withdrawal of the senses is declared to be the supreme austerity. ||1||
The mind is exceedingly fickle; its restraint, O twice-born ones, [is the means].
This must be accomplished by a wise person through the practice of withdrawal (pratyāhāra). ||2||
Having withdrawn the mind from sensual desires, O best of the twice-born, a person [should practice].
He would become a vessel for sensual pleasures in this world, and likewise for liberation. ||3||
He who, having abandoned all desires, moves about among men free from longing;
Free from the sense of "mine" and free from the sense of "I," he attains peace. ||4||
In this way, a person should perform the withdrawal of the mind from sensual desires.
One attains whatever one desires and finds the means to liberation. ||5||
For the mind, O Brahmins, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate.
The wise, applying diligent effort, must effect its restraint. ||6||
As long as the mind does not attain supreme detachment, so long does the man remain [in bondage].
O twice-born ones, he is indeed not capable of withdrawal until then.
The world is afflicted by the sufferings of birth, death, old age, disease, and grief.
Seeing this, O Brahmins, one becomes weary; through such detachment, one attains perfection.
Thus, he repeatedly perceives the impermanence of this world.
Having established oneself in the state of dispassion, one shall thereafter attain perfection. ||9||
Of the deities, the sages, the kings, and the hosts of spirits.
Having seen this destruction, O fortunate one, the dispassionate person is liberated.
There is great suffering in dwelling in the womb, and again and again in hell.
Whether in the animal realm or among humans, one who desires the state of an animal is liberated. ||11||
O twice-born ones, he who is exhausted day after day by subsisting on the food of others;
Thus, being weary of urine and excrement, he attains dispassion.
But when the cessation of sufferings has been cultivated with the thought, "This is happiness," [then it truly becomes so].
He who becomes weary of sufferings in a very short time becomes dispassionate toward them. || 13 ||
Then, having established himself in detachment, he should practice withdrawal of the senses without sloth.
If one should withdraw the mind from sensual desires, by that means one attains everything. ||14||
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in immobility;
In the same way, he into whom all desires enter attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires. 15.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-first chapter, titled "The Description of Pratyāhāra," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
The mind's abiding together in one place occurs with respect to an external object.
That is designated as dhāraṇā, which effects the binding of the mind. || 1 ||
That [form] should be fashioned for the worship of the deity, wherein his mind may become steady.
Having, however, found a single object for the fickle mind, || 2 ||
One should diligently restrain the fourth [state] for the sake of favoring the mind.
Alternatively, one who understands should compose a poetic composition (lakṣyabandha) on this earth.
But one who has attained the target in the yoga of the earth should abandon the yoga of the earth.
O best of men, a man who has attained his goal should act with vigor toward other men.
Then, having emitted it into the wind, one should cause it to enter into space.
In this manner, by gradually ascending through the stages of being an object of focus, a person [attains the goal].
Having performed concentration on external objects, one attains perfection of the mind.
And as long as there is the binding and holding of this flickering mind.
For as long as one has not ascended to that meditation, O twice-born ones, it cannot be attained by anyone.
Having attained unwavering concentration (dhāraṇā), one should thereafter attain meditative absorption (dhyāna).
He abandons this body at that place where concentration (dhāraṇā) has been firmly established.
One attains identification with that; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 8 ||
Having attained dhāraṇā and cast off the body, that best of men—
One attains liberation in due course of time, but through meditation it is attained quickly; such is the established rule.
But once a person established in dhāraṇā has attained that state of identification (yanmayībhāva), from that [point onward...]
When he enters into a person, then he takes possession of him. || 3.282.10 ||
Having attained concentration upon the Fixed One, a human being obtains liberation.
However, through meditation, it is established that [liberation] occurs quickly after a long period of time. || 11 ||
In all the world, those who destroy external objects should be known as such.
One should practice the concentration (dhāraṇā) upon them, which is the cause for seizing the mind.
Having attained an unwavering binding of the mind, the Supreme Person—
Therefore, through the practice of dhāraṇā, one certainly attains liberation.
Whatever is eternally established in his heart, that indeed shall be his state at the time of death.
For whatever one meditates upon at the time of death, that indeed one inevitably becomes, being absorbed in its nature. (14)

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-second chapter, titled "The Description of Dhāraṇā," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
But when the concentration is upon an external object, it is proclaimed as external concentration (bāhyadhāraṇā).

O best of the twice-born, it is facing downward within the pericarp of the heart-lotus.
The wise man should perform meditation upon the sun, that mass of splendor.
The moon resides in the midst of the sun, and fire resides in the midst of the moon.

The Person is imperishable, eternal, all-pervading, and the Great Lord. ||4||

The Svastika, the Sarvatobhadra, the Paryaṅka, and the Kamalāsana [postures].
Having assumed one of those [postures], one should remain unwearied in a yogic seat. ||6||
Having likewise brought the two hands to the base of the thighs, they should be held level and directed sideways.
O best of the twice-born, having placed the right hand upon the left with the palms facing upwards.
The two hands should likewise be made with the thumbs slightly contracted.
Having raised it up and rendered his arms utterly limp, he made it false.
The wise practitioner should place the back against his shoulder and raise his body upward.
Then the neck should be made steady and very firm, and the head held level.
He gazed at the tip of his own nose, without looking toward the directions.
Closing one's eyes slightly, one should completely cast off everything external.
Having completely renounced everything external, [one should realize] the Supreme Self by means of the self.
The heart-lotus is in the center of its pericarp, and light is offered into light.
Having seen the Lord Puruṣa, one is liberated from all bonds. || 11 ||
Having first achieved restraint of the mind through withdrawal (pratyāhāra),...
But the person who has attained the target through concentration ascends to meditation.
Having achieved mastery over the senses and having likewise restrained the mind, then—
And having thus conquered the vital air, the person ascends to meditative absorption.
One who has ascended to meditative absorption (dhyāna) then attains that state, having gone to which one does not grieve.
At the end of the night and likewise at dusk, a person should exert effort in meditation.
But having seen the Supreme Person through meditation, one who has been liberated from the body attains wholeness.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-third chapter, titled "Description of Meditation," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Haṃsa said:
Then, having ascended to meditative absorption, he shall attain concentration of the mind.
After attaining meditative absorption, a person should not think of anything at all. || 1 ||
Devoid of sound, touch, and taste, and bereft of smell and form.
One should know that as the Supreme Person, having gone to whom one does not grieve. 42.
O Brahmins, that which is empty and supreme in meditation is proclaimed as samādhi.
Having attained that, one shall never again be overcome by other men. || 3 ||
There is no happiness whatsoever in the three worlds superior to meditative concentration.
And established in samādhi, he is not shaken even by heavy suffering. || 4 ||
Even if hundreds of conch shells were blown right into his ears.
And even if drums are beaten, they do not perceive an external sound. || 5 ||
Likewise, one who is struck by blows or whose body is burned by fire [is tormented].
Even when situated in an extremely terrible cold, he does not perceive any external touch.
If this is true even regarding external scents and tastes, what need is there to speak of such a person?
Having seen [this] by himself, he again attains meditative concentration.
Neither thirst nor hunger ever pursues him at any time.
Even for one who has completely abandoned craving, who does not enjoy [sensual pleasures], and who observes [the truth]. || 8 ||
That best of men understands that there is only one kind of disenchantment.
Arising from meditative concentration, he is intensely tormented by it.
Neither in heaven, nor in the netherworld, nor among humans is that happiness found.
The joy that a person experiences upon attaining unwavering meditative absorption (samādhi).
Having attained samādhi, a person abandons the bondage of the body.
It pervades all the worlds—the three realms, including all that is moving and unmoving.
And that Puruṣa pervades even that which is outside the three worlds.
Having attained samādhi, a human being reaches infinity.
He is entirely free from birth, death, old age, disease, sorrow, and suffering.
All-pervading, the destroyer of all, and the essence of the qualities of all the sense organs. ||13||
O Brahmins, he is present there at all times and in all places; of this there is no doubt.
Then he attains the state of a Puruṣa and also attains omnipotence.
Having indeed restrained the mind in the dhāraṇās, one should then subsequently ascend to dhyāna.
By relying on meditative concentration, the person of great power attains equality with the Supreme Being. 15.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Samādhi," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
O best of the twice-born, that which is the root for attaining a great station—
Therefore, explain to us everything regarding the definition of direct perception.
The Swan said:
All men, preceded by resolute effort, attain their goals.
For those who have resolve as their companion, nothing in this world is difficult to attain.
Resolve is the supreme kinsman; assistance follows immediately after that.
It is certain that a person endowed with that [knowledge] attains [the goal] correctly. || 3 ||
O best of sages, regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
But a man who possesses perseverance should always be known as a worthy vessel. || 4 ||
For those devoid of resolve, even the slightest object is difficult to obtain.
Of those who are devoid of resolve, indolent, and evil-minded. || 5 ||
Even when wealth has come into one's hand, it may suddenly and quickly perish.
But one devoid of resolve does not differ from a mere tree stump. || 6 ||
Therefore, those men who are devoted to vice are said in the world to be partakers of desire.
For them, both this world and the next belong; likewise, the path to liberation is not far for them.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of Resolve," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
They bestow honor upon perseverance, which is the foremost of all actions.
The root is declared to be one alone—namely, volitional intention (saṃkalpa); of this there is no doubt. || 1 ||
Desire indeed has its root in volition; knowledge is bound by volition.
The Vedas have conceptualization as their bond; Dharma has conceptualization as its bond.
The object of desire is bound by intention; liberation is also bound by intention.
This entire world, consisting of the moving and the unmoving, is bound by volitional construction (saṃkalpa).
First, having determined with his mind what action is to be performed, a wise man—
He who subsequently applies himself with perseverance is to be known as a wise man.
Whatever objects have been determined by anyone’s mind anywhere;
Until then, it cannot be accomplished; therefore, a higher resolve is required.
Success is declared to belong to those who are endowed with resolve, having first formed their intentions with the mind.
Therefore, the wise declare that all undertakings in this world have their root in intention.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-sixth chapter, titled "The Definition of Saṃkalpa," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
Regarding the attainment of the state of supreme beatitude, you have taught the practice of withdrawal.
And the yoga of retention and meditation, as well as the supreme samādhi. || 1 ||
Speak further, however, concerning men who wander through the cycle of existence.
The supreme path for the sake of welfare, which brings happiness to both worlds. || 2 ||
The Swan said:
Agni is the mouth of the deities and the ultimate refuge of all beings.
By merely serving him, one attains all desires.
That supreme form of Viṣṇu, which was given by Him, the Sun attains.
From the sun comes rain; from that comes food; and from food, the world arises.
The celestial deities rain downwards, while those of the earth rain upwards.
The principal earthy [substance], raining upwards, was offered into the fire.
Having first uttered the syllable Oṃ, whatever deity a Brahmin [addresses],...
He offers the oblation, and she remains ever pleased with him.
The deities attain satisfaction through the oblation offered by Vahnidatta.
Being satisfied themselves, they satisfy that man with the fulfillment of his desires.
An oblation offered in the sun is supremely meritorious; by it, one is glorified in heaven.
Therefore, one shall obtain eightfold merit by offering oblations with sacrificial fuel.
Therefore, it is ten times more [efficacious] with grains, and twice as much again with rice.
Just so much merit is traditionally held to result from an oblation performed with white mustard seeds.
From that, [the merit] is fourfold with barley; from that, tenfold with sesame seeds.
The fruit should be known as being exactly that much; from that point on, it increases tenfold with each *bilva* fruit.
And at that very moment, O twice-born ones, it was said by the lotuses with curd and milk:
Then, O knower of Dharma, by means of supreme food and ghee, the merit is eightfold.
The wise one [should offer] with a mantra purified by the syllable Oṃ and ending in Svāhā.
At the conclusion of each "svāhā," one should offer oblations while meditating upon the deity of the mantra.
An oblation should be offered only so long as the finger-joints can still be filled [by the grains].
The sacrificial fuel (idhma) is desired to be one span (vitasti) in length and the thickness of a thumb (aṅguṣṭha). || 13 ||
And likewise in the case of bad dreams, ill-omened sacrifices, and unfavorable portents.
There is no rite accompanied by mantras that destroys evil as effectively as this. || 14 ||
Through burnt offerings a person abandons evil, and through burnt offerings he likewise ascends to the celestial realm.
Indeed, the fire-oblation destroys all evil in this world; there is no doubt about this. || 15 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-seventh chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for Fire Offerings," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
All creatures are subject to destiny; this entire world is dependent upon the gods.
The happiness and suffering of human beings likewise depend upon the gods.
Human beings, however, consume both the auspicious and the inauspicious as ordained by the gods.
Therefore, with every effort, one should be devoted to the worship of the deity. || 2 ||
The gods are pleased by devotion as well as by supreme faith.
The gods are pleased only when worshipped by one who is pure, and not otherwise.
Through service to the gods comes heaven; through service to the gods comes happiness.
Through service to the gods, both sovereignty and even liberation may be attained.
In this world, the deities always desire their devotees in such a manner.
The gods, who are compassionate toward their devotees, are certainly so both in this world and in the next.
O best of the twice-born, the gods certainly provide protection for one who is devoted.
Through the gratification of the deity, one obtains whatever desires one wishes for in the mind.
Whichever deity one should worship constantly with devotion from the very moment of birth;
But when the time of death has arrived, he too will certainly be his protector.
Or rather, do the deities quickly become pleased with one who is free from evil?
Therefore, a man who takes refuge in the gods should not commit sin.
For those who have taken refuge in the gods, evil is swiftly destroyed.
Indeed, no sinful action ever arises in vain for them. || 9 ||
Likewise, great fruit residing in the thirty [gods] has been proclaimed in the world.
One should worship all the gods, or one may take refuge in a single deity.
Having performed the worship of the deity with faith, one will certainly attain that world.
O Brahmins, by building a temple for the gods, a man shall attain that world.
As many atoms as there are in the celestial abode, [so many...]
For that many years he attains those worlds; of this there is no doubt. || 12 ||
For as many times as one whitewashes a temple here with lime, [so many times does one attain merit].
He shines with glory throughout as many other births as those.
Having thus established the banner in the abode of the gods with such devotion,
It swiftly dispels all evils, even those born of the great sins (mahāpātaka). || 14 ||
Having likewise performed the work of painting, he rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
By removing the garlands from the deity, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow. || 15 ||
One is liberated from all sins by sprinkling water upon the temple of the deity.
Likewise, by sweeping [the temple], one undoubtedly dispels evil; of this there is no doubt. || 16 ||
One obtains desired objects of pleasure by smearing the temple of a deity.
Having established it with the lines of Sudhā, one does not overstep the boundary. || 17 ||
Having had it painted with various colors, one shall obtain great good fortune.
By sprinkling with fragrant scents, men attain the state of a Gandharva. || 18 ||
By scattering flowers, one is reborn endowed with beauty.
By anointing an image of a deity, one is liberated from all sufferings. || 19 ||
Having dried it up, one is liberated from those very evils.
Having likewise bathed with medicinal herbs, he rejoices together with the Nāsatyas.
In this world, having bathed the deity with the Vedas, one goes to Prajāpati.
By bathing [the deity] with water mixed with flowers, one attains great good fortune. || 21 ||
Having bathed [the deity] with water containing fruit, one finds that one's ritual action is fruitful.
Having bathed [the deity] with the juices of the betel vine (nāgavallī), he goes to the world of the Nāgas.
By bathing with water containing jewels, one shall attain the world that bestows all desires.
With excellent scented water, he rejoices together with the Gandharvas. || 23 ||
By means of the meritorious water of sacred fords (tīrtha), one shall attain the heavenly world.
Having likewise anointed himself with fragrances, he is honored in the world of Śakra.
By the gift of ornaments, one becomes a king upon the earth.
Indeed, by the granting of royal insignia, one becomes a king upon the earth. || 25 ||
By the gift of clothing in this world, one is born well-attired.
By offering garlands to the deity, one attains supreme prosperity. || 26 ||
Likewise, by the offering of incense, one shall attain the supreme state.
By the gift of a lamp, one becomes possessed of sight and indeed becomes luminous. || 27 ||
He attains an upward course and likewise preeminence everywhere.
Likewise, O Brahmins, one should diligently offer food to the deities.
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
Then the deity attains complete satisfaction through the offering of the bali-oblation.
Being satisfied, they gratified him with the fulfillment of all his desires.
By the offering of heart-pleasing drinks, one attains eternal satisfaction.
By paying homage to the deities, some degree of evil is destroyed.
In the same way, even excessive sin is destroyed by prostration. || 31 ||
Then, having performed even more than that, he circumambulated the deity.
The act of praising the deities bestows the fruit of all desires.
O best of the twice-born, the deities attain satisfaction through song.
Likewise, through instrumental music and dance, especially for a man. ||33||
O twice-born ones, he himself performs dancing, singing, and likewise instrumental music.
He attains the same world as the gods of that wise man. || 34 ||
By reciting the Itihāsas and other such works, one shall attain liberation from sin.
If one causes a song to be performed for a price, one shall attain the state of a Gandharva. || 35 ||
Having given musical instruments to one who knows the Dharma, one enjoys the world of the Vasus.
Through dance, one attains the world of the high-souled Śaṅkara. || 36 ||
By the gift of history, a man becomes wise.
Whoever offers an oblation into the sacrificial fire, dedicating it to the deity; || 37 ||
That god gratifies him with desires, or he is gratified by him.
He who gives food here to Brahmins with the deity in mind. || 38 ||
That god, being pleased, bestows upon him his desired objects.
Whatever is given to the Brahmins with reference to the deity, ||39||
That very thing is obtained in great abundance in this world when the Thirty-three Gods are pleased.
A vehicle, a bed, a seat, an umbrella, as well as sandals and shoes.
He who, knowing the Dharma, gives a vehicle and a cow to the gods;
From each one of these, a person obtains the fruit of a Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice. || 41 ||
Having offered fruits to the gods, one finds that one's ritual action becomes fruitful.
By offering grains in this manner, one attains the unsurpassed state.
The God does not attain such pleasure from gifts, dances, or fruits as He does from this.
Just as Brahmins experience joy through the honoring of those who depend upon them. || 43 ||
O twice-born ones, the deities are not at all pleased by giving in many ways.
Since they are pleased by devotion, one should therefore take refuge in devotion. || 44 ||
Likewise, by giving vessels filled with ghee at a śrāddha, a man [obtains great merit].
One attains a long life and is not overcome by diseases. || 45 ||
By giving vessels filled with honey, one shall obtain good fortune.
O best of beings, it comes about through the giving of vessels in whatever manner possible. ||46||
It is indeed a vessel for all desires; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
By the gift of flowering trees, a human being obtains a home. || 47 ||
By the gift of a fruit-bearing tree, one shall become the lord of a village.
Likewise, from the gift of a house, one becomes the lord of a district.
A house provided with beds and seats, and equipped with vehicles and carriages.
It was prosperous, filled with wealth and grain, and crowded with male and female servants. || 49 ||
Having bestowed that delightful [gift], endowed with all desirable things, during the performance of the śrāddha rite.
Falling away from the heavenly world, he becomes an earthly king.
Whatever gift one bestows, even if it be but a small thing, with the ancestors in view;
Through their grace, he obtains even greater merit than theirs. || 51 ||
Therefore, acts of faith should be performed at sacred fords and holy shrines.
And gifts indeed should be given according to one's ability, dedicated to the ancestors. ||52||
Through śrāddha rites, men obtain prosperity, and through śrāddha, the brahmins attain residence in the third heaven.
Thereafter, one should diligently perform the *śrāddha* ceremony exactly as prescribed in one's own *kalpa-sūtra*. ||53||

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-eighth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Worship of the Ancestors," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
The Vaiśyas are the deities of the Śūdras, and likewise, the Kṣatriyas are the deities of the Vaiśyas.
The Brahmins [are the teachers] of the Kṣatriyas, and the sacrificial fire is likewise for them.
The spiritual teacher is celibate, and women have their husbands as their deities.
A householder has the guest as his deity; therefore, he should always honor him.
Having performed the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice at home, being composed in mind, both morning and evening.
Having performed the offering of the funeral rice-ball (piṇḍa) and having given alms to a mendicant, [he should proceed].
By giving alms with due respect, one obtains the fruit of the gift of a cow.
And one should scatter [food] on the ground for dogs, for those who cook dogs, and for birds.
All beings, both stationary and moving, depend upon the householder for their livelihood.
A householder should provide sustenance for those who have died as well as for those who are still living.
Because he provides nourishment here constantly, he is glorified in heaven by that very act.
The worm, the moth, the fallen one, the enemies, and the best of the twice-born.
A householder must not show contempt toward [guests] when the Vaiśvadeva sacrifice has been undertaken.
A householder should diligently honor a guest who has come to his home.
Rising and walking toward the east from this place, one shall obtain the fruit of the gift of a cow.
And having likewise offered a seat, that best of men obtained a place to stay.
And having made inquiries regarding one's welfare, the wise man is born.
Then, by washing his feet and by massaging him when he was weary, [he served him]. || 9 ||
By fanning with a yak-tail whisk or by fanning with a palm-leaf fan.
Either by the offering of an oil massage for the feet, or likewise by the offering of a lamp.
By the gift of a bed at night, as well as by massaging [the feet], [one obtains great merit].
From each one of these, he obtains the supreme fruit of giving a cow. || 11 ||
By worshipping him with discourses, one shall attain union through glory.
And having caused him to hear the historical narratives (itihāsas) according to his desire, [he should proceed].
One attains the world of the gods through song, dance, festivals, and other such celebrations.
By worshipping [it], one attains the state of a Gandharva without a doubt. || 13 ||
By the gift of shelter, one attains all desires.
Having given him clay, a tooth-stick, and likewise water for purification; || 14 ||
Having given [it] at the proper time according to one's pleasure, one shall obtain great good fortune.
And having heated this [body] which was afflicted by cold, he experiences happiness everywhere. || 15 ||
Having first provided him with an oil massage, he untiringly gave him a bath.
One obtains health, beauty, charm, wealth, and grain. || 16 ||
Having offered all the principal baths, O best of the twice-born.
One attains the world of the Nāsatyas; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. ||17||
Likewise, having given fragrant substances, one rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
By the gift of a bracelet, one enjoys great good fortune. || 18 ||
The merit arising from bathing a guest is equal to that produced by giving away ten cows.
By uniting with one who desires anything at all, one obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 19 ||
And by giving him whatever he desires, one enjoys that very thing in an inexhaustible manner.
Therefore, a man should always honor a guest with all his power.
When a guest has been satisfied, whatever that noble-souled person merely thinks of for himself, [that is his reward].
One obtains all that without delay; therefore, a guest must always be honored by one devoted to dharma.

Thus ends the two hundred and eighty-ninth chapter, titled "The Worship of Guests," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
The Brahmins are the deity on earth; the Brahmins are the deity in heaven.
There is no being whatsoever in the three worlds superior to the Brahmins. || 1 ||
They can make a non-god into a god, and they can make a god into a non-god.
For the highly fortunate Brahmins, the twice-born, are constantly honored.
According to the sacred tradition (śruti), the gods were first produced from the Brahmins.
The entire world belongs to the Brāhmaṇas; therefore, they are always most worthy of worship.
The deities and likewise the ancestors eat from their mouths.
And what is the nature of those highly fortunate sages that makes them superior even to him? || 4 ||
Whatever a person bestows upon the Brahmins with devotion, [that alone is what truly matters].
Those who know the Dharma obtain that very same thing in birth after birth. || 5 ||
Thus, by means of the breeze from palm-leaf fans and by the fanning of those who were weary;
By the rubbing of the limbs as well as by the application of collyrium. || 6 ||
By the offering of water for washing the feet and by the cleansing of the feet.
O best of the twice-born, by means of service alone, according to one's desire.
One obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice and goes to the heavenly world.
Having carried out the auspicious command of a Brāhmaṇa, one is honored in the heavenly world. ||8||
Whatever the Brahmins, being most satisfied, declare, that the deities approve in return.
When those whose deities are perceptible are satisfied, those whose deities are imperceptible always become satisfied as well. ||9||

Thus ends the two hundred and ninetieth chapter, titled "Service to Brāhmaṇas," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Cows are purifying and auspicious; in cows, the worlds are established.
Just as the gods, just as the Vedas, and just as the Brāhmaṇas and the twice-born. || 1 ||
In the same way, cows are declared to bring happiness to all the world.
Each one of them should be known as a Brāhmaṇa; in them both, the sacrifice is established.
The mantras abide in the Brahmins; the sacrificial oblation resides in the cows.
O best of the twice-born, the gift of cows removes evil deeds. ||3||
Cow’s urine, cow dung, milk, curd, and ghee as the fifth;
This has been declared as the supreme purifier for men, a means of purification.
They are auspicious, purifying, destroyers of demons, and likewise illuminating.
O Brahmins, the water from their horns is like the water of the Ganges.
By scratching cows, a mortal casts off all evil.
By giving them morsels of food, one shall obtain great merit.
And having prepared their path in that very manner, they likewise reached the reservoir of water.
They indeed enjoy the heavenly world for many groups of years.
By making these their sphere of activity, a person attains [the goal].
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of the horse sacrifice (aśvamedha). || 8 ||
Having established a dwelling for them, one should become the lord of the city.
Likewise, by the gift of salt, one enjoys great good fortune.
One who is afflicted by illness, or mired in mud, or tormented by the fear of thieves and tigers;
O best of the twice-born, having liberated [them], one obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
By giving them medicinal herbs, freedom from disease arises for them.
And having been liberated from fears, no fear exists for them anywhere. || 11 ||
And by purchasing [it] from the hand of a Caṇḍāla, one obtains the fruit of a cow-sacrifice (gomedha).
And Gopaka likewise purchased this and another from his hand. || 12 ||
Having provided them with protection from cold and heat, one shall attain heaven.
When they have risen, he should remain standing; and when they are seated, he should likewise remain seated.
But one should eat when they have finished eating, and drink when they have drunk their water.
One should perform a bath with cow urine, as well as with cow dung and barley.
Or else, O twice-born ones, one should maintain the journey of the body with cow's milk products.
For this cow-vow, when observed for a month, destroys all impurities.
One should maintain a single cow for a month and likewise give her barley to eat.
One should eat those [leavings] made of cow dung for one month; thereafter, one becomes pure.
At the end of the month, the devoted person should give that cow to a Brahmin.
This vow has been fully described as the destroyer of all impurities. || 17 ||
This vow is even more superior than the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
By performing this vow, one shall attain all desired objects. || 18 ||
And he goes to the world of Brahmā by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
Even without the gift of a cow, this vow yields great fruit. ||19||
For three nights or seven nights, according to one's own ability and strength.
Having likewise made his livelihood with barley that was free from being carried away by cattle.
One attains liberation from evil and enjoys great merit.
And dust raised by the hooves of cows destroys all impurities. ||21||
