From whatever kind of place it may be, no deliberation should be made regarding this matter.
It is auspicious, purifying, and the destroyer of misfortune. ||22||
For by the dwelling of cows, the earth indeed attains purification.
For that house is indeed pure where the cows reside. ||23||
By the wind of their breath, the city shall be consecrated with the lustration rite.
Touching them is meritorious and destroys the evil of bad dreams. ||24||
At the joint of the neck and the head, however, Gaṅgā is established among them;
cows consist of all the gods and likewise consist of all sacred fords.
O twice-born ones, their hairs are likewise meritorious and purifying.
A place smeared with cow dung is proclaimed to be pure. || 26 ||
One should smear the fire-chamber and the temple of the gods with cow dung.
In cow dung, however, Lakṣmī herself is always personally present. ||27||
Likewise, the Gaṅgā resides in cow urine, as well as in curd, milk, and ghee.
Sarasvatī is eternally established in the luminous realm of Soma.
Viṣṇu is declared to be the sacrifice, and he is established in cows.
Therefore, cows have been designated as Viṣṇu himself by the ancients.
They are indeed worthy of worship, they are to be saluted, and likewise they are to be glorified.
And one should provide them with food and likewise perform service for them.
O best of the twice-born, by serving cows in this world, one attains stainless realms free from sorrow.
Therefore, men devoted to dharma should indeed perform the service of cows with diligent effort. ||31||
Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-first chapter, titled "Service to Cows," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. ||291||
The swan said:
That man who is compassionate is considered a human being, while he who is merciless is regarded as a Rākṣasa.
O best of the twice-born, even among the Rākṣasas, compassion is found.
The merciless ones quickly fall into a terrible hell.
Then, in the human state, they experience slaughter, bondage, and affliction. ||2||
They become afflicted by disease, suffering, miserable, and poor.
Endowed with compassion, those men shine forth having attained heaven. ||3||
Therefore, a wise person should cultivate compassion even toward blades of grass.
One should not cause injury even to blades of grass that possess life. || 4 ||
Compassion should be shown toward insects, moths, domestic animals, and likewise toward wild beasts.
Whether among those of the highest caste, those devoid of caste, the outcaste, or those of mixed caste; || 5 ||
Compassion should be practiced in all circumstances; it bestows the fruit of all desires.
Of all vows as well, the single vow of compassion is the most excellent.
O twice-born ones, he liberates some living being afflicted by suffering from that very suffering.
The fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice is proclaimed; no deliberation is required here.
Having thus performed service, O twice-born ones, one should comfort living beings.
By that deed, the compassionate one attains the world of Brahmā.
He is not repulsed by the phlegm, urine, or excrement of one who is ill.
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled. ||9||
Those men who do not feel revulsion toward a dead person or one who is destitute.
And at the conclusion of the funeral rites, men who are destined for heaven perform these very acts.
From fire, water, weapons, and likewise from other calamities.
Having brought about the liberation of living beings, one is glorified in the heavenly world.
Likewise, O twice-born ones, having liberated living beings from their bonds, one attains that state.
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
For it is because a person might at some time liberate a living being from suffering.
He does not encounter that suffering wherever he may be born. ||13||
The gift one gives to all beings, and the compassion one has for even a single being—
For compassion is to be known as yielding great fruit through the gift of all beings. ||14||
The worlds of the Lord of the Thirty-three belong to those endowed with compassion, as do the worlds of the Grandfather for those endowed with compassion.
O best of Brahmins, it is ordained that those endowed with compassion shall have all their desires fulfilled in both worlds. ||15||

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-second chapter, titled "The Description of Compassion," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Courtesy is the supreme means of winning over people in this world.
Likewise, for one endowed with courtesy, there is the act of doing what is pleasing to others. || 1 ||
That best of men who performs what is pleasing to others,
O twice-born ones, he attains only what is dear in both worlds.
One should perform what is pleasing for others, both in their presence and in their absence.
One destroys what is unpleasant through what is pleasant; one attains what is pleasant through what is pleasant. || 3 ||
One overcomes the harsh with gentleness; one overcomes gentleness with gentleness.
For everything is overcome by gentleness; therefore, gentleness is sharper than the sharp.
In this world, the gods destroy the enemies of a generous person who is mild.
That is the subjugation of enemies, as is gentleness for a man. ||5||
Those who have been burnt by a mild person, however, are [burnt] on all sides by that very mildness.
Those Brahmins do not sprout, just like seeds that have been burnt.
Courtesy alone is the cause of good fortune; courtesy alone is the cause of the celestial realm.
One should conquer enemies by resorting to courtesy, and one should always remain endowed with courtesy. ||7||

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-third chapter, titled "The Description of Courtesy," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
A forest pierced by an arrow or struck down by an axe grows back again.
A loathsome evil spoken by speech does not take root once it has been uttered.
Friends turn into enemies for the man who speaks unpleasantly.
Misfortunes come of their own accord, and when dead, one goes to hell.
Therefore, a person should always speak with a smile as a preliminary.
Both directly perceived and beyond perception, it belongs to all those who speak kindly.
Enemies become friends for those men who speak kindly.
Even Rākṣasas are subdued by men who speak with conciliatory words.
In this world, there is no greater means of winning others over than pleasant speech.
Likewise, that man who speaks kindly becomes beloved by the worlds.
This entire world remains under the control of those who speak kindly.
In enmity toward those who speak kindly, there is no one [to be found] in the three worlds.
Those who speak kindly attain happiness in this world; those who speak kindly go to heaven thereafter.
Those who speak kindly obtain everything; therefore, one should always be a speaker of kind words. (7)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-fourth chapter, titled "The Praise of Priyaṃvada," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
For idle men, poverty is constant suffering.
In this world, laziness is a sin; laziness is the destroyer of prosperity.
Those lowest of men who are indolent do not obtain what is to be enjoyed.
Even wealth that has been acquired perishes for those who are indolent. ||2||
Therefore, a discerning person should always exercise skillfulness.
The skillful person attains everything whatsoever that he desires in his mind.
O best of the twice-born, [this applies] regarding dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.
A man who is always skillful is indeed a worthy recipient at all times.
The skillful one drew Śrī by her hair, even though she was turning her face away.
The highly fortunate one accepts it; everything is established in Dakṣa.
A man who is steadfast in exertion surpasses those who are merely eloquent in speech.
Those firm in speech delight in attending upon one who is steadfast in exertion. || 6 ||
Only the industrious person goes to heaven; only the industrious person attains the supreme state.
Only a man who possesses the spirit of exertion shall be victorious; therefore, one should always be intent upon exertion. (7)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-fifth chapter, titled "The Praise of Rising," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
O Acyuta, tell us of our external duties and our merits.
For by the gift of knowledge from you, we have indeed been further increased. || 1 ||
The swan said:
This entire triple world, with all its moving and unmoving beings, is water.
This world of the stationary and the moving is likewise a transformation of water. (2)
In this world, there is never any subsistence whatsoever without water.
For worms, insects, and moths, water alone is their ultimate refuge.
Wherever there is water, there all the gods are established.
Where there is water, there likewise are the sages of great vows.
And that is difficult for people to attain in the next world, O best of the twice-born.
Without water, there is no subsistence at all in either of the two worlds. || 5 ||
At that time, reservoirs for water should be constructed by a wise man.
Wells are equal to the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice, and a lake is equal to the Aśvamedha sacrifice.
A well with flowing water removes half of one's misdeeds.
Having reached heaven by means of the well-digger, he enjoys the pleasures of the gods.
Even there, a deficiency of enjoyments is proclaimed due to the place and lack of practice.
A large oblong pond (vāpī) is likewise proclaimed to be equal to ten wells. || 8 ||
And by constructing a pond, one likewise enjoys the world of Varuṇa.
O best of the twice-born, for ten thousand years it was only the size of a *nalva*.
There too, one obtains great merit from the act of leaving that place.
By performing that [rite] at the grazing ground of cows, one will certainly attain Goloka.
One attains the world of Śakra by constructing a pond on a path.
O twice-born ones, he indeed possesses water in a lake within a desert.
He goes to the world of Brahmā by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
But during the rainy season, he whose water remains in his pond—
The fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice is proclaimed for that person.
The fruit of that [act] belongs to him on the twelfth day, and indeed to him during the autumn season.
A human being, however, obtains the fruit of the Gosava sacrifice during the winter season.
The fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice belongs to him in whose house the Śiśira remains. ||14||
He obtains the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice at that place where the twice-born reside during the spring.
He who possesses it during the summer heat gains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
When a river channel had likewise been constructed for the purpose of irrigating the crops.
He shall indeed become a giver of food, a giver of life, and likewise a giver of protection.
He undoubtedly attains those worlds of Bhagīratha.
Having purified the water in a region fashioned by the gods. ||17||
O twice-born ones, a person obtains the fruit arising from the gift of ten cows.
A reservoir of water, constructed with stones donated by others, which is pleasant to use. || 18 ||
Having composed the Purāṇa of Manu, he is glorified in the heavenly world.
By the construction of water-channels, one attains unsurpassed satisfaction. || 19 ||
By thus making the water pure, one attains great merit.
Having dispelled the thirst of even a single embodied being here in this world, (verse 3.296.20).
One obtains a great fruit and rejoices in the world of the gods.
The wise man who should cause a tank to be dug by his own arm [shall gain great merit]. || 21 ||
One obtains from a Nalva the fruit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices.
One obtains the merit of bathing in a river by bathing at a bathing-ghat (snānasetu) in a reservoir of water.
Then, having bathed at Bahukhāta, a person obtains the merit of bathing in the Gaṅgā.
Furthermore, whoever should create even a small meritorious lake (jalāśaya) shall [reap its fruit].
For he who possesses that reservoir of water becomes a sharer in a portion of its merit. ||23||
A person attains supreme satisfaction and likewise reaches the highest worlds of the Lord of Waters.
O best of the twice-born, therefore water should be provided in the world of men, even if only a small reservoir is constructed. (24)

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-sixth chapter, titled "The Construction of Reservoirs," in the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, within the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and [Yama] in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
By planting trees, a mortal enjoys great fruit.
O twice-born ones, by planting shrubs, creepers, and climbing plants, a person [attains merit]. ||1||
One obtains each of those fruits that are proclaimed to result from the gift of a cow.
By planting a flowering tree, one attains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
One obtains the merit of a Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice by planting a fruit-bearing tree.
Even he who might establish a grove for others without any selfish motive, || 3 ||
Likewise, for the sake of green vegetables, he shall obtain the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having established a beautiful flower garden for the sake of the deities, a man [attains great merit]. || 4 ||
He rejoices in all the divine gardens, such as Nandana and the others.
One may dwell according to one's desire; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 5 ||
Having thus established a fruit orchard, one obtains an even greater reward.
Having established a grove of a hundred trees, one shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
One should assign the fruit [of the rite] in a grove of a thousand trees or in a grove of a hundred thousand trees.
The campaka, mallikā, and jātī are considered the best among those that bloom in the spring.
Another person obtains even more by giving these; there is no depletion here.
Likewise, both the Bhavya and the Pomegranate (Dāḍima) are said to be excellent for treating Gulma.
O Brahmins, the banyan and the holy fig tree are proclaimed to be the most excellent on the path.
By the gift of an orange, a person becomes endowed with beauty.
By the gift of a citron fruit, one shall obtain great good fortune.
By giving a copper vessel filled with pālevata fruit, one attains unsurpassed satisfaction.
By the gift of mangoes and walnuts, one shall obtain all desires.
Furthermore, whatever man here should establish a grove of mango trees numbering one hundred thousand; || 11 ||
Resembling an immortal, he sports in the delightful gardens of the gods.
Surrounded by apsarases, he does not turn back from that.
Even a single tree, when planted, can perform the function of a son.
She gratifies the gods with flowers and likewise honors guests with her shade.
Through its fruits, it delights human beings; for a tree, there is no hellish state.
Even on a tree devoid of flowers and fruit, there is rest for the traveler.
In the shade, one bestows great merit in a short time.
When it rains, just as water drips from the leaves of a tree, so [does it flow]. || 15 ||
By that, one certainly attains satisfaction when gone to the other world.
By that means, the man who plants trees attains the celestial realm.
Even from the watering of a tree planted by another.
One obtains a great fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point. || 17 ||
One should treat the diseased tree according to the sequence prescribed in the science of tree-life (vṛkṣāyurveda).
By making a person free from disease, one shall attain the heavenly world. || 18 ||
The suffering of cold, wind, and heat, as well as cutting and piercing;
Trees endure the greatest [injury], for that indeed is their great austerity. || 19 ||
By their leaves, flowers, fruits, and even by their shade, the trees constantly [benefit others].
That which is beneficial to others is indeed their great austerity.
One should always show compassion toward them, and likewise, one should show devotion.
Whosoever among them is constantly devoted, for him that forest deity [is always present].
He attains supreme satisfaction and likewise grants all desires.
Likewise, upon the dissolution of the body, he attains the world of the Vānaspatyas.
In the auspicious world of the Vanaspatis, [there is a place] for all trees indeed.
The deities abide as if possessing bodies; there is no doubt in this matter. || 23 ||
Those who have been described as possessing self-conceit have, moreover, attained supreme splendor.
Likewise, the world of Yama is proclaimed as the Vānaspatya world. || 24 ||
All those tree deities attend upon the realm of Yama.
And [the merit goes] to the one who planted the tree when he has departed to the next world. || 25 ||
They wait upon him, delighting him with divine song and dance.
Just as there is a deity for a tree that has been planted here in this world.
In this world, it yields fruit in the southern quarter as well as in the western quarter.
O highly fortunate ones, one becomes a deity when a meritorious reservoir of water has been constructed. || 27 ||
O twice-born ones, when the scripture was thus perfectly established, it was likewise so in the world of Brahmā.
The highly fortunate ones, who are deities of the scriptures, are born very quickly. || 28 ||
A treatise, a reservoir, a tree, and likewise a temple;
Even for a deceased person, the body is said here [to be] "mṛta" (dead). ||29||
And by reciting it by another person, a human being shall attain heaven.
A person desiring imperishable heaven should perform each respective duty.
Sons are declared to be the trees created by a man himself; a man must dwell within them.
They constantly satisfy a man with affection until he dies, and they gratify him with divine pleasures. || 31 ||

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Planting Trees," in the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, within the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
O best of the twice-born, it meets its destruction by water wherever it may be.
Whoever constructs a bridge there for the purpose of warding off the flood of water; || 1 ||
But those worlds which belong to the gift of land—those eternal realms he attains.
Having made the path easy to traverse like a bridge, one obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
That best of men who constructs a bridge for crossing over water—
Having crossed over both pleasure and pain, he attains the heavenly world. || 3 ||
By likewise providing a water-station on the road, one is glorified in the world of the gods.
Having performed the meritorious act of establishing a water station, one attains an eternal abode.
Through its maintenance as well as its relinquishment, the increase of fruit is proclaimed.
By performing its anointing, one is liberated from all sins. || 5 ||
Having given a rope at a place where water stands, a person becomes a possessor of cattle.
Likewise, by giving a water-vessel, one obtains that very same fruit.
By the gift of a water-pot, one's desires always become fulfilled.
And having likewise established water-stations, he appointed a man as an attendant.
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled.
O best of the twice-born, he who should give increasing [offerings] at a water-station (prapā)— || 8 ||
One attains a threefold increase through splendor, fame, and prosperity.
By the gift of salt, one obtains eternal flavors.
In that regard, by the gift of green vegetables, one shall attain the world of cows.
Likewise, by the offering of fruit, one obtains the merit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
And by the gift of barley meal, a man obtains the fruit of the Gosava sacrifice.
By the gift of cow-products, one shall attain the world of cows.
Having prepared various beds and seats at the water-station (prapā), he provided them.
One attains the heavenly world as well as a place among human beings. || 12 ||
Having constructed a windless shelter, beautiful to behold, at the site of the water-station.
One attains a world well-guarded by the Vasus; of this there is no doubt.
Having thus prepared the fire there, men [used it] for protection against the cold.
One shall likewise attain the radiance of the bodily fire, brilliance, and good fortune.
By providing fuel, one is not overcome by enemies.
There too, by giving suitable vessels, one shall attain heaven. || 15 ||
By the installation of snow, however, one attains the world of the moon.
Likewise, a man [should avoid] gravel, clods of earth, stones, and thorns. || 16 ||
Having removed [the image] from the path with effort, one shall obtain the fruit of the gift of a cow.
By massaging one who is weary, one obtains that very same fruit. || 17 ||
Having fanned the exhausted man with a palm-leaf fan.
Even by merely carrying [the image] on one's shoulder, though exhausted, one shall obtain the fruit of the Vājapeya sacrifice. || 18 ||
Then, leading him who was thus exhausted by his own vehicle or conveyance, he brought him along.
Having reached the world of the Sādhyas, he enjoys the pleasures of the gods.
By giving food to one who is weary, one obtains eternal desires.
But a human being who is exhausted finds satisfaction when satiated with waters. || 3.298.20 ||
A person who provides sandals and an umbrella to one who is weary, [attains great merit].
By means of these two, one obtains great fruit in an instant even in uneven places. || 21 ||
Likewise, he who, having taken up a burden from one exhausted by the weight, carries it himself.
By that action, O best of Brahmins, one attains the heavenly world.
Even when carrying the burden of another for a fee, the wise person remains discerning.
By giving the price for that, one shall obtain a tenfold fruit.
That best of men who provides protection for travelers on the road,
Having obtained a livelihood from that source, he is glorified in the world of Rudra. || 24 ||
Just as a man ferries travelers across at riverbanks along the path, so too does that person [help others].
He swiftly crosses over difficult terrains and mountains with edges as sharp as razors. || 25 ||
He who always performs purification and likewise offers a boat on the riverbank;
By that deed, a man obtains the fruit of an Aśvamedha sacrifice.
The wise man who constructs beautiful assembly halls.
He is honored in the world of Śakra in various wonderful gardens. ||27||
By the gift of beautiful objects to behold, one obtains memory and intelligence.
For one must show compassion toward travelers by whatever means possible. ||28||
The traveler who has departed from his own home is the supreme object of compassion.
Whether he be a bearer of sectarian marks (liṅgin) or a student (varṇin), he should be treated as a guest by the wise.
No consideration whatsoever should be made; rather, all travelers are to be honored in every way. ||29||
Having performed worship for the traveler, the man then reached the abode of Purandara.
They obtain meritorious divine enjoyments in heaven; therefore, they are most worthy of worship in the world of men, like travelers on the path.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-eighth chapter, titled "The Praise of Water-Stations," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the third section of the *Māghamāsa-saṃvāda* of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
The wise have declared that the fruit of all merits is fourfold.
Those actions performed contrary to the rules, or for the purpose of deceiving another; || 1 ||
One who is overcome by anger and greed should designate them as belonging to the quality of darkness (tamas).
But those performed with passion (rājasa) become characterized by supreme attachment.
O twice-born ones, these become characterized by goodness (sāttvika) here through supreme faith.
Having recognized other qualities, however, they were performed according to the desire for ritual injunctions. || 3 ||
A human being always experiences the fruit of tamasic actions in the state of an animal.
Whether by reason of the intermixture of castes, or again, in old age; || 4 ||
Whether in childhood or in a state of servitude, there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Otherwise, one would obtain the fruit of those characterized by passion (rājasa) within the human state. || 5 ||
One enjoys the fruit of those characterized by sattva while in a divine state; of this there is no doubt.
And the liberation resulting from those actions performed through superior qualities is proclaimed as the fruit. || 6 ||
For actions that are accomplished through wealth, wealth is traditionally said to be of three kinds.
And Kṛṣṇa, Śabala, and Śukla as well, O best of the twice-born.
Its threefold fruit is proclaimed to be likewise threefold.
Whatever was done by Kṛṣṇa while he was in the state of an animal, that indeed is now being experienced.
For among the social classes, white wealth is indeed that which is acquired through one's own duty.
But the variegated [state] is taught as resulting from the immediately preceding action.
The action of one who is of the highest caste but performs a base deed is called black.
Nevertheless, O best of the twice-born, I shall describe the white [complexion] among the castes.
That which is obtained through receiving gifts, from a patron for whom one sacrifices, or from a pupil;
For a Brahmin endowed with virtues, that threefold wealth is pure.
And wealth acquired through war, as well as from fines and legal proceedings.
The pure wealth of a Kṣatriya is proclaimed to be of three kinds.
Likewise, the Vaiśyas, having performed agriculture, trade, and cattle-rearing, [attain] purity.
That which is obtained through service to the twice-born is declared to be pure for a Śūdra. 13.
A Brahmin should never, under any circumstances, perform the work of a Śūdra.
A Śūdra may perform either Brāhmaṇical rites or those that cause mutual degradation.
For them, neither superior nor inferior karma exists.
Having abandoned the two intermediate actions, which are beneficial to all in common. ||15||
I shall describe the various kinds of wealth for all social classes [varṇas]:
[wealth acquired] through association with associates, gambling, theft, forgery, and violence. (16)
That which is acquired by means of deceit is called "black" for everyone.
Whatever wealth has been acquired through the practice of a craft, as well as by means of usury; || 17 ||
And that which is obtained from one who has rendered assistance is declared to be "spotted" (śabala).
Together with his wife, he received the hereditary gift that had come down through their lineage.
The wealth of all [these] is declared to be "white" (śukla) without distinction.
Merit performed with wealth acquired through righteous means shall yield abundant fruit. ||19||
Then, having performed meritorious deeds with wealth acquired through righteous means, the wise man enjoys divine pleasures in heaven.
The one of great power enjoys for a long time; therefore, wealth acquired through righteous means is imperishable.

Thus ends the two hundred and ninety-ninth chapter, titled "The Consideration of Wealth," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the third section of the *Māgha-saṃhitā* of the *Śrī-Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
The gods praise generosity, as do humans and likewise the twice-born.
Through generosity, one obtains whatever desires one wishes for in the mind. || 1 ||
Due to taking what was not given, people become miserable here upon seeing those who are dependent on others.
A person should make gifts to Brahmins as wealth for the sake of the next world. ||2||
A gift given equally to non-human beings and to cows should be known as yielding great fruit.
And that same [penance] is said to be double in the case of a mixture of castes (varṇasaṅkara). || 3 ||
For a Śūdra it is declared to be fourfold, and for a Vaiśya it becomes eightfold.
In the case of a Kṣatriya, it is sixteenfold; but for a mere Brahmin (brahmabandhu), it is exactly that same amount.
It is taught that thirty-two gifts should be given to one who is devoted to the study of the Vedas.
But that which is mastered by one who has studied extensively is a hundred times more distinguished than that, amounting to a hundred thousandfold.
And that very same [state] is called "infinite" by a Brāhmaṇa who has mastered the Vedas.
The domestic priest, however, may be a recipient for himself alone, but not for anyone else.
But a gift given to one's own domestic priest is said to be inexhaustible.
A man [should behave thus] toward a sacrificer, a priest, and likewise toward his teacher. || 7 ||
One should not take account of caste with respect to one's mother or father.
Likewise, [the same applies] to maternal aunts, sisters, and paternal aunts. || 8 ||
Likewise, [one should not approach] one's maternal grandmother, a sister's daughter, or a sister's son.
Among them, a gift given to a daughter's son and to the husband of a Vaiśya wife becomes inexhaustible. || 9 ||
Whatever is given in such a manner to one who has fallen from prosperity is also said to be inexhaustible.
The man who restores one who has fallen from his position to that very status once again— || 3.300.10 ||
One attains the world of the gods through long-performed action in this world.
He who shall restore a king fallen from his kingdom back to his own sovereignty; || 11 ||
He goes to the same world as Śakra for as long as fourteen Śakras reign.
Then, having attained human birth, he becomes a righteous king. || 12 ||
Therefore, one who desires prosperity should give a gift even if it is devoid of wealth.
That which is given to those bereft of fortune is proclaimed to be infinite. || 13 ||
Wealth that has been acquired by righteous means [should be given] at the proper time, to a worthy recipient, and in a suitable place.
O best of Brahmins, that which is given there is proclaimed to be infinite.
But whatever is given on the twelfth days, especially those of the bright fortnight, [yields great fruit].
But even among those women who are devoted to listening, O best of the twice-born, [there are some]. || 15 ||
Especially on days conjoined with Mercury, as well as at the ends of the fortnights, it is likewise so.
But especially on all the third days of the bright fortnight. || 16 ||
Especially during the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, they bestow honor.
Especially during the months of Āṣāḍha, Kārttika, and Phālguna. || 17 ||
O Brahmins, these three full-moon days yield great fruit when gifts are given.
O best of the twice-born, whatever is given during the Vyatīpāta yoga or on one's birth star (janmarkṣa), [that becomes inexhaustible]. || 18 ||
At the time of the transit of the planets, and specifically during the renunciation of the sign of Gemini.
The gift given at night yields great fruit; even greater fruit shall accrue from those [who give] to them. || 19 ||
O best of the twice-born, when the sun enters Capricorn, [then...]
Likewise, in the bright fortnights of Āṣāḍha, Aśvayuja, Pauṣa, and Caitra.
The merit of the four days beginning with the twelfth has been declared.
Likewise, Gemini, Virgo, Sagittarius, and Pisces. || 21 ||
O twice-born ones, when the sun has entered [the zodiac], the merit for each [day] has been described.
The gift known as the "Mouth of the Eighty-six" lasts for four days. || 22 ||
O best of the twice-born, that which is given when the umbilical cord has not yet been severed upon the birth of a son—
And for a son who performs these consecratory rites, that merit is proclaimed to be inexhaustible. || 23 ||
When either the moon or the sun is eclipsed by Rāhu, the great planet.
That which is spoken and given there is said to be inexhaustible; among those, one in particular is especially so.
At Puṣkara, at Prayāga, at Prabhāsa, and likewise at Naimiṣa;
In Dharmāraṇya, at Gayā, and likewise at Amarakaṇṭaka.
At Gaṅgādvāra, Kuśāvarta, Bilvaka, and the Nīla mountain;
Likewise at the Kanakhala tirtha, and similarly at Śāligrāma. || 26 ||
In Vārāṇasī, at the Sarasvatī, and at the confluence of the Gaṅgā and the ocean.
And at the confluence of the Sindhu and the ocean, as well as at Tritakūpa, O sinless ones. || 27 ||
Likewise, at the meritorious Plakṣaprasravaṇa and at Camasonmajjana;
Likewise at Mahālaya, Kedāra, and Bhṛgutuṅga. || 28 ||
And likewise in the meritorious Mānasa, and similarly in Uttaramānasa.
And whatever [merit] may arise from these and other such sacred sites of curd (dadhi-tīrthas), [that too is obtained]. || 29 ||
And it should be known that on the banks of rivers, that [practice] indeed yields abundant fruit.
Likewise, that which is given to the wretched, the blind, the miserable, the helpless, and those deprived of speech; || 3.300.30 ||
Likewise, toward others who are impaired—such as the dull-witted, the dwarfish, and the lame—[one should behave similarly].
And wealth given to those afflicted by disease shall yield great fruit.
Whatever is given while providing assistance for the Dharma, as well as during a sacrifice;
For the purpose of performing a marriage, that is proclaimed to be inexhaustible.
But with whatever wealth has been acquired, a man may enjoy festivals and happiness.
Wherever he may be born, he shall be a partaker in festivals.
And by that wealth which has been given, one may overcome future calamity.
That best of men does not encounter any misfortune whatsoever. || 34 ||
A woman, a ram, a goat, a cow, a horse, a steed, and a human.
But one [gift] should be given to each individual, or even many [gifts] may be given to a single person. 35.
If one person gives [a gift] to many, that gift certainly leads [the giver] to hell.
O best of the twice-born, that [gift] would lead the receiver to hell, and likewise the giver. || 36 ||
But he who, having given the fee for his life, enters into a sale [of himself], [is not released].
Thus, at the proper time, in the proper vessel, and in the proper place, [one should give] wealth acquired through pure means. || 37 ||
By giving wealth, one obtains [the favor of] gods, Brahmins, and Kṣatriyas.
Wealth is the life-breath that moves outside; everything is established in wealth. || 38 ||
From wealth comes food, and by means of food, indeed, every person lives.
A donor excels all the merits that exist in the world.
Through giving, one obtains whatever is desired by the mind. || 39 ||
Through generosity one attains popularity in the world; through generosity a person goes to heaven.
And having attained human birth, one who is characterized by generosity obtains enjoyments that are pleasing to the mind.

Thus ends the three hundredth chapter, titled "The Praise of Charity," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
O best among all upholders of dharma, [explain] the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of gifts.
Relate this to the Brahmins, for you are indeed a treasure-house consisting of the Vedas.
The Swan said:
O Brahmins, during a death-impurity or a birth-impurity, no gift should be accepted.
And even there, one should give in that same manner the gift of fearlessness.
They do not praise giving at night, except for the gift of fearlessness.
O best of the twice-born, what other knowledge, lamp, food, or shelter [could there be]?
Even at night, that which is beneficial should be given, as well as whatever else was previously mentioned.
In the honoring of guests and also in the honoring of travelers on the road.
And that [time] at night should be understood in the same way as that which has been declared for the worship of cows.
All time has been fully described, as well as all worthy recipients who bestow honor.
But regarding the granting of fearlessness, no deliberation should be made here.
Whether pure or impure, one should give the gift of fearlessness.
The gift of fearlessness should be accepted by one who is either pure or even impure.
That very time is the moment for seizing [the opportunity] when danger has arisen. || 7 ||
Furthermore, other gifts should always be accepted by one who is pure.
O best of the twice-born, [these] must not be accepted during a death-impurity or a birth-impurity.
And likewise, O knower of dharma, by one who has anointed himself and whose topknot is loosened.
Having bathed and properly performed the ritual sipping of water, one who is self-restrained and pure should take hold [of it].
Likewise, the giver should offer water; this is remembered as the rule for giving.
But the recipient should recite the Sāvitra mantra in every case.
Then, one should recite the name of the deity of the substance together with the substance itself.
Thereafter, one should conclude with the recitation of the Kārmastuti and the formal acceptance of the gift.
Having accepted a gift, the best of the twice-born should recite the *pratigraha* formula aloud.
A member of the royal caste (Kṣatriya) should recite it softly, and likewise a member of the merchant caste (Vaiśya) should recite it in a whisper.
Likewise, one should mentally perform the recitation of the *svastivācana* for a Śūdra.
One should utter the syllable "Oṃ" when addressing a Brāhmaṇa, but omit the "Oṃ" when addressing a king.
In the case of a Vaiśya, it should be done in a whisper; for a Śūdra, "Svasti" is proclaimed.
Fearlessness has all the gods as its deity; the earth indeed has Viṣṇu as its deity.
The giving away of a daughter, as well as [the gift of] a maidservant, are proclaimed as the Prājāpatya form.
And likewise, all single-hoofed animals are said to have Yama as their presiding deity. || 15 ||
Likewise, that which belongs to the buffalo, the sheep, and the camel would indeed be of the nature of Nirṛti.
Raudrī is designated as the cow, and the goat is said to belong to Agni.
One should know that the ram belongs to Varuṇa, while the boar is remembered as belonging to Viṣṇu.
All wild animals are said to have Vāyu as their presiding deity. || 17 ||
All reservoirs of water, water-jars, and water-pots;
O best of the twice-born, both the water-jar (kumbha) and the small vessel (karaka) belong to Varuṇa.
O best of the twice-born, these are the jewels born of the ocean, belonging to Varuṇa.
Gold is said to belong to Agni, as do all other metals.
O twice-born ones, grains belong to Prajāpati, as does cooked food.
All perfumes and the arts of the Gandharvas are to be known by the discerning.
The garment is remembered as belonging to Bṛhaspati, and likewise the juices belong to Soma.
And likewise, all birds are proclaimed to belong to the Vāyavya [class]. || 21 ||
The Brahma-vidyā has been fully described, as well as the requisites for that knowledge.
Scholars should know that books and other such items belong to Sarasvatī. ||22||
Viśvakarman is indeed the presiding deity of all craft implements.
Then, with trees, flowers, and various kinds of vegetables and greens; || 23 ||
In the same way, the Vanaspati is to be known as the source of all fruits as well.
Fish meat is likewise specified as being dedicated to Prajāpati.
An umbrella, a black antelope skin, a bed, a chariot, and likewise a seat;
Likewise, sandals, a vehicle, and whatever else is devoid of living beings. ||25||
O Uttaanangiras, may this man accept it from you.
Likewise, [he should offer] a rain-cloud, a plow, weapons, armor, banners, and so forth. || 26 ||
All the equipment for battle has been described; the discus is its presiding deity.
O best of the twice-born, let them seize whatever has been declared as belonging to all the deities.
O best of the twice-born, that which is to be known is either Viṣṇu as its deity or everything is so.
One should accept the gift of land after circumambulating the land clockwise.
O best of the twice-born, having likewise taken the hand of the maiden, as well as the female and male servants;
Having placed [the gift] upon the heart, it should be understood that such acceptance is in accordance with Dharma. || 29 ||
Having mounted the elephant, he spoke into its ear, and it was proclaimed to the horse.
And likewise, for all single-hoofed animals without distinction. || 3.301.30 ||
Accept the cow by the tail, and likewise the black antelope skin at its end.
Goats and other animals should be seized by the ears, while those with tails should be seized by the wise at the tail. || 31 ||
Furthermore, the acceptance [of the gift] of a camel should likewise take place while actually mounting it.
Having taken a handful of seeds and having gathered jewels from all sides, || 32 ||
One should take up the *vasu* formula from the end of the ten [syllables], or alternatively, after having put it on.
Having put on his sandals, he likewise ascended the two wooden shoes while reciting the mantra.
One should cause [the mantra] to be recited over the chariot while holding the pole, and over the umbrella while holding the staff.
Then, O twice-born ones, he placed his hands at the roots of all the trees.
Having taken up his weapons and likewise removed his ornaments.
Likewise, having touched his armor and banner, and having entered his house; ||35||
Having descended, O twice-born ones, they indeed entered all the reservoirs of water.
Having taken other substances and touched them, the Brāhmaṇa should recite [the mantra]. || 36 ||
But at the giving away of a daughter, one should recite [the mantras] separately for each of the articles.
O best of the twice-born, they are included right there within the category of receiving gifts.
Furthermore, by hearing the names of all these substances, men [attain their goals].
Then, taking water in his hand, he should recite the formula for the acceptance [of the gift].
That twice-born man who does not know the dharma and the rule regarding the acceptance of gifts.
One who is joined with the theft of property goes to hell. || 39 ||
But a Brāhmaṇa redeems that object from the act of acceptance.
But having understood the righteous rule regarding the acceptance of gifts, a Brahmin [should act accordingly].
A donor, likewise, should apply himself to his own spiritual welfare.
The earth, a cow, and likewise a horse, as well as jewels and gold. || 41 ||
One should not give sesame seeds to an elephant without first ascertaining its merits and faults.
Out of compassion for all beings, the wise man should give food.
And one should give clothing to everyone, for it is beneficial to all in common.
But he who should accept a gift without knowing the dharma-ordained procedure, [is at fault]. (43)
O twice-born ones, he certainly crosses over all difficulties together with the giver.
Therefore, with every effort, the rule regarding the acceptance of gifts should be understood.
The acceptance which is received according to the rule should bring about the supreme union of the two.
Having accumulated merit in the other world, he likewise attains prosperity in this world; there is no doubt about this. || 45 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and first chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Accepting Gifts," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the third section of the *Māgha-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
Tell me separately, however, the supreme fruit of each of these gifts.
O best among the upholders of all dharmas, you are indeed considered by us to be omniscient. || 1 ||
The Swan said:
Indeed, no other gift excels the gift of fearlessness.
Of all forms of giving, the gift of life is preeminent. || 2 ||
The gift of life may indeed be accepted even from a Caṇḍāla or a Pukkasa.
Living, one attains everything; living, one performs dharma.
But a man who remains alive shall become a vessel for desires.
But by means of the vessel, indeed, the state of being a vessel for everything perishes.
One should strive with diligence to protect the entire essence of the body's nature.
Dharma flows from his body just as water flows from a mountain. || 5 ||
By the granting of fearlessness, a man becomes a granter of all desires.
He who protects one who has come for refuge obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
But that lowest of men who abandons one who has come for refuge—
He falls into hell for many thousands of years. || 7 ||
Likewise, once released from hell, he is born among the animal species.
And even there, he likewise undergoes slaughter and bondage many times over.
Having attained a human birth by chance, one may yet fall into the state of a Caṇḍāla.
And there too, he is afflicted by terrible diseases, bonds, and fears.
But he who provides protection for one who is afraid and seeks refuge—
He alone is the one person in the world, the best among all upholders of dharma.
That best of men who provides protection for one who fears execution, [attains great merit].
His world is known as Śakraloka, extending as far as fourteen Indras.
By providing protection to one who fears entering into darkness, a human being [attains merit].
One attains the world of Brahmā; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. || 12 ||
There is no sin greater than killing; however, one may deprive [an enemy] of his sight.
A king should never, under any circumstances, perform that act for anyone. || 13 ||
Having caused others to enter into darkness, that lowest of men—
He certainly incurs blindness wherever he is born. || 14 ||
Even for thousands of eons, one is not separated from darkness.
Having provided protection for one who was terrified of the severing of his limbs, those blameless ones— || 15 ||
"He attains the world of Rudra for the remainder of a kalpa; such is the Vedic revelation."
Then, at the beginning of the creation of the eon, that man becomes endowed with knowledge. || 16 ||
Having provided protection for one who was afraid of bondage, that best of men—
Released from all bonds, he is glorified in the world of Vāyu. || 17 ||
For by providing protection to one who is afraid through repeated practice, a man likewise [attains that same state].
Completely liberated from all suffering, he shall attain the world of the Sādhyas. || 18 ||
But one who provides protection for someone terrified of being beaten or otherwise harmed [should be honored].
Freed from all bonds, he attains the world of the Bhṛgus.
Likewise, a man who provides protection for one who is afraid of being exiled, [attains merit].
He attains the heavenly world and the highest station among human beings.
Having provided protection for one who was afraid of the theft of his wealth, that best of men—
One attains the heavenly world as well as worship from the hosts of gods. || 21 ||
When a person who has provided protection performs some meritorious deed, [the merit belongs to him].
Such a man becomes a sharer and a protector of that meritorious deed. || 22 ||
And likewise, O twice-born ones, [the slaughter] of domestic animals, wild beasts, and birds.
And by providing protection for grasses, trees, and creepers, one becomes a possessor of heaven.
The best of men, having purchased a beast that had fallen into the hands of a slaughterer, [departed].
He attains the world of the gods and is born happy everywhere. || 24 ||
For as many hairs as there are on the animal, for that many years does the human [suffer].
He who provides protection attains the heavenly world.
Even by providing protection to a mere insect or moth, one enjoys all [the fruits of merit].
For many thousands of years; there is no need for deliberation on this point. ||26||
One should liberate those seized by thieves, seized by kings, or seized by enemies.
Likewise, O Brahmins, one who has been seized by a serpent shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. ||27||
Likewise, in uneven terrain, in difficult passes, in water, or amidst fire;
He who rescues one who has sunk [therein] shall obtain the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice. ||28||
By giving medicine to one who is diseased, one obtains the fruit of bestowing the gift of life.
By attending to one afflicted by disease, one obtains the fruit of giving the gift of life. || 29 ||
O twice-born ones, having thus performed the medical treatment, the physician [should do so] without payment.
The fruit of giving life is honored for him in the heavenly world.
Those men who, while being protected, were slain, have gone to the world of the Lord of the Thirty-three, filled with fear.
Yet those heroes among men have not fallen even now; for them, there is no falling away even when their time has come.

Thus ends the three hundred and second chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of the Gift of Fearlessness in the *Haṃsagītā* to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Knowledge is the cow that milks all desires; knowledge is the supreme eye.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of knowledge.
A man who possesses knowledge becomes a vessel for all desires.
Therefore, by one who bestows knowledge, everything indeed is bestowed here in this world. || 2 ||
When a man experiences affliction as a result of teaching others.
That is his supreme austerity; the world of Brahmā is known as his highest goal.
It is the supreme among gifts in the world, and likewise the supreme among ascetic practices.
O fortunate ones, the gift of knowledge bestows the fruits of all desires. || 4 ||
By the gift of the Veda, a person obtains the fruit of all sacrifices.
By the gift of an Upaveda, one rejoices together with the Gandharvas. || 5 ||
And by the gift of the Vedāṅgas, one shall attain the world of Śakra.
By the gift of the Dharmaśāstra, one rejoices together with Dharma.
By imparting the established doctrines, one attains liberation without a doubt.
And by giving other treatises (śāstras), a man is glorified in heaven.
One obtains [the fruit] from the gift of knowledge and from the gift of a book.
He who teaches the arts shall obtain the fruit of the Pauṇḍarīka sacrifice.
Having taught the science of archery, one obtains the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
By the gift of artistic implements, one obtains the fruit of the gift of craftsmanship. ||9||
Likewise, having restrained one who is engaged in what is harmful, [one should act].
The fruit of the gift of knowledge has been proclaimed; there is no need for deliberation on this matter. ||3.303.10||
Likewise, having restrained a man who is engaged in evil, a person [attains merit].
Having obtained the fruit of the gift of knowledge, one is honored in the heavenly world.
A man should train himself in that work by which he lives.
Having instructed [them], those highly fortunate ones are honored in the heavenly world. || 12 ||
The giver of that merchandise by which one lives is the heir to that merchandise.
He enjoys the fruit of a sacrifice in which all desires are fulfilled. || 13 ||
O best of the twice-born, all gifts indeed bear fruit in this world.
The gift of knowledge should be known as yielding one great fruit that is infinite. || 14 ||
Having bestowed upon a person the knowledge desired, whether it be an auspicious mantra or even a craft.
O best of the twice-born, whether it be the materials for his craft or whatever world he desires in his mind, he shall obtain it.

Thus ends the three hundred and third chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of the Gift of Knowledge," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the Māgha-saṃhitā of the third section (*Khanda*) of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
But he who bestows a maiden as a gift for a Brahmin upon a man, [is guilty].
The seven ancestors who have passed away and the seven descendants yet to be born in his own lineage. ||1||
By that gift of his daughter, he will undoubtedly cause [them] to cross over.
And likewise, he attains here the world of Dakṣa Prajāpati.
By giving [this] according to the divine ordinance, a man [elevates] his lineage for three generations.
He delivers [beings] from misfortunes and goes to the world of Dakṣa. ||3||
Having surrendered oneself according to the Prājāpatya rite, one should effect one's own deliverance.
One attains great merit and goes to the heavenly world. || 4 ||
The gifts of land, female elephants, and horses, as well as the gift of cows, likewise.
Since all [virtues] are indeed contained within it, what gift could be superior to that? || 5 ||
Having given her to one devoid of caste, he sinks into terrible darkness.
In that very same way, the man eats impure things for many thousands of years.
He who gives [this] to one of equal caste shall indeed partake of the aforementioned fruit.
And having given [the land] to one of superior complexion, [he should give] twice or likewise thrice as much.
He who would perform the consecration rites for an orphaned son of a twice-born man, and he who [performs them] through ritual acts.
And by means of the tonsure ceremony, the initiation, and other rites, he shall obtain the fruit of the horse sacrifice.
Having given away a maiden who is without a protector to a suitable or superior bridegroom.
One obtains double the fruit that is proclaimed for the gift of a maiden.
When the wedding had arrived, he prepared all the necessary articles.
O twice-born ones, one attains the world of the gods even through other ritual acts.
He gives clothing, a vehicle, ornaments, and what is required for marriage.
One obtains a great fruit and is glorified in the heavenly world. || 11 ||
Whatever wealth was given along with the daughter at the base of the fire;
The ancients have declared that his fruit is double that of the fruitful [action].
By the gift of a daughter in marriage, the best of men attains the world of Dakṣa.
The merit resulting from the worship of her husband shall be equal to the merit of the worship of Viṣṇu. || 13 ||
Having ascended a celestial chariot that delights the mind and is made charming by the playful songs of divine maidens.
The giver of a daughter attains the worlds of the highest of the thirty-three gods; there is no doubt about this. ||14||

Thus ends the three hundred and fourth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of Giving Away a Daughter," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the third section of the *Māgha-saṃhitā* of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 304 ||
The swan said:
The earth is the supporter and the sustainer; everything is established upon the earth.
For the earth is the mother of all, the supreme bestower of all desires. (1)
The deities attain satisfaction through the oblation produced from that [fire].
For the earth, O Brahmins, is declared to be the foundation of the three worlds.
For everything exists in the earth; everything is established upon the earth.
O best of men, the gift of land should be known as that which grants all desires.
But he who gives even a span's length of land, O best of men—
By that very act, a person certainly obtains the fruit of the gift of land. || 4 ||
O twice-born ones, whatever a man eats that has been produced [as a result of such acts] for the duration of a year;
However, the wise have declared that even a single area of ground the size of a cow-hide is [sufficient]. || 5 ||
Having given it then to a Brāhmaṇa, one shall attain the world of the Vasus.
Then, having given a plot of land for vegetables, one shall go to the world of Aṅgiras.
And by giving a grove of trees, one enjoys the world of Maruta.
He who gives for the purpose of a reservoir of water shall attain the world of Varuṇa.
Having given wealth for the temple of that deity, he indeed enjoys its fruits.
O best of the twice-born, that world which exists there is indeed eternal.
And having given away a pleasure grove, he rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
But by giving a jewel-mine, one is indeed honored in the world of Śakra. ||9||
And having given land made of gold, one is glorified in the world of Agni.
He who bestows upon others the source-land of metals, [attains great merit]. || 3.305.10 ||
O twice-born ones, his mind is also declared to be like that of the sacrificial fire in this world.
Having given land containing a granary, one is honored in the heavenly world.
O twice-born ones, he who indeed bestows land containing mines of collyrium—
That best of men is honored by his ancestors while residing in the world of Yama. || 12 ||
And by [giving] a salt-mine, one is honored in the world of Soma.
Having given land where leguminous crops are sprouting, that best of men [attains great merit]. || 13 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Gift of Land," in the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, within the third section of the *Māgha-saṃhitā* in the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

One who has missing limbs, one who drinks milk, one who is old, one whose milk has been milked dry, and one who is devoid of virility. ||3||
One who is diseased, one who is erratic, one who is like a serpent, and likewise one who is fleeing.
Furthermore, they were taken from that bull among the twice-born by means of prices that were not even partially purified. ||4||
It is traditionally taught that a cow should not be given away; having given one, one would fall into hell.

O best of the twice-born, a single [portion] should not be given to many, nor to two.

Having placed a single vessel, it is traditionally taught that many [gifts] may be given.

"May we attain preeminence by means of the cows previously released. || 23 ||

Those who bestow a leader of the herd along with a thousand cows.

Thus ends the three hundred and sixth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruit of the Gift of a Cow," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

Thus ends the three hundred and seventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Ghee-Cow," within the *Haṃsa-gītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighth chapter, titled "The Description of the Ritual for the Gift of the Sesame-Cow," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

Thus ends the three hundred and ninth chapter, titled "The Description of the Water-Cow," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
