O twice-born ones, he who indeed bestows gold equal in weight to his own body—
Completely liberated from all sins, he shall attain whatever destination he desires. || 13 ||
Whether he be a slayer of a Brahmin, a drinker of liquor, a thief, or one who violates the teacher’s bed;
Even one who is burdened with all manner of sins is liberated by that gift.
This is the highest among acts of faith and the most excellent of all gifts.
By giving gold to a Brāhmaṇa, one becomes happy everywhere. || 15 ||
After a long time, having fallen from the celestial realm, he was endowed with beauty and good fortune.
But in their highly prosperous family, there was a man endowed with all virtues. || 16 ||
By the gift of a golden vessel, a man becomes possessed of sons.
Of all desires, as well as of fame and the third heaven.
One who gives silver obtains beauty, and one who gives copper obtains wealth.
By the gift of iron and copper, one undoubtedly obtains base metals. || 18 ||
By the gift of tin and lead, one shall obtain an increase in fire.
And whoever should give a vessel of iron to a twice-born man according to his desire, || 19 ||
It becomes a vessel for desires, and it is superior even to iron.
O twice-born ones, he who duly gives implements for crafts and metals [attains merit]. || 3.310.20 ||
The fruit of the gift of knowledge for him has been declared; there is no doubt in this matter.
A man who gives leather always attains protection. || 21 ||
By the gift of weapons, one shall attain the destruction of enemies.
By the bestowing of royal insignia, one becomes a king upon the earth. || 22 ||
And by the gift of jewels, one is born here indeed as a king.
O twice-born ones, having enjoyed that world which results from the gift of jewels for a very long time, [one falls]. (23)
The giver of a diamond goes to the world of Śakra, while the giver of a ruby goes to the world of Ravi.
By giving emerald immediately, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu. || 24 ||
By the gift of pearls, one enjoys the world of Varuṇa.
By the gift of lapis lazuli, one rejoices in the seven continents. || 25 ||
And having given other jewels to the king of kings, O twice-born ones, |||
Among all jewels, gold is said to be the most excellent. || 26 ||
The wearing, the praising, and the giving away of gold are highly commended.
This gift pacifies bad dreams and destroys the effects of ill-performed sacrifices. || 27 ||
It should be known as the supreme remover of sins, as well as the pacifier of misfortune.
Having given gold, one rejoices in whatever worlds one desires. ||28||
By means of a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans.
By means of the sky-going vehicle, which was rich with hosts of celestial nymphs and moved according to one's will.
Having enjoyed pleasures in heaven for a long time, one shall obtain happiness in the human state.
Gold is the first offspring of Agni; the earth belongs to Viṣṇu; and cows are the daughters of Brahmā.
For everything has indeed been given by him here who would give gold, a cow, and land.

Thus ends the three hundred and tenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Procedure for the Gift of Gold," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 310 ||
The swan said:
But a man, by the gift of a seat, finds a place everywhere.
O best of Brahmins, by the gift of a bed, one obtains a wife.
Having given to a twice-born man a well-spread bed with an upper cover, one attains the world of Brahmā.
Born into a great family, she was endowed with beauty and wealth.
Likewise, he likewise obtains a capable woman who possesses [virtuous] qualities and is submissive to his will.
By this very gift, a wife shall obtain a husband. || 3 ||
By the gift of a canopy, one is liberated from all sins.
And likewise, O Brahmins, there is the Chatra; no doubt should be entertained in this matter. || 4 ||
Having indeed given an umbrella with a hundred ribs as protection against the heat of the sun.
Freed from all suffering, he is glorified in the heavenly world. || 5 ||
O best of the twice-born, he likewise proceeds along the southern path with ease.
Likewise, having given a pair of sandals that are smooth and provided with oil. || 6 ||
A chariot yoked with she-mules reaches the third heaven.
Freed from all sins, he shall proceed happily along the path of Yama.
By the gift of a palm-leaf fan, one is liberated from all sins.
By the gift of sandals, one attains an auspicious state. || 8 ||
By the gift of a footstool, one finds a place everywhere.
Having bestowed punishment upon a twice-born man, he likewise attains his proper place.
By the gift of a sacred thread (yajñopavīta), one obtains the fruit of the gift of clothing.
Thus has this fruit of the gift of a turban been declared. || 3.311.10 ||
By the gift of a tooth-stick, one shall obtain great good fortune.
By the offering of earth, one becomes pure in every respect. || 11 ||
By offering water for purification and bathing, one becomes free from disease.
Likewise, one who always provides oil for anointing attains the destruction of disease.
In the same way, by the gift of medicine, one attains the destruction of disease.
By offering fragrant substances native to the region, one attains good fortune.
By the gift of ointments, one is born endowed with beauty.
The body was ablaze with fire, and there was manifest radiance as well as the most excellent state of rebirth.
But he who gives to a Brāhmaṇa for the purpose of accomplishing [his] goal;
He attains the same world as Agni and achieves the destruction of his enemies. || 15 ||
Having given metallic vessels along with salt, [one obtains the following merit].
One becomes worthy of desires and shall attain great beauty. || 16 ||
But for one who gives metallic vessels containing oil, [the reward is as follows].
Supreme health has been proclaimed, and supreme beauty as well. (17)
But for one who offers vessels made of refined metal that are covered with soot, [the following occurs].
Supreme beauty has been proclaimed, and supreme good fortune as well. || 18 ||
By the gift of sandalwood, a person is liberated from all sins.
In the same way, by the gift of agallochum, one shines with glory upon the earth. || 19 ||
The gift of saffron is said to bring about good fortune.
Likewise, by the gift of camphor, one shall obtain all desires.
By the gift of a deer-skin, one shines with glory upon the earth.
O Brahmins, by giving nutmeg, one finds that one's ritual action becomes fruitful. || 21 ||
They are the providers of baths, mouth-fresheners, and incenses.
In this world, they attain popularity and become fragrant. || 22 ||
O Brahmins, by giving betel nuts, one finds that one's ritual action becomes fruitful.
By the offering of betel-leaf, one also attains good fortune. || 23 ||
He is the bestower of ocean-born treasures, such as conch shells and other precious objects.
He becomes a vessel for desires and for glory; of this there is no doubt. || 24 ||
By the gift of a comb, one utters excellent speech.
The gift of a bed is likewise the supreme provider of a dwelling place in the worlds. || 25 ||
Whatever may be desired by a petitioner, whether it be very little or much.
By giving that, one obtains the merit of the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 26 ||
Having gone to the world of Brahmā from among the Brāhmaṇas, [he is honored] by the Brāhmaṇas who worship with curiosity.
Being honored by gods and brahmins, one shall be happy; therefore, that which is requested should be given to the brahmins. || 27 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and eleventh chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of the Gift of Various Objects in the *Haṃsagītā* to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Jaimini within the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
But that man who properly bestows human carriers upon a twice-born person, [attains great merit].
O best of the twice-born, the fruit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice is said to belong to him.
Likewise, by the gift of a palanquin, one obtains the fruit of the Vahniṣṭoma sacrifice.
By giving away a servant as a laborer, one obtains the fruit of the Gosava sacrifice. || 2 ||
He who provides a warrior for battle goes to the same world as Śakra.
But he who gives a female servant who performs manual labor to a Brāhmaṇa— || 3 ||
The worlds of the Vasus are declared to be his auspicious realms.
He who gives away a young maidservant endowed with beauty, || 4 ||
Accompanied by celestial nymphs and filled with joy, he sports in the Nandana grove.
O Brahmins, he who gives a camel or a donkey to a twice-born man [is likewise reborn as such]. ||5||
Having reached Alakā, he rejoices together with the lords of the Yakṣas.
Among all forms of giving, the gift of a horse is declared to be the most excellent.
Likewise, it is recorded that the gift of a mare yields abundant fruit.
Those who give a horse go to the world of the Sun.
For as many hairs as he has, for that many hundreds of years [he shall dwell there].
By giving a white horse, one shall obtain tenfold the fruit.
Just as a white cow is the most excellent, so too is [the white horse] among horses.
He gives a horse equipped with a saddle and adorned with ornaments. || 9 ||
It is declared to be the fruit of the white lotus; no doubt should be entertained in this matter.
Yoked with four horses and equipped with all necessary implements.
By giving a chariot to a twice-born man, one obtains the fruit of the Rājasūya sacrifice.
By properly giving a female elephant, one shall obtain this very same fruit. || 11 ||
By the gift of an elephant, one is honored in the heavenly world.
In this world, he becomes a king endowed with glory and valor.
O twice-born ones, having indeed given an elephant with a golden girth to a Brahmin, [one attains great merit].
One undoubtedly obtains the fruit of both the Rājasūya and Aśvamedha sacrifices. || 13 ||
Having given a chariot yoked with four elephants to a twice-born man.
One undoubtedly attains the fruit of a gift given on all stages. || 14 ||
For by him, the earth with its mountains, forests, and waters has indeed been given here in this world.
And that high-souled man, being honored by the gods, proceeds to the worlds he has desired. || 15 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and twelfth chapter, titled "Description of the Ritual for the Gift of a Vehicle," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 312 ||
The swan said:
Among all forms of giving in the world, the gift of clothing is proclaimed to be the most excellent.
For clothing belongs to all the deities; it partakes of everything that is consumed. ||1||
A giver of clothing shall be well-attired and endowed with beauty and wealth.
O twice-born ones, he was likewise endowed with beauty and good fortune, and free from disease.
One should not give blue, red, or faded cloth to a Brāhmaṇa.
Having given a gift of fine linen to Bṛhaspati, who is of the lineage of Aṅgiras,
one is honored in the heavenly world after giving a garment made of cotton.
Having given that even with its hairs, the fruit shall be tenfold.
By giving a garment made of wool, one attains the world of the Bhṛgus.
Having given a goat to Aṅgiras, and having given linen to Bṛhaspati; || 5 ||
One attains the world of the Vasus by giving garments of kusha grass and silk.
And having given [the gift] produced from worms thereafter, one is glorified in the world of Soma. || 6 ||
By giving even a single woolen garment made from deer hair, one obtains the merit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice.
Having given clothing made of bark, one shall attain the world of the Vasus.
And likewise, having given Sumeraka, Kadali, and so forth, as well as the antelope skin;
as well as armor for the body, a helmet for the head, and likewise finger-guards for the hands.
And for one who gives footwear, it is recorded that the fruit is distinct [from that of giving shoes].
The gift of clothing is purifying and brings liberation even to the ancestors. ||9||
By offering [an object] dyed with safflower, one shall obtain great good fortune.
From the gift of saffron-red [powder], one shall obtain great beauty.
By applying red dye with other colors that are not blue, one shall become happy.
But in whatever measure a garment attains high value here in this world, [in that same measure does its merit increase]. || 11 ||
To whatever extent there is whiteness, to that same extent one shall obtain the fruit of merit.
This alone is proclaimed as the foremost among all other gifts.
One who gives clothing is declared a giver of everything, since one who possesses clothing is provided for everywhere.
Those who know the Dharma receive worship; therefore, that [knowledge] is indeed superior. || 13 ||
The giver of clothing, having enjoyed divine pleasures in heaven for a very long time, [attains liberation].
By means of a radiant celestial chariot, sun-colored and drawn by swans.
Having attained human birth, one becomes free from disease, endowed with purity, devoted to happiness, and humble.
Likewise, he is delightful to people, well-attired, and always honored in the world by the wise. (15)

Thus ends the three hundred and thirteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Praise of the Gift of Clothing," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Bhārgava and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:
O best of the twice-born, the gift of grain is said to be the most excellent of all gifts.
Among all grains, red śāli rice is proclaimed to be the supreme grain. (1)
By giving red śāli rice, a person is honored in the world of the Sun.
Having given fragrant scents in that manner, he rejoices together with the Gandharvas.
By the gift of *kāla* rice, one is glorified in the world of Śakra.
By the gift of a large house, one shall attain the world of the Vasus. || 3 ||
Likewise, by giving a wooden rice-offering, one finds favor in Alakā.
By the gift of rice and other grains, one shall attain heaven.
By the gift of barley, a man is glorified in the world of Śakra.
Likewise, by the gift of wheat, one shall attain the world of the Vasus. || 5 ||
He who gives priyaṅgu becomes beloved by the world.
The deities are pleased with him who gives śyāmāka grain.
A person who delights in giving other types of awned grain [attains great merit].
One attains the heavenly world; there is no need for deliberation on this matter.
One who gives mung beans goes to the world of Śakra, while one who gives black gram goes to the world of Yama.
O Brahmins, the giver of sesame seeds attains the world according to his desire.
By the gift of sixty-day rice, one shall attain the world of Nirṛti.
By giving chickpeas mixed with salt, one attains the world of Varuṇa.
Lentils belong to Vāyu, and king-beans (rājamāṣa) bestow strength.
By giving other kinds of grain, one shall attain heaven.
By the gift of sugarcane and grapes, one shall attain supreme good fortune.
Likewise, the giver of jaggery obtains health, and the giver of white sugar obtains his desired wish.
By the offering of molasses, one shall attain supreme satisfaction.
The giver of sugar-candy gains good fortune, and the giver of honey obtains all desires. || 12 ||
The giver of ghee obtains long life, and the giver of oil likewise obtains freedom from disease.
He who bestows salt obtains all his desires. || 13 ||
By giving roasted barley flour one attains satisfaction, and likewise by giving sand one attains prosperity.
By giving other gifts that have not been specifically mentioned, one shall attain heaven.
For it is said that in the world of men, the gift of cooked food yields fruit because even there, dry food is indeed obtained from it.
The best of the twice-born constantly perform sacrifices there; therefore, it is declared to be most meritorious.

Thus ends the three hundred and fourteenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Gift of Grain," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
Of all gifts whatsoever, the gift of food is preeminent.
There has never been, nor will there ever be, a gift superior to the gift of food.
In this matter, there should be no examination of the recipient, nor likewise any restriction regarding the time.
Nor should the location be scrutinized here; that food must always be given.
And from dogs, from those who cook dogs, and likewise from those who have fallen [from their caste].
Food should always be given to worms, insects, and moths. ||3||
For food is life in this world, and the vital breaths are dependent upon food.
In this world, the giver of food is the giver of life, and the giver of food is likewise the giver of everything.
And likewise, O best of the twice-born, he whose food one has eaten shall have offspring.
O best of Brahmins, it should be known that the offspring belongs to him whose food one eats. ||5||
Gifts should be given to all castes, and food should be eaten by the Brāhmaṇa.
O twice-born ones, when a Brahmin dies with someone else's food remaining in his stomach, [that person is held responsible].
He enters that very womb; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
The giver of solid food attains heaven, while the giver of soft food reaches the world of Śakra.
He who gives things to be licked shall attain the world of the Apsarases, and he who gives things to be sucked shall attain the world of the Vasus.
Likewise, the man who provides a drink attains the world of Varuṇa.
They offered fragrant and cooling drinks.
One shall have all desires fulfilled; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
Through the offering of *paramānna*, eternal satisfaction is attained.
Dying of thirst, he is honored in the world of cows.
Whoever should give unblemished food to one traveling on a journey;
For one who is weary and has never seen [it] before, the fruit of that merit is great.
Even if he feeds a thousand people, he does not go to hell.
He is honored in the heavenly world by means of a celestial chariot with the brilliance of the sun.
O Brahmins, one should destroy [the merit of] that [act] which is done for the sake of a single person afflicted by hunger.
By that action, he enjoys a great fruit after passing away. ||13||
Whatever is most beloved in the world, and whatever is dear to him in his home—
One who desires that very gift to become inexhaustible should give it to one who possesses those respective qualities.
Having observed the many kinds of gifts and their manifold fruits, a person [should act accordingly].
Endowed with faith, one should bestow it upon Brahmins; then, with a satisfied mind, one shall attain even more of that very thing in the world of men. (15)

Thus ends the three hundred and fifteenth chapter, titled "The Praise of the Gift of Food," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 315 ||
The sages said:
O Mahāmati, tell me: what gift has what recipient as its worthy vessel?
In which country and at what time does even a small gift yield great fruit? (1)
The Swan said:
One should not give a gift for the sake of fame, nor should one give to a benefactor.
A righteous person should not [give] to those habituated to dancing and singing, nor to atheists. || 2 ||
Nothing whatsoever should ever be given to one of evil character.
But that which is given to one of evil character brings harm to the donor.
By that sinful act, the Giver of Wealth (Kubera) is swiftly joined with suffering even in this world.
Therefore, having acquired wealth, one should practice virtue and cultivate a virtuous character.
By that merit, he undoubtedly attains union with the Giver of Wealth.
In the giving of food, one should examine the recipient, even if only slightly.
O twice-born ones, food indeed must be given everywhere by one who desires the Dharma.
But even in that which is faulty, [the teaching] is faultless; even in that which possesses qualities, it brings forth further qualities.
Therefore, with every effort, food should always be given.
The gift of food to those devoted to the study of sacred knowledge yields great fruit.
And likewise, O best of the twice-born, regarding other auspicious karmas as well.
A man who consumes whose food may accomplish his tasks.
Just as one who accomplishes a ritual action attains merit, so too does the giver of food enjoy its fruit.
Having given wealth to those who were afraid of kings and likewise to the wealthy, || 9 ||
And for those who are afraid of thieves, he enjoys imperishable fruit.
Likewise, it was given by one desiring to sacrifice and by one wishing to kill in a time of distress.
It is proclaimed that for those afflicted by suffering and the wretched, it is inexhaustible.
In rites such as marriage, the tying of the girdle, and consecrations, ||11||
And that which is given to those who have fallen into distress is declared to be inexhaustible.
O best of the twice-born, the sacrificial materials and implements belong to the Kṣatriya.
That which is useful for merit [is appropriate] for a Vaiśya; for a Śūdra, one who subsists by his craft.
Whatever substance is useful to someone should be given to that very person; it shall belong to them alone.
And by whichever vessel the livelihood of anyone has been prescribed, [that is what they should use].
That indeed should be given by the wise person who desires merit.
The staff, the black antelope skin, and likewise the water-pot, O Brahmins.
One obtains great merit by giving this garment to a student of sacred knowledge (brahmacārin). || 15 ||
Clothing, bedding, seats, grain, wealth, a house, and household utensils.
But that which is given to a householder should always be known to yield great fruit.
Nīvāra grain, bark garments, vegetables, fruits, roots, and cow's milk.
That which is given to one who has entered the forest-dwelling stage of life (vānaprastha) is proclaimed to be infinite. || 17 ||
The giving of alms to an ascetic, as well as the gift of a begging bowl, is likewise beneficial.
For women, there are auspicious substances such as betel, red garments, and so forth. || 18 ||
The giving away of women must be performed by placing them into the hand of the husband, and not otherwise.
For this is declared to be adultery when one gives oneself secretly to a husband who is offering himself [in marriage]. || 19 ||
Both food and shelter given to a traveler yield great fruit.
At the time of rites such as marriage, it is the cause for the successful completion of those rites.
O knowers of dharma, he who bestows [this] shall obtain the merit of an Ashvamedha sacrifice.
By giving wealth to those who are afflicted with illness, one obtains a gift of great fruit. || 21 ||
Having given toys to the child, as well as sweet food, likewise.
Or even by [giving] a charming fruit, one obtains the fruit of the Agniṣṭoma sacrifice. ||22||
A man, having given sweet food to those who desire sweet foods, [obtains great merit].
One obtains inexhaustible fruit and goes to the heavenly world. || 23 ||
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, having given food to one who is destitute of fortune, [one incurs sin].
Or by giving auspicious clothing, those who know the Dharma attains great merit. || 24 ||
O Brahmins, that man was preeminent in objects of compassion and was radiant with splendor.
Compassion for him must be shown by one who stands upon the path of the virtuous. || 25 ||
When an undertaking has been commenced and others have arrived [to assist], one should exert effort in the task.
One obtains inexhaustible fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point. ||26||
By the gift of fodder to brahmins who possess cows.
And the knower of dharma who gives salt enjoys imperishable fruit. ||27||
Then, during the procreations, both [groups] were subsequently afflicted by calamities.
That gift is declared to be inexhaustible for a wise man. ||28||
Having given even a mere handful of water to a petitioner, O tigers among brahmins.
One obtains inexhaustible fruit; there is no need for deliberation on this point. ||29||
Furthermore, it is declared in the world that a gift given to a seeker, even without [the giver's] afflictions, indeed bears fruit.
Therefore, when entreated, one must not show disrespect toward a petitioner according to one's ability. (3.316.30)

Thus ends the three hundred and sixteenth chapter, titled "The Description of Specific Gifts According to Specific Recipients," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
The gift that has been proclaimed as having great fruit at a particular time—[that is the one to be given].
Tell us the truth, for you are said to be all-knowing.
The swan said:
Likewise, the gift of sesame seeds for a year yields great fruit.
Likewise, O best of the twice-born, there was a gift of barley preceded by the word "pari. || 2 ||
In the sequence beginning with *iḍā*, there is the successive arrangement of garments and grains.
In the year Udāsa, a gift of silver yields great fruit. ||3||
During the northern course of the sun (uttarāyaṇa), the gift of clothing is declared to be fruit-bestowing.
O best of the twice-born, [this applies] to bathing, anointing with unguents, and so forth, during the spring season.
Likewise, [the gift] of beverages in the summer, and of umbrellas immediately thereafter.
Those who know the Dharma [should give] food in the autumn and also garments in the winter.
Having performed the offering of fire at the rising of the sun, a man [attains the fruit].
Likewise, during the cold season, one should constantly satisfy the fire with sesame seeds.
Having given kulmāṣa with ghee to the twice-born according to one's ability.
One attains the radiance of bodily fire, brilliance, and the destruction of enemies. ||7||
Barley meal mixed with white sugar-candy, along with cucumber and gourd.
One who has prepared water-pots [for the deceased] enjoys inexhaustible fruit. ||8||
O best of the twice-born, he constantly bathes at midday during the rainy season.
By the gift of sesame seeds during the month of Māgha, he attains that world and goes there.
By giving priyaṅgu in the month of Phālguna, one becomes beloved on the earth.
In the month of Caitra, one who wears variegated garments attains great good fortune.
By the offering of cakes in the month of Vaiśākha, one attains heaven.
Likewise, by giving an umbrella in the month of Jyeṣṭha, one obtains all desires.
And having given sandals in the month of Āṣāḍha, one certainly attains heaven.
The very great fruit of giving clothing in the month of Śrāvaṇa has been proclaimed.
Likewise, by the offering of molasses in the month of Proṣṭhapada, [one obtains great merit]. || 12 ||
By the gift of ghee during the month of Āśvina, one is born handsome.
By offering lamps during the month of Kārttika, one shall obtain vigor everywhere.
By giving salt in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, one attains good fortune.
Likewise, by the gift of gold in the month of Pauṣa, one attains supreme nourishment.
And the gift of flowers during the bright fortnight is remembered as bringing about prosperity.
Likewise, the gift of fruits during the dark fortnight yields great fruit. ||15||
On a Sunday, one should offer a cake prepared with salt, clarified butter, and molasses.
By giving it along with gold, a person is not overcome by diseases. ||16||
By giving such [a gift] on a Monday, one shall obtain good fortune.
By giving wood on a Tuesday, one shall obtain the destruction of enemies. || 17 ||
The gift of toys for the sake of awakening is praised when given to children.
By the gift of clothing on the day of Jīva (Wednesday), one attains supreme nourishment.
Having given pleasure to his wife with semen, he obtains delight everywhere.
By applying an oil massage on a Sunday, one shall obtain long life. ||19||
The gift of gold under the constellation Kṛttikā is remembered as yielding great fruit.
Red cloth under Rohiṇī, and salt under the lunar mansion of Saumya (Mṛgaśiras).
Likewise, on the day of Ārdrā, one should eat kṛsara, and on the day of the Sun (Sūrya), silver.
Likewise, [the offering] of ghee should be made under Puṣya, and of perfumes under Āśleṣā.
Sesame seeds under the Maghā conjunction, and priyaṅgu under the constellation presided over by Bhaga.
And for Āryaman, cakes; and for Savitṛ, milk-rice. || 22 ||
Under Citrā, one should give variegated garments; under the deity Vāyu, one should give parched grain flour (saktu).
And for metals, it is on the day of Indra and Agni; for garlands and fruit, on the day of Mitra.
Likewise, [the same applies] to an umbrella, a leafy vegetable, a root, and a root-fruit.
The gift of honeyed water during the month of Āṣāḍha yields great fruit. || 24 ||
In hearing of the gift of food at Viśveśvara and in [the merit of] clothing, as well.
O Brahmins, [the asterism] Vāsava is for grain, and Vāruṇa is for medicinal herbs.
And [the worship] of the seed-syllables is at Ajapāda, and that of the grains immediately thereafter.
Likewise, [the month] Pauṣa is for dairy products, and Āśvina is for ritual ablutions. || 26 ||
Likewise, the gift of sesame seeds under the asterism Bharaṇī yields great fruit.
On the second day of the month of Puṣpa, you should likewise partake of ghee. || 27 ||
On the third day, however, one should give garments; on the fourth, gold.
On the fifth day, they indeed grant fruits; on the sixth, they bestow honor for bathing.
And on the seventh day, one should offer cakes, and on the eighth, molasses.
On the ninth day, [the gift] is of kulmāṣa; on the tenth, it is of silver. || 29 ||
On the eleventh day [one should give] gold, and on the twelfth day, clothing.
On the thirteenth day, [one should offer] fragrant substances; immediately after that, white [substances].
And the gift of excellent food on the fifteenth day yields great fruit.
O best of the twice-born, on the third day of the bright fortnight of the month of Vaiśākha, || 31 ||
O best of men, whatever one gives, that very thing one enjoys inexhaustibly.
In particular, likewise, the gift of unbroken grains yields great fruit.
When the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) in the month of Māgha is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism, it is so endowed.
The gift of sesame seeds brings great merit, even without hearing [this teaching]. || 33 ||
O best of the twice-born, it was on the ninth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Bhādrapada.
By giving wheat-rice mixed with jaggery, one shall obtain merit.
O best of the twice-born, these meritorious gifts have been described by me as appropriate for their specific times.
All these gifts should be given even without [the practice of] yoga; however, through yoga, merit is declared to be even greater. || 35 ||

Thus ends the three hundred and seventeenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Giving in the Yoga of Time," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*. || 317 ||
The sages said:
Tell us of the vow known as the Nakṣatra-sattra, together with its associated gifts.
O best among all upholders of the Dharma, O you of direct and stainless vision!
The swan said:
O highly fortunate ones, under the asterism Kṛttikā, he [should offer] milk-rice with clarified butter.
Having satisfied virtuous Brahmins, one attains the unsurpassed worlds.
Under Rohiṇī, one should offer well-known beans, rice, and clarified butter.
Milk should be given as a drink to the twice-born for the sake of discharging one's debt.
Having given a milch cow together with her calf under the lunar mansion presided over by Soma, one obtains great merit.
One shall go to the worlds of men after [attaining] unsurpassed residence in heaven.
Having fasted, one should give kṛsara mixed with oil under the constellation Ārdrā.
A man crosses over difficult terrains and even mountains with edges as sharp as razors.
Having given cakes and likewise excellent food under the constellation Punarvasu, one attains prosperity.
He is born into a family that is illustrious, endowed with beauty, and possesses abundant food.
But by giving gold, whether wrought or unwrought, under the asterism Puṣya, one attains [the fruit].
In worlds devoid of light, he shines like the moon. || 7 ||
And he who gives silver or a bull under the asterism Aśleṣā, [attains great merit].
He is liberated from all fear and attains auspiciousness as well. || 8 ||
Under the Maghā asterism, a person [should offer] vessels filled with sesame seeds.
Having given [these], one possesses sons and cattle in this world and rejoices after death.
Having fasted on the occasion of the full moon of Phālguna, one should honor the Brāhmaṇas.
By giving food mixed with molasses, one attains good fortune.
Rice of the ṣaṣṭika variety, prepared according to the rules and combined with ghee and milk.
Having given [a gift] in the region of Uttara, one is glorified in one's own world. || 11 ||
Whatever gift is bestowed by men in the region of Uttarā;
And it is the certainty that there will be great fruit in the future. || 12 ||
Having fasted, he gave an elephant-chariot yoked with four animals into the hand [of the recipient].
A man crosses over difficult terrains and mountains with edges as sharp as razors. || 13 ||
Having given a bull and sacred perfumes under the asterism Citrā, a person [attains great merit].
He wanders in the world of the Apsarases and delights in the Nandana grove.
Then, having given wealth under the Svāti asterism—whatever is most dear to oneself—
He attains auspicious worlds and, even in this very world, great renown. || 15 ||
And under Viśākhā, having given a bull and a milch cow that yields milk;
And a cart, complete with its harness, filled with grain, and provided with clothing. || 16 ||
He gratifies the ancestors and the gods, and having attained [this state], he enjoys infinity.
And he does not encounter difficulties; he goes to his own world. || 17 ||
Having given the desired means of subsistence to the Brahmins as prescribed, he obtains it for himself.
And it is certain that he does not fall into the afflictions of hell and other such realms. || 16 ||
Under the asterism Anurādhā, one who has fasted should offer an upper garment as a cloth-offering.
Having given it, even for a hundred ages, a man is glorified in heaven. || 19 ||
Having given kālaśāka together with its roots to brahmins, a mortal [attains great merit].
In Jyeṣṭhā, one attains desired prosperity and goes to a desired state of existence. ||3.318.20||
Having given roots and fruits at the base to the Brahmins, he remained composed in mind.
He indeed delights the ancestors and attains his desired destination. || 21 ||
Then, under the constellation Pūrvāṣāḍhā, having fasted, one should offer vessels of curd.
In a family endowed with proper conduct, among Brahmins who have mastered the Vedas. || 22 ||
Having given [this], he is born after death in a family possessing many herds of cattle.
A water-pot containing ghee, along with abundant honey and molasses. || 23 ||
Having given [a gift] under the Uttarāṣāḍhās, one attains all the worlds.
But when the Abhijit yoga occurs, one should offer it with milk, having first poured honey and ghee over it. ||24||
One who constantly wears this armor is honored in the heavenly world by the wise.
Having given a woolen blanket to Śravaṇa, it should indeed be covered with a cloth. || 25 ||
He travels by means of a white vehicle to the unobstructed worlds of heaven.
Having given a vehicle yoked with oxen under the asterism Dhaniṣṭhā, being composed in mind, ||26||
By means of the Vastraraśmi, one immediately attains a new kingdom after passing away.
Having offered perfumes along with aguru and sandalwood during the Śatabhiṣaj conjunction, || 27 ||
Having passed away, he attains the worlds of the Apsarases and eternal fragrances.
And having given rajamāṣa beans during the conjunction with Pūrvābhādrapadā. || 28 ||
Endowed with all kinds of edible fruits, he indeed becomes happy after passing away.
But he who offers the meat of a sheep under the Uttarā constellation [attains the fruit]. ||29||
He truly gratifies the ancestors and, after death, attains infinity.
He who gives away a cow with a bronze milking vessel under the asterism Revatī—
Having departed, it returns to the giver, bringing with it those desires.
Having given a chariot yoked with horses under the asterism Aśvinī, that best of men [attains the fruit]. || 31 ||
Endowed with elephants, horses, and chariots, he is born into a family of radiant splendor.
Having indeed bestowed a sesame-cow upon the twice-born under the asterism Bharaṇī, one attains great merit.
Furthermore, such a man obtains well-prolific cows and likewise attains glory after death.
I have thus described this Nakṣatra-sattra for men who desire to attain their desired worlds.
Having performed this once, he goes to the world of the gods and remains there for a kalpa, like that lord of the gods.

Thus ends the three hundred and eighteenth chapter, titled "The Procedure for the Nakṣatra-satra," within the *Haṃsa-gītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
Speak further to me regarding gifts according to their proper timing.
O best of the twice-born, O you of pure vision, the fruit for us is now manifest.
The Swan said:
Having reached the fifteenth day of the bright fortnight of the month of Caitra, a person...
Having given a pair of variegated garments to a twice-born man while observing a fast, ||2||
And by honoring other Brahmins, O learned ones, one shall attain great good fortune.
On the full moon day of Vaiśākha, [he should feed] seven or five Brāhmaṇas.
One should cause [the patient] to recite [the mantra] while using black sesame seeds mixed with honey, or else with other [seeds].
"May Dharmarāja be pleased," or whatever else dwells in your mind. || 4 ||
One is liberated at that very moment from the sin committed throughout one's entire life.
At that very time, he [discharged] a black arrow with a hoof-shaped tip.
Having covered it with sesame seeds and cloths, it was adorned with all kinds of jewels.
And to those performing austerities, the earth with its groves and forests must be given.
Having placed sesame seeds upon a black antelope skin, together with gold, honey, and clarified butter;
He who gives to a Brahmin overcomes all evil deeds.
Likewise, having fasted when the full moon of the month of Jyeṣṭha has arrived, he who bears the mark of the hare (the moon).
Likewise, by giving sandals and an umbrella, one shall become exceedingly happy.
By giving food on the full moon day of Āṣāḍhā, a man obtains abundant food.
By the gift of a water-cow on the full moon day of Śrāvaṇa, one shall attain heaven.
The gift of a cow on the full moon day of the month of Proṣṭhapada yields great fruit.
On the full moon day of Āśvayuja, one should give a bronze vessel filled with clarified butter to a twice-born man.
And likewise, by giving gold, one is born radiant.
On the full moon day of Kārttika, [one should worship] the one who has the luster of the moon or even another color.
With jewels, perfumes, grains, seeds, and likewise with garments.
Having prepared the bull according to the rules and having offered lamps accompanied by mantras, || 52 ||
By giving at the rising of the moon, a person is liberated from all sins.
By means of that, he travels easily through the wilderness on the path of Yama. || 13 ||
And he bestows all his enjoyments upon him there.
Likewise, in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, when the moon was full during the winter season.
O best of the twice-born, [he should honor them] with garments adorned with great silver.
Having covered it and placed a prastha measure [of the substance] in a bell-metal vessel, he should remain composed. ||15||
But of the finest salt, O best of the twice-born, when it has been ground into powder—
Having given Suvarṇanābha to that very same twice-born man. || 16 ||
That person becomes endowed with good fortune, beauty, and charm.
A man who has been empowered on the full moon day of the month of Pauṣa by means of a paste of white mustard seeds, || 17 ||
Immediately thereafter, he was consecrated with a jar of cow-derived clarified butter.
Likewise, he should bathe after being scrubbed with water containing all types of seeds and medicinal herbs.
Immediately after that, [one should offer oblations] with clarified butter together with fragrant gems and fruits.
Having seen that golden face, he should give it to a member of the twice-born caste.
Then, one should worship Viṣṇu, who has been bathed with ghee, according to one's capacity.
One should offer clarified butter into the fire and give clarified butter to the twice-born.
Fasting and composed in mind, one should give a pair of garments to the performer.
By this action, those who know the Dharma attain unsurpassed nourishment.
Having performed a śrāddha with sesame seeds on the full moon day of Māgha, one is liberated from all sins.
Having given a well-spread bed to a Brāhmaṇa on the full moon day of Phālguna, [one obtains great merit].
A wife endowed with beauty and wealth, as well as one who is devoted to her husband.
A man who knows the Dharma attains this; he obtains unsurpassed prosperity. || 23 ||
Likewise, a wife [should not abandon] her husband; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
And on these full-moon days, conjoined with the lunar mansions of the respective months. || 24 ||
The fruit of these very same gifts shall be tenfold.
And when these [rites] are preceded by the word "great" (mahat), one enjoys inexhaustible fruit. || 25 ||
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Caitra, a man who gives variegated garments [attains great merit].
One obtains inexhaustible fruit and goes to the world of the gods. || 26 ||
Likewise, by the gift of gold on the twelfth day of the month of Vaiśākha.
O best of the twice-born, by the gift of an umbrella and sandals in the month of Jyeṣṭha, [one attains great merit].
Having given a well-spread bed, one should please Him who reclines upon the serpent-king.
On the twelfth day of the bright fortnight of Āṣāḍha, one is glorified in Śvetadvīpa.
By giving a gift of clothing in the month of Śrāvaṇa, one is glorified in the world of Viṣṇu.
O twice-born ones, one who gives a cow goes to Goloka in the month of Bhādrapada.
Likewise, one should please Aśvaśiras by giving a horse during the month of Āśvina.
He attains the world of Viṣṇu and uplifts his own lineage.
By the gift of cotton cloth in the month of Kārttika, one shall attain heaven.
The gift of salt in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa yields great fruit. || 31 ||
Likewise, there will be a terrible famine of grain in the month of Pauṣa and in the one immediately following it.
In the month of Phālguna, one should offer all types of fragrant substances; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter. ||32||
The twelfth day (Dvādaśī) of the month of Caitra, when conjoined with the lunar mansion of Bhaga, yields great fruit.
Then Vaiśākhī is conjoined with Hasta, and likewise [Jyeṣṭhā] in Jyeṣṭha with Svāti.
Likewise, when Jyeṣṭhā and Āṣāḍha are conjoined with Mūla, it belongs to Viṣṇu.
Likewise, in the month of Bhādrapada, it is conjoined with the Śravaṇa asterism.
In the month of Āśvina, the twelfth lunar day (dvādaśī) joined with the constellation Ārdrā is meritorious.
In the month of Kārttika, [the day] joined with Revatī, and likewise in the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, joined with Kṛttikā. || 35 ||
In the month of Pauṣa, when joined with Mṛgaśiras, and in the month of Māgha, when conjoined with Āditya (the Sun).
In the month of Phālguna, the twelfth lunar day conjoined with the Puṣya asterism is supremely purifying.
Likewise, one who has fasted should give gifts under these lunar mansions when they are in conjunction with them.
O best of the twice-born, it should be known that its fruit is the fulfillment of all desires and is infinite.
When the sun enters Aries, the gift of a ram yields great fruit.
Likewise, the gift of cows is prescribed for the transit of the sun into Taurus.
And the gift of beds and seats should be given when the sun has entered Gemini.
Likewise, upon the sun's entry into Cancer, [one should offer] parched grain flour mixed with sugar. || 39 ||
Likewise, O twice-born ones, [the offering] of molasses, inspissated juice, candied sugar, and white sugar.
And likewise of salt, clarified butter, fruits, and yellow myrobalan.
In the same way, the gift of water-pitchers should be known to yield great fruit.
Likewise, upon entering the lion [palace], there were vessels made of metal. || 41 ||
Likewise, at the entrance of a maiden, there should be fragrant garments.
At the entry of the sun into Libra, it is most excellent for grains and seeds as well.
And when insects enter one's clothes or dwellings, one should indeed give gifts.
Entering at Dhanvi yields great fruit for garments and vehicles. || 43 ||
At the entrance of the deer, there is likewise the offering of wood and of fire.
At the time of entering the water-jar, however, one should give a gift of grass for the sake of the cows.
Upon the entry of the Fish [into the zodiac], it is the most excellent of all places and even of garlands.
O best of the twice-born, these gifts have thus been described by me; and a man, having bestowed them at the proper time, [attains the highest reward].
One obtains the desires cherished by the mind; therefore, they praise this great gift.

Thus ends the three hundred and nineteenth chapter, titled "The Description of the Fruits of Giving on the Twelve Full-Moon Days," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
The performance of meritorious sacrifices has been prescribed for those men who are endowed with wealth.
Likewise, various gifts were given to those of middling conduct. || 1 ||
And various kinds of gifts have been described for those of limited means.
Tell me about the performance of dharma for those men who are destitute of wealth.
The swan said:
For them, the practice of fasting is the supreme cause for attaining the Dharma.
Likewise, for those endowed with wealth, that [gift] is praised and yields great fruit. || 3 ||
Eating only in the evening and in the morning, he did not drink water in between.
Within six years, a person attains the world desired by his mind.
This is the most excellent among auspicious acts; performed daily, it becomes a source of merit.
This merit, which grants whatever one desires in the world, yields great fruit even among human beings.
O best of the twice-born, a man performing the fast month after month—
Having dwelt in the world for a very long time, when he is born again in the human state, || 6 ||
Then one becomes long-lived, wealthy, and endowed with beauty.
Acting in this manner during every fortnight, one enjoys double the fruit.
That best of men who should observe a three-night fast month after month,
Having descended from the heavenly world, he attains the status of a leader of the Gaṇas.
By performing this for three nights during each fortnight, one becomes a king.
After a very long time, that one of great strength fell down from the heavenly world.
A twice-born man should observe the three-night rite, but a Śūdra should never do so under any circumstances.
Eating only at the sixth mealtime is said here to be his supreme austerity.
In the territory of whichever king a Śūdra observes a three-night fast, [that kingdom suffers].
His kingdom perishes through disease, famine, and thieves. || 11 ||
A Śūdra, however, should perform austerity on every first and second day.
O best of the twice-born, by means of that [practice] performed according to one's capacity, one attains all desires.
But after this, O best of the twice-born, [the duties] of the social classes [are described] month by month.
Now listen to the supreme fruit of those who eat but one meal a day. || 13 ||
Furthermore, he who passes the month of Caitra subsisting on a single meal a day is disciplined.
He is born into a great family, enriched with gold, jewels, and pearls. || 14 ||
That best of the twice-born who passes the month of Vaiśākha by eating only one meal a day, [attains the highest state].
Whether a man or a woman, he or she shall attain preeminence among their kinsmen.
He who subsists on a single meal throughout the month of Jyeṣṭhāmūla, [attains great merit].
Whether a man or a woman, one is born with incomparable and supreme sovereignty. || 16 ||
Having remained for the month of Āṣāḍha with a single meal per day, free from sloth.
He is born with abundant grain, abundant wealth, and many sons. || 17 ||
He who, being disciplined, passes the month of Śrāvaṇa eating but a single meal a day;
Wherever one is consecrated by sprinkling, there one increases their kin. || 18 ||
He who observes the practice of eating only one meal during the month of Proṣṭhapada—
He attains abundant wealth and incomparable, flourishing sovereignty. || 19 ||
Likewise, he who passes the month of Āśvayuja eating but one meal a day;
He becomes intelligent, wealthy in vehicles, and blessed with many sons. || 3.320.20 ||
The man who observes the practice of eating only once a day throughout the month of Kārttika, [attains great merit].
He is born as a hero, one who has many wives, and indeed one possessed of fame. || 21 ||
He who passes the month of Mārgaśīrṣa by eating but a single meal [per day], [attains great merit].
He becomes a sharer in the fruits of agriculture, possessing great wealth and abundant grain. || 22 ||
O best of Brahmins, he who passes the month of Pauṣa with a single meal [per day], [attains great merit].
He becomes fortunate, handsome to behold, and a partaker of glory. || 23 ||
Whoever should spend the month of Māgha with a fixed diet of a single meal per day;
One is born as a sharer in agriculture, possessing much wealth and abundant grain. || 24 ||
He who passes the month of Bhādrapada eating but one meal a day has Bhaga as his presiding deity.
In a noble family, he attains greatness among his kinsmen. ||25||
He becomes beloved by women, and they come under his control.
And these are recorded as bestowing the aforementioned fruits within twelve years. ||26||
But he who, for a full year, should always eat but a single meal a day;
A person obtains the fruit of the Atirātra sacrifice. ||27||
Likewise, for a full year, he should eat at intervals of one day.
O twice-born ones, he certainly attains the sacrifice known as Bahusuvarṇaka. ||28||
And likewise, a man who eats only on every third day for one year.
O best of the twice-born, the Vājapeya sacrifice has been described.
But eating only once a day for one year, on the fifth [day], [he attains that fruit].
And he rejoices in heaven for twelve padmas of years.
Likewise, a man who, being self-restrained, eats only once every sixth year for a full year;
He rejoices in heaven for eighteen padmas of years.
And on the seventh day of the year, he should eat only one meal.
He rejoices in heaven for thirty-six padmas of years.
And on the eighth day of every month, he should always eat while remaining self-restrained.
He rejoices in heaven for fifty years upon the celestial lotuses.
But he who eats [only] on every tenth day for the duration of a year, [attains a specific merit].
O best of Brahmins, he rejoices in heaven for one kalpa like a god.
But on the arrival of the eleventh day, he who obtains the sacrificial oblation—
For two hundred kalpas, he rejoices like a god in heaven, in the celestial realm.
He who indeed consumes the sacrificial oblation when the twelfth day has arrived;
For three kalpas he enjoys the celestial realm, endowed with divine happiness.
But on the thirteenth day, when it has arrived, he who receives the oblation—
For him, four kalpas are proclaimed as his destination in heaven.
But on the fourteenth day, when it has arrived, he who obtains the oblation—
His course in the celestial realm is proclaimed to last for seven kalpas.
A man who eats the fifteenth oblation for a full year [attains this].
The righteous-souled one dwells in the celestial realm for kalpas, without a doubt. || 39 ||
Likewise, he who eats once every fortnight for one year, along with ten days [of fasting].
But he, O brahmins, rejoices like a god in heaven for a hundred kalpas.
When the seventeenth day has arrived, he who should eat but a single meal;
O Brahmins, he rejoices in heaven for five hundred kalpas.
And on the eighteenth day, he who should eat a single meal;
In the Nāka-kalpa, the man who performs this act rejoices for a thousand years.
On the nineteenth day, he who eats but a single meal;
He, moreover, rejoices in heaven for a thousand kalpas and a half.
And eating at a single time, when the twentieth day has arrived.
For two thousand eons, he dwells in heaven and is honored by the gods.
But on the twenty-first day, he who should take only one meal;
For three thousand kalpas, his course shall be in the celestial realm.
When the twenty-second day has arrived, he who eats but a single meal;
And he shall attain [residence] in heaven for four thousand kalpas.
And on the twenty-third day, he who should eat a single meal;
He, dwelling in heaven, rejoices for five thousand kalpas. || 47 ||
But on the twenty-fourth day, he who eats a single meal;
He indeed rejoices, dwelling in heaven, for seven thousand kalpas.
And on the twenty-fifth day, he who eats a single meal;
Remaining in heaven, he indeed rejoices for ten thousand kalpas.
He who eats only one meal on the twenty-sixth day, [attains the fruit].
But that man shall become [one who has attained] twenty-four thousand kalpas.
On the twenty-seventh day, however, he who eats but a single meal;
But he rejoices for thousands of kalpas, even while dwelling in heaven.
But on the twenty-eighth day, he who eats a single meal;
He indeed rejoices for forty thousand kalpas.
On the nineteenth day, he who eats but a single meal;
He shall become a lord of the sky for fifty thousand kalpas.
But he who, when the thirtieth day has arrived, should eat only a single meal;
But he, remaining in heaven for a hundred thousand eons, is honored for a hundred [eons].
When each month has passed, one should generally eat only one meal.
He rejoices like a god in heaven for as many days as there are hairs on a man's body.
Indeed, all these vows bring happiness for one year dedicated to the ancestors (Kavya).
In the year [of the planet], they are declared to be fruit-bearing; no deliberation is required in this matter. || 56 ||
Bathing must be performed in all cases, and likewise, the fire sacrifice (homa) must be performed.
One should not eat meat in that manner; thus one enjoys the fruit of the vow. || 57 ||
Or else, by resorting to a sacred ford or a deity, these vows likewise yield great fruit.
These rites should not be performed after more than these months have passed; beyond that, fasting unto death is not prescribed.

Thus ends the three hundred and twentieth chapter, titled "The Description of the Rules for Fasting in the Haṃsa-gītā to the Sages," in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra within the third section of the glorious Viṣṇudharmottara.
The sages said:
At what time, and by what action, do the best of men attain [this]?
Tell us the truth, for you, being all-knowing, ought to do so.
The Swan said:
[One should not look at] an elder sister, a father, a mother, or a teacher.
One should worship [it] constantly with devotion; such a person is honored in the world of Yama.
One should honor the guest with food, clothing, and other such necessities.
He rejoices among the worlds of the king of kings; of this there is no doubt. || 3 ||
Indeed, proceeding toward Meru, he remained constantly devoted to his Vedic studies.
And where that Jambū tree named Sudarśanā stands, O twice-born ones.
Skilled in dance and song, they go to the Nandana grove.
Having passed through the Himālayas, they likewise proceed to the Northern Kurus.
The virtuous who are constantly devoted to giving go to the eternal world.
Likewise, those who remain steadfast in austerity go to the world of Āditya.
Likewise, those devoted to pilgrimage to sacred fords go to the world of Pracetas.
Those slain in battle go undoubtedly to the world of Śakra.
Likewise, by conducting themselves properly, the rulers of the earth attain the realm of Prajāpati.
In this way, those best of men go to Goloka by means of the Lord of Cows.
And those who always speak the truth go to the world of the Sun.
And those men who have desisted from accepting gifts, even from the Vasus.
Those who attend to the sick are honored in the world of Vāyu.
Then those who are devoted to the service of the fire go to the world of Agni.
Those who are intent on guarding water-stations go to the world of Nirṛti.
Even among the worlds of the Bhṛgus, those who sleep in the open air rejoice.
And by this vow, human beings go to the world of Aṅgiras.
Likewise, those men who give vehicles go to the world of the Maruts.
Those who give medicinal herbs likewise rejoice in the world of the Nāsatyas.
Those who are affectionate toward cows, Brahmins, and human beings attain the world of Rudra.
Those devoted to their own proper conduct go undoubtedly to Vaiśvadeva.
Those compassionate men, however, rejoice together with the Ādityas.
The world of Brahmā, the world of Viṣṇu, and likewise the world of Rudra.
O best of the twice-born, they are attained only by those devoted to Him, and not otherwise. ||15||
Whatever devotion a human being always bears toward whichever deity, [that deity protects him].
All his perfections attain the same world as his; there is no doubt about this. ||16||
O brahmins, I have described the course of a person through the divine worlds according to their karma.
What more than this shall I say? Tell me that, O you who are foremost in asceticism.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-first chapter, titled "The Description of the Divisions of the World," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The sages said:
O wise one, tell me further the dharma of women.
We wish to hear that, for you are said to be all-knowing.
The Swan said:
This duty of women was established by their kinsmen at the very outset of marriage.
The wife should follow her husband in the practice of the true Dharma near the sacred fire. ||2||
Of excellent nature, of excellent mind, well-proportioned, and beautiful to behold.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-second chapter, titled "The Description of the Duties of Women," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages by Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

Of peace, war, giving, and likewise of remaining seated;

In that regard, one should construct fortresses and make one's own stronghold particularly secure.
The desert fort, the earth fort, and likewise the mountain fort.
The fortress of the waterless wilderness, the fortress of trees, and likewise the fortress of men. || 16 ||

Various gardens, as well as cattle-pens and the houses of Brahmins.
Punishing the wicked, honoring the virtuous, and acquiring wealth through righteous means. || 25 ||
Protection of the kingdom, impartiality, and [the administration of] legal proceedings—this is the pentad.
The great sacrifices of the rulers of the earth destroy all impurities.
One should consecrate both the troop endowed with auspicious marks and the horse.

And stationed in the fort, he should appoint guardians in every village.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-third chapter, titled "The Exposition of the Duties of Kings," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.

By facial expressions, gestures, gait, movements, and speech.

A scribe who writes falsehoods should be deprived of all his property.
And whoever reviles the scribe, the members of the assembly, or the witnesses. ||38||
In summoning one who has not been summoned, and in releasing one who has been summoned;

The king should punish those Brahmins with double the fine.
Either one should not enter the assembly, or one should speak what is improper.
Whether one speaks falsely or even speaks the truth, a person becomes guilty of sin.
One quarter of Dharma goes to the doer, and one quarter likewise to the witness.

Let him be a king by this [means]; however, he is worthy of reproach where he is reproached.

The staff, one's own wager, and the wealth itself [should be returned] to the creditor. ||44||
That is no assembly where there are no elders, and they are not elders who do not speak according to dharma.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-fourth chapter, titled "The Description of Conduct," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and the sages, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The swan said:

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-fifth chapter, titled "The Description of the Characteristics of Enjoyment," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the *Śrī Viṣṇudharmottara*.

And by means of castes, the marks produced by them, the attainments, and the logical arguments.

Thus ends the three hundred and twenty-sixth chapter, titled "Description of the Characteristics of Painting," within the *Haṃsagītā* addressed to the sages, in the dialogue between Mārkaṇḍeya and Vajra, in the third section of the glorious *Viṣṇudharmottara*.
The Swan said:
The wise have observed in the scriptures that there are eleven kinds of witnesses.

The written witness, the reminded witness, and the witness who knows by chance.

He who is always an insider in affairs, being constantly dispatched by the petitioner; || 3 ||

When two parties are disputing over a matter and there are witnesses present for both sides. ||4||

That [topic] upon which the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) must be based by virtue of the force of the subject matter. || 5 ||
